That should be accepted without hesitation—O God, how could that which you have spoken be false?
And the worlds have been destroyed by you, O Bhairava, through your illusory form.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly wise one, you who inquire about the nature of reality!
Those mantras which were previously spoken by me are the bestowers of the accomplishment of all desires."
O Goddess, those [mantras] which were hidden by me have now been revealed according to their colors and forms;
therefore, they do not succeed even if recited hundreds of millions of times. (Kubjika-tantra 4.8)
O beautiful lady, they are protected by the syllable *oṃ* and by the act of salutation;
when that is protected, they are protected, while the remaining castes are merely unprotected.
Those consisting of one syllable, those of two syllables, and those of four, five, or nine syllables;
whatever peak-mantras (kūṭamantra) there may be, as well as likewise the lump-mantras (piṇḍamantra).
Others consist of eighty-one syllables, ending at one thousand, or numbering fifty;
all of these are declared to be fruitless, for they are devoid of the vital breath (jīva).
For it is well known in the world that those devoid of life are indeed dead;
and what living could there be for them through the mere figurative designation of "dead"? (KubjT 4.12)
Thus, O lady of excellent hips, mantras are established in the meaning of their syllables;
they are not accomplished by mere observances of vows—this is what has been declared as the truth. (Kubjikātantra 4.13)
Those joined with the living beings (the vowels) are indeed perfected; what more is there to deliberate upon here?
They are mutually entwined and differentiated by the twelve vowels.
O lady of excellent complexion, when colored by the seed-syllable of Śakti, they all become perfected;
they are said to be bestowers of desires, and all possess unfailing power.
All [mantras] originate from the mouth of Śiva and possess the nature of both reflection (*manana*) and protection (*trāṇa*).
Protection is said to be guarding, and that is devoid of phonemes (*varṇa*).
Resembling pure crystal, devoid of movement or utterance,
blazing with its own radiance, it is firmly established within the heart-lotus.
One should meditate upon the self as empty and unified with her,
rising like the orb of the sun through the practice of moving within the Suṣumṇā.
Having pierced [the centers] in the sequence of O-JĀ-PŪ-KĀ, [the practitioner] stands in the station of the Vidyā-Kubjā;
at that moment, that yogin trembles and attains *stobha* instantly. (KubjT 4.19)
One knows in reality all mudrās, mantras, and likewise languages;
having attained the state of Kubjīśāna, the state of deep sleep arises. (KubjT 4.20)
Established in the state of deep sleep, one perceives only a slight degree [of consciousness];
then the Command (ājñā) residing in the aperture of Brahmā remains like a piece of wood.
It is of the size of a barley grain, triangular in shape, and excellent;
it possesses the qualities of closing and opening like the organ of the submarine fire (vaḍavāmaṇi).

Therein, when the mind has reached the middle state, the stage of "wood" (kāṣṭhāvasthā) arises through various kinds of sounds such as those of kettledrums and clay drums, and through songs and instrumental music.
He hears not, he sees not, nor does he perceive another as his lord;
even when being cut by weapons such as swords and discuses, he feels no pain.
O fair-faced one, in the state of Śakti, one perceives only slightly;
but when one has reached the end of Śakti, then one rises up in an instant.
In this manner, O Goddess of the gods, one should practice the upward resonance of Śakti in sequence;
through the yoga of constant practice, mastery over speech is produced. (Kubjikātantra 4.26)
When practiced for one month, one becomes a composer of poetry; of this there is no doubt.
After two months, one possesses a radiant body and is not afflicted by hunger, thirst, or other such ailments.
One may wander through all the worlds until the dissolution of all beings;
this is clearly the procedure specifically for those mantras whose meaning is based on the syllables. (Kubjika-tantra 4.28)
The venerable Kubjikā said: "O God Bhairava, show me your grace so that the instruction on the meaning of the syllables and the Kaula tradition may be understood."
The venerable Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim clearly the definitive determination of mantras;
those mantras which have been enjoined, O Beloved, by means of various methods such as the *prastāra* and others. (KubjT 4.30)

O Goddess worshipped by the gods, those mantra fragments taught by Śiva are to be understood by you according to the literal meaning when joined with the *rañjaka* [the coloring agent]; this is the oral instruction (*upadeśa*).
O Goddess, that oral tradition (sampradāya) is also divided into six types:
Pallava, Yogarodha, Sampuṭa, and likewise Grathana; KubjT_4.32.
Vidarbha—these six are indeed proclaimed as the traditions;
Mālinī, Śabdarāśi, and the Kaulika, which is the supreme method.
O lady of excellent hips, O observer of good vows, she should be known through fifty divisions;
the Kula, moreover, is to be known as sixfold, and I shall state its characteristics.
The supreme seed, likewise the root, the tradition, and the ritual procedure—
endowed with the collection of phonemes, this is the sixfold lineage transmission (kulakrama).
He is both with parts and without parts, as well as both with and without parts;
he is subtle, possessed of distinct parts, and beyond all parts, O fair-faced one.
The mantra should be known to be of six types by one who desires accomplishment: pure, born of a couple, and mixed; the instruction is threefold according to these divisions.
The venerable Kubjikā said:
"Those mantras endowed with the proper characteristics that have been indicated on the path of mantra should be known through your grace by means of meditation, concentration, and yoga."
O God, how does it come to be that one has entered the path of the family?
And how is the yoga of the sprout [divided] into six types from the beginning? KubjT_4.39 //
What, however, is the sixfold Kaulika? What is the sixfold course of mantras? And what is the threefold instruction? This is what I wish to know.
The illustrious Bhairava said: "The *pallava* is at the beginning; for one who knows, the *yoga* is in the middle;
the *rodha* is at the beginning, middle, and end; and the *sampuṭa* extends from the beginning to the end. (Kubjikātantra 4.41)
The interlacing (grathana) should be known as occurring between [the two parts] through the union of the syllable and the non-syllable;
O Vīranāyikā, the vidarbha [occurs] at the beginning of the mantra and at the end of the mantra.
Indeed, this stringing together of the garland must be understood by the practitioner of mantra;
however, the sprout within the awakening of the mantra should always be known as yoga.
O Dear One, yoga has indeed been described in this way for the purpose of making [the breath] stainless and for the procedure of rejoining; now the "obstruction" (rodha) is likewise being explained.
It is proclaimed for the immobilization of fierce mantra-words, for the immobilization of speech, for the immobilization of an army,
and for [the destruction of] elephants, chariots, machines, and even ships.
Among these, the *rodha* (obstruction) is praised for the transgressions of cattle;
one should employ the *sampuṭa* (encasement) for the protection of mantras and for the purpose of subjugation.
In the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), regarding poisons both stationary and mobile,
and in rites such as pacification (*śāntika*), the *sampuṭa* [arrangement] is recommended.
In the rites of form-making, such as the acts of attraction and so forth,
O lady of excellent hips, "grathana" is declared to mean "joining together."
O Goddess, if one desires success, one must always perform the Vidarbha rite in all undertakings, whether they have been specifically mentioned or not.
O Goddess, O Mother of the Gaṇas, this auspicious procedure of the oral tradition has been fully explained; it has not been told by me to anyone—this is the truth, the absolute truth.
Now listen to how the path of the Kula actually is:
O leader of the gods, the supreme *bindu* is said to reside in the heart-lotus.
Its grasping is the means; that supreme Kaulika reality is to be known as the seed, the power Kuṇḍalinī, who performs the coming and going.
Having then understood its end, the supreme Kaulika seed-syllable is known as the Root Power (Mūla-śakti), Kubjī, whose nature is the cause of the universe. (KubjT 4.53)
O lady of beautiful hips, everything born within her, up to the very limits of the world of Brahmā, is created by her through the conjunction of cause and effect.
The state of being the subject (dharmitva) within the object of knowledge (dharmi) is to be understood, just as heat belongs to fire;
this, O fair-faced one, is declared to be the Kaulika [tradition], known by the name "the Root" (mūla).
In that regard, the scripture is the meaning of the Sūtra, and the procedure is prescribed therein;
the sequence of the collection of letters is to be known according to its essential nature from *na* to *pha*.
O Goddess of gods, the wise know the sequence of the mass of sounds (śabdarāśi) from *a* to *kṣa*.
O fair-faced one, this is declared to be the sixfold Kaulika [tradition].
Understand now that which will be explained according to the sequence beginning with the Sakala:
the Sakala mantra, residing in Brahman, is endowed with thirty-eight kalās.
O Goddess, for the one who knows, [the Self] is endowed with the eight perfections when situated in the state of emergence; it is partless when situated in the throat, devoid of both parts and time.
O auspicious lady, the mantra situated in the station of Rudra is joined with two states of being,
endowed with the subtle and the gross, and with the manifestations of the bindu and the other [phonemes].
For that one, called Touch, which abides in the subtle support, is the knower of the mantra;
O lady of good vows, this mantra should be known as both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala).
Dissolved into the Bindu-deity by virtue of its nature as the form of the Yoni,
the mantra— freed from sound and touch— is to be known as partless (niṣkala).
O Goddess, subtler than the subtle, he is called the Subtle;
the Bindu is known as the form of Time. If one penetrates that, one proceeds [to liberation].
For one who has set out upon the upward path, [the breath] rests within the locus of the support of the Suṣumṇā;
it dissolves into the deity of sound, awakened by the power of consciousness.
For it is taught that when the timing is disrupted, one is subject to dissolution; however, when it transcends dissolution, it bestows liberation.
Thus, five states have been fully described for mantras of immeasurable power.
As long as one does not find it thus, how could there be accomplishment?
The letters arise from the heart, throat, palate, tongue, lips, teeth, and nose.
O Goddess, for those things that perish in an instant, their destruction is just as their arising;
for they are produced, insentient, empty, impermanent, and mere fabricators of speech.
But when distinguished by its five states, it is then called "mantra" here;
having thus understood the nature of mantra, men achieve success effortlessly. (Kubjika-tantra 4.68)

In the state of emergence (udbhava), it is said to be pure; in separation (viśleṣa), it is remembered as born of duality; and in the state of dissolution (laya) within the mixed state, instruction is indeed remembered as being threefold. // KubjT 4.69 //
Touching, gazing, conversing, seeing oneself [in the disciple],
and entering oneself— transference has these five characteristics.
Touching is situated in the heart, while looking is from the region of the throat;
speaking is located in the place of the palate, and seeing is in the center of the bindu.
O Goddess, there is no doubt that self-penetration occurs in the aperture of the humpbacked one (kubjīrandhra);
trembling is to be known upon touch, and shaking occurs in the light.
By conversing with him, there is a sudden awakening, and one understands the very meaning of the scriptures;
by merely seeing him, one attains qualities, namely the eightfold supernatural powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā).
O Goddess, by entering [the mantra] oneself, one will fly up; there is no doubt in this.
Having thus understood the course of the mantra, one attains accomplishment; there is no doubt in this.
Henceforth, O fair-faced one, I shall explain the extraction of the mantra;
[it should be performed] in a well-concealed, pure place on the ground smeared with cow dung.
In a place rich with heaps of flowers and fragrances, one should delineate the mandala-pit;
with twenty-seven divisions, six lines are to be erased in a sequence of six.
And just as there is one on one side, so indeed is there a second;
likewise one, three, five, seven, and nine in the same way.
Likewise, starting from eleven and ending at thirteen,
one should perform [the rites] according to the rule, omitting one up to fifty.
One should write [the letters] starting from the vowel 'a' in Kāmarūpa and so forth in this sequence:
the vowels and consonants according to their respective order, until they have reached the center.
O Goddess, the great-souled one known as Haṃsa, located in Oḍḍiyāna,
arises through union with the king of mantras known as Ka-ṣa.
When the ritual placement (nyāsa) has been performed in this manner, O Goddess, one should extract the auspicious Mālinī;
listen to how it occurs according to the sequence from *na* to *pha*.
In the middle of Pa and Dha, Śikhā is to be known as situated with its head downward;
the four vowels beginning with E are declared to be the Śiromālā.
One should fashion the head of the Goddess, endowed with auspicious marks, between the letters *ai* and *śa*;
furthermore, the third eye of the Goddess is located between *ṅa* and *cha*.
O fair-faced one, it should be known that [the letter] situated between *na* and *da* becomes twofold;
these are remembered as the two eyes of the Goddess, located respectively on the right and the left.
The nose is to be known as preceded by *ṭa*, conjoined and situated in the middle;
having taken that which is situated between *ḍha* and *ta*, it is uttered with a double repetition.
The letters preceded by *ṭha* and *ḍa*, joined with the vowel *u* and adorned below, are known as the ornaments of the ears;
they are situated here on the paths of the left and right as ear-ornaments.
And that face situated in the middle belongs to the Goddess Vīranāyikā;
it stands between the *kha* at the end of the *visarga* and, furthermore, between the *ka* and *ga*.
One should extract the auspicious syllable indicated by the letter *kha*, the western direction, the north-western direction, and that which is situated between *gha* and *ca*. KubjT_4.88.
These five letters are known as the five divisions of the Goddess's teeth:
the letter preceding *ña* is the goddess Rasanā, and the letter above *jha* is Sarasvatī.

One should extract [the syllable] situated between *sa* and *ta*, that which is located between *ma* and *cha*, and likewise that which is situated between *ra* and *ma*; these two syllables are auspicious in nature.
O auspicious lady, those two peaks are known to be on the left and right, which are auspicious;
having taken the one situated between *ū* and *ḍha*, the second is between *ḍa* and *ṇa*.
The two arms of the goddess, worshipped by the gods, extend to the left and right;
one should cause the letter situated between *ṭa* and *ḍa* to be manifested in two ways.
The two palms of the Goddess are known by those who understand them as being on the right and left;
the auspicious fingers, beginning with *ja* and *ma*, are located on the left and right respectively.

One should visualize [the letter] situated between *aṃ* and *ka* on the back of the hand as being split in two; having taken that which is located between *ña* and *ṭha*, one should place it upon the left hand.
The skull-cup with its opening facing upward, filled with that which is called nectar, should be known to be in the right hand; meanwhile, the staff is between the letters *ya* and *ḍha*.
O auspicious lady, the trident has been described; it is extracted by means of its extraction.
The trident situated between the letters *a* and *cha* is turned upward, facing upwards.
The wise should know that the heart of the Goddess, which grants all desires, is situated between the letters *gha* and *na*, as characterized by its defining marks. (Kubjika-tantra 4.97)
O auspicious lady, having taken the seed-syllable of the Self, which consists of Śiva and is situated between *ma* and *ṣa*,
this supreme mantra is extracted together with the *visarga*.
O Vīranāyikā, one should take the vital breath situated between *ya* and *sa*,
and likewise that which is situated between *ja* and *ca*, as well as that which is at the junction of *ra* and *va*.
The two syllables situated on the left and right are of the nature of breasts;
that which precedes *jha* should be known as milk and is declared to be nectar.
O sinless one, having grasped the *na*, *sa*, and *ma* situated in the middle, and having extracted the *u*,
one should arrange the *ka* and *ṣa*— the king of principles— at the navel of the Goddess.
O Goddess, the hip consists of all [the letters] situated between *bha* and *ña*;
the secret place consists of those between *va* and *ṣa*, joined with the letter *au* at the end.
O sinless one, the seed-syllable situated between *ṇa* and *tha* should take the form of the thighs;
one should fashion the two knees with the seed-syllables located to the right of *ṇa* and *ta*.
O one of auspicious gaze, the two movements to the left and right are to be known in their respective order;
the two shanks, however, extend to the right and left, corresponding to the letters *tha* and *da*.
O Goddess, the middle of the letter *tha* and likewise the middle of *pa* and *ba*—these two seed-syllables, O Blessed One, should be known as the feet by the wise. *KubjT_4.105*
The two [lines] on the left and right are said to be endowed with their defining characteristics;
thus, O Dear One, Mālinī has been correctly extracted according to the proper ritual procedure.
Of the seventy million vidyās and mantras of immeasurable power,
this Mālinī alone is the supreme source, granting all desires.
Because she remained there having formed a garland (mālayitvā), she is known as Mālinī;
O lady of beautiful countenance, those beings who have been and those who will be are immeasurable.
O fair-eyed one, she alone is declared to be the Mother of the Rudras and the Yoginīs;
she is to be known as colorless, yet the union of all colors.
"O Dear One, all mantras have Rudra as their essence, and the Rudras have Śakti as their essence;
Śakti is to be known as Mātṛkā, and she is to be known as having Śiva as her essence. (Kubjikātantra 4.110)
Thus, O beautiful one, the measure of the mantra has been told to you;
this is declared to be the first [measure], which must be guarded with great effort.
The ritual procedure for the Solitary Hero (Ekavīra) has already been explained previously in another scripture.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Extraction of the Mālinī from the Abyss of the Determination of Mantras," in the *Śrīkubjikāmata*, according to the tradition of the Kulālikas.
The venerable Bhairava said: I shall now explain with certainty the wheel of Umāmāheśvara.
He who knows both the steps and the divisions of the steps attains success.
Aiṃ, "namo bhagavate rudrāya" is the ten-syllable foot;
"namaś cāmuṇḍe" is declared to be the second, consisting of five syllables. (Kubjika-tantra 5.2)
"Salutation to the Mothers of Space"—this is another third step, declared to consist of eight syllables, distinguished by its specific characteristics. (Kubjikātantra 5.3)
And the fourth word is that which accomplishes all desires and goals;
O Goddess, this is the nine-syllable word that has been proclaimed. (Kubjika-tantra 5.4)
And here the state of those who are ageless and immortal is described as bringing five qualities;
in brief, the number of tastes among the syllables has been illustrated.
O fair-faced one, the sixth state belongs to those whose movement is everywhere unimpeded.
O Vīranāyikā, the ten-syllable mantra has been fully described and explained.
The seventh word consists of those [syllables] that transform one's own form and the form of others;
in brief, these syllables constitute the supreme triad of ten.
The eighth position shall be the locus for all activities—the subjugation, concealment, and uprooting of all sentient beings;
[it consists] of letters in total, numbering forty-two. (KubjT 5.8)

The ninth state is the supreme, perfected heart-essence secret of all Mothers; O fair-faced one, it consists of syllables numbering thirty-three in total. Likewise, O Goddess, it is proclaimed to be the performer of the rites of others and the instrument of destruction.
And here, the word that brings about accomplishment consists of ten syllables.
Thus, the number of syllables has been declared together as being measured by fourteen; this is clear, O Mistress of the Kula. (Kubjikāmata-tantra 5.11)
Listen to another auspicious word of the Mothers, O lady of excellent hips: it consists of two groups of four syllables each, O fair-faced one. (Kubjikātantra 5.12)
O beloved, this eleventh word, beginning with "tadyathā," brings all virtues; it is the second auspicious one. (Kubjika-tantra 5.13)
The first word is Brahmāṇī, the second is Māheśvarī, the third should be Kaumārī, and the fourth is Vaiṣṇavī. (KubjT 5.14)
The fifth is to be known as Vārāhī, the sixth is Aindrī;
the seventh is declared to be Aiśānī, and the eighth, O Dear One, is Āgneyī. (KubjT 5.15)
O beautiful one, these and other goddesses have been described to you;
they abide in the words "Aghore," "Amoghe," "Varade," and "Vicce," which are indeed auspicious.
For all the Mothers as well, [the mantra] is joined with *svāhā* and the *praṇava*;
first the word *aiṃ cāmuṇḍe*, and secondly *ūrdhvakeśi*. (Kubjikātantra 5.17)
The third is Jvalitaśikhā, while Vidyujjihvā is the fourth;
likewise, O Goddess, Tārakākṣī is proclaimed as the fifth. (Kubjikātantra 5.18)
The sixth is indeed named Piṅgalabhru, O fair-eyed one;
this seventh step is proclaimed as Vikṛtadaṃṣṭrā. (Kubjikātantra 5.19)
"Being angry," and likewise another, the eighth auspicious mark;
the ninth is being fond of meat, blood, wine, and spirits, while the tenth is the pair of smiles.
Likewise, O lady of good vows, the pair of dances is said to be the eleventh.
And likewise, the pair of twenty-two is revealed as the yawning.
"O Supreme Goddess, 'Māyātrailokyarūpā' is the best of the three decads; 'Sahasraparivartinī' is the seventh of the two. (Kubjikātantra 5.22)
O Bhadrā, there are two *nudās*, five *kūṭas*, twice eight [syllables],
and likewise two *cirīs*, all together numbering seventeen.
When there is an auspicious aspect upon eighteen [syllables] in one place, there is a pair of *hiri*s;
and by repeating that twice, there are twenty-one *bhiri*s. (KubjT 5.24)
The two [syllables] of *trāsani* constitute the twentieth step;
this pair of *bhrāmaṇī* syllables is indeed the twenty-first and supreme.
O sinless one, from the double repetition of Vidrāvaṇī, twenty-two [syllables] arise;
likewise, from the double repetition of Kṣobhaṇī, twenty-three is declared.
The two [mantras] for the destruction of Māra consist of forty and twenty syllables respectively;
however, O Dear One, there are two for the Sañjīvanī-pada, and the fifth consists of twenty-five syllables.
O auspicious lady, the pair *heri* is remembered as the twenty-sixth, unsurpassed;
likewise, the pair *geri* is declared to be the twenty-seventh word.
O fair-faced one, by repeating the *ghurili* twice, it becomes twenty-eight;
thus, the *ghurili* is likewise declared to be twenty-nine.
"Salutation to the host of Mothers"—thus the thirtieth [mantra] has been clearly explained.
"Salutation, salutation! Aiṃ! Vicce! Svāhā!"—this is the thirty-first word. (Kubjikātantra 5.30)
O fair-faced one, from the conjunction of all the words, the measure is fifty; and of the syllables, it is two hundred and ninety-two.
O auspicious lady, more has been told regarding the Mothers, excluding their names;
however, the practitioner must understand the various divisions of the words of the Vidyā.
O lady of excellent limbs, by diligent effort he becomes a protector of the tradition of the Tantras;
once this Vidyā has been uttered, he becomes a knower of the Samaya.
Listen, as I explain to you in this secret place the extraction of the five *praṇavas*:
having extracted [the letters] from between *e* and *o*, it is adorned with the *bindu* and the *nāda*.
The first seed-syllable called Bhaga, the supreme syllable, has been extracted;
it is taken as situated between *va* and *ṣa*, and rests upon a seat between *ṇa* and *ṭa*. (KubjT 5.35)
"O Goddess, the second [syllable] is said to be the *i* and *u* joined together, adorned by the middle of *aḥ* and *au*; the third is situated between *va* and *ma*."
Seated upon the *ṭha-la* middle-seat, differentiated by the fourth vowel, with the *bindu* crowning its head, and the fourth [consonant] in the middle of *na-ca*. (Kubjika-tantra 5.37)
The fourth Praṇava is that which is situated between the letter *ī* and preceded by the letter *ai*, and is pervaded by the Bindu and Nāda. (Kubjikātantra 5.38)
The fifth [consonant], situated between *ya* and *sa*, standing upon a seat between *ba* and *ha*, joined with the letter preceding *aṃ* and adorned by the one following *au*. (KubjT 5.39)
Having formed it with a half-moon, make it joined with the Bindu and Nāda;
the extraction of the five Praṇavas has been told to you as a secret.
O Goddess, one should employ the illuminator of mantras according to the specific rite;
furthermore, in connection with the Vidyā, the five-fold *praṇava* has been extracted. (Kubjikātantra 5.41)
Now listen, O auspicious lady, to the supreme majesty of this Vidyā;
it shall come about gradually through its practice, recitation, fire-offerings, or meditation. (Kubjikātantra 5.42)
O Goddess, by performing this which has been declared as the truth, one is liberated within six months;
having committed the faults born of imperial power, it removes the stain through its recitation.
For treachery against a deity or treachery against a guru, he is purified by thirty million [repetitions];
however, for the cutting of flowers or leaves, he is purified by a single cycle (āvarta).
O Goddess, when the twilight prayer (sandhyā) has been omitted, one is purified by performing it three times;
when the daily rite (āhnika) is interrupted, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times.
O Goddess, for transgressing the rules of time, for eating what is not to be eaten,
and for speaking what should not be spoken, purification is held to occur through a thousand [repetitions].
If the killing of crows, owls, pigeons, or other birds has been committed, one is purified by two thousand [repetitions]; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
O Goddess, according to what Bhairava has declared, purification for goats, sheep, and others such as deer, jackals, and bears occurs after three thousand [repetitions]. KUBJATĀNTRA 5.48.
A killer of snakes, a killer of cats, a drummer, and a fisherman—
these four indeed attain purification quickly by means of [the gift of] four thousand [cows].
Whether it be a dog, a pig, a mongoose, and so forth, or even a rat—
if five thousand of these [are killed], purification is desired for one's entire lineage.
One is purified by killing ten million cows;
but when, O Goddess, a Brāhmaṇa is killed through negligence by the wise, [the following applies].
One who eats only at night and has conquered the senses is purified by twenty hundred thousand [repetitions];
and one who kills a follower of the Buddha or an Arhat is purified by twice that amount compared to a twice-born.
Having killed those who belong to the Lākula, Mauṣala, or other Lātapāṇi sects,
one attains purification by means of three koṭis of recitations.
Having killed a guru out of negligence, one is purified by five crores [of recitations];
but he who kills a woman and is of evil conduct, O Dear One, should recite ten crores.
Eating only at night, he attains purity if he wanders through the sacred fields and seats;
for those of other castes and lineages, there are the inferior, superior, and middling [categories].
Purification occurs through two, three, or four hundred thousand [recitations];
for each of the castes, it should be performed in sequence, decreasing by one.
He who reviles a Yoginī, he who reviles those devoted to Śiva, he who censures the scriptures, and he who strikes a woman; KubjT_5.57.
O Goddess, if a thousand girls cry out, purification is required;
likewise, one who observes the Śiva-vow is slain according to the Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, and Siddhānta traditions.
O Goddess of the gods, one who is devoted to recitation is purified by forty million [repetitions];
moreover, one who knows the reality (tattva) and is skilled in the sixteenfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa) [is purified even more]. (Kubjikātantra 5.59)
"Purity is desired through recollection; Bhairava has declared this to be the truth.
But when, O Goddess, one speaks with loud cries out of anger," (Kubjikātantra 5.60)
If one recites this vidyā three times, it quickly bestows peace for children afflicted by the diseases of lūtā, cipita, and gaṇḍa once the ritual has been performed.
From fevers, seizing spirits, poisons, and the like, as well as for the purpose of proclaiming medicinal herbs,
one who follows the teaching shall be purified by means of the *pañcāvarta*.
Furthermore, he who knows the sequence is not afflicted by pure or impure [influences],
whether he be a teacher, a spiritual son, a practitioner, or one who knows the observances (samaya).
O beloved, he who censures through negligence is purified from ten rebirths;
likewise, he who feels revulsion toward a bee or even a small insect [is purified].

Food becomes pure by a single utterance [of the mantra], as does that which one finds loathsome; likewise for the *kanduka*, the *mallakoṣāḍhya*, the *chippaka*, and the leather-worker’s [utensils]. (Kubjikātantra 5.65)
Dhvaja, Sūnākara, or Matsyaghāta, as well as Lubdhaka;
Koṅkaṇa, Cīna, Bāhlīka, Vaṅgāla, and Kāmarūpaka.
Whether from Māgadha, Saindhava, Gurjara, or the region known as Lāṭa,
or even others dwelling in the midst of various lands, such as forest-dwellers and those of the lowest castes (antyajāti).

O Goddess of the Gods, for all [those who have approached] prostitutes and so forth in sequence, purification is desired through three repetitions [of the rite], whether done unintentionally or intentionally. KubjT_5.68.
O Goddess, one who desires accomplishment must perform double the penance for an act committed out of desire;
such is the penance prescribed in the Kula lineage for the three-sectioned [tantra].
In the same way, those who know reality should perform [the rite] with the thirty-two syllables.
These forms of cessation have been revealed for the sake of practitioners.
For their sake, I have declared this Vidyā by which practitioners attain success;
it has been taught by me for those seeking the highest good who are my devotees and firm in their resolve.
O sinless one, this knowledge has been fully declared for those who abide in the pursuit of non-attachment; it shall never belong to others, O lovely-faced one, due to its practical application.
Now, O Bhairavī, I shall tell you in brief how the division of the words is to be applied; listen to that.
The knowledge that was previously described according to the sequence from *na* to *pha* consists of the phonemes residing within that body, differentiated by the five *praṇavas*.
The five wombs, according to their own nature, have one letter each;
Bhairava, however, is the mass of sounds (śabdarāśi) in the sequence from A to KṢA.
Those phonemes, enclosed individually by the five *praṇavas*, are declared to be joined according to the sequence from *a* to *kṣa*. KubjT_5.76.
O beautiful one, the binding of the entire [mantra] should be performed with two [syllables];
one should place seven syllables at the beginning and the word of the Vidyā in the middle. (KubjT 5.77)
Again, at the end of the seven steps, there is a step at its conclusion;
having again uttered the group of seven, the step follows immediately thereafter.
By this sequential method and through this process,
O Mistress of the Gods, one should apply [the practice] only as long as patience indeed persists.
In the *Mālinī* meter, which is illuminated by both the completion and the execution of the total number of syllables, there are twelve varieties; however, in the *Śabdarāśi*, there are sixteen.

By this sequence, when one worships the science of words (*padavidyā*), all the castes (*varṇas*) individually, according to the division of the moving wheel (*calacakravibhāga*). (Kubjikātantra 5.81)
Then, O Dear One, it quickly causes agitation among the divine, the non-divine, and others;
all the fivefold wombs become moistened, and not otherwise.
O Goddess, when he becomes equal to Śakti, he effects all of those: causing flight, agitation, delusion, yawning, and likewise withering.
O fair-faced one, O Supreme Goddess, she who resides at the navel should likewise be visualized in the form of a sleeping serpent at the *dvādaśānta*. 5.84.
Within the center of the body and at the end of the void, the Parāparā is seen;
before her, one should then visualize the mantra in the form of a spark of fire.
Then, O Dear One, one should utter the mantra in the form of sound within the heart;
at the end of the sound, the Śakti should be uttered, moving very slowly like a gentle breeze.
Having a form resembling a lotus fiber, it should be pronounced with a nasal resonance;
at the end of the pronunciation, it should be understood as being like a whirling firebrand.
Therein, O Goddess, consciousness situated in the center is conjoined with the mantra,
abiding in the ten directions by means of many millions of quivering rays.
O Goddess, at the end of that as well, there is the primordial power Manonmanī;
when she has indeed transcended that, she is then designated as Bindu.
At the end of the *bindu* is the all-pervading Lord, beyond *māyā* and free from affliction;
he is Śiva, transcending all mental constructs, devoid of qualities yet the source of all qualities.
The authorized practitioner, the universal sovereign, and the great lord who transcends all power—
by this sequential yoga, the sequence should be performed by those who are well-resolved.
O Goddess, the self, the mind, the mantra, Śiva, and likewise Śakti— these must be understood by those seeking perfection as having attained a state of oneness.

Therefore, the recitation of the mantra, which is equal to the vital breath, occurs at the end [of the breath] within the sphere of *nāda*; having understood that it occurs at the end of *nāda*, this is called "recollection. (Kubjika-tantra 5.93)
Recollection is designated as the power (śakti) which effects coming and going;
at its end, however, is the supreme, subtle digit (kalā), whose nature is nectar.

But that which transcends the latent impressions (layātīta) is formless and self-cognizable through non-discursive inquiry; O Goddess, it has no defining characteristic, no object of definition, and no application.
There is neither decay nor growth, nor indeed the bright or dark fortnights;
there is neither night nor day, nor twilight, nor likewise the solstices.
O Goddess of the gods, there is no equinox nor indeed any transition (saṅkrānti);
having known the movement of all states, higher knowledge (vijñāna) arises. (Kubjika-tantra 5.97)
This, O beloved, is declared to be the Kaulika [practice] of Umā and Maheśvara;
there is no doubt that one who is unsteady will fly up after a hundred thousand recitations.
The power called Calā has been fully described and illustrated by its characteristics;
she who is colorless yet a union of colors is illustrated as Mālinī.
For a single [mantra] existing through the division of its syllables is indeed innumerable, O fair-faced one;
thus has that which is called "the grasping" been explained, which produces immediate conviction.
O beloved, I have not revealed this Umāmāheśvara to anyone;
however, he who constantly recites it shall become a favorite of the Yoginīs.
O Goddess, within six months even a slayer of a Brahmin is purified, without a doubt;
he beholds Virajā, peaceful, in the form of light, and of great splendor.
O Goddess, listen now at this moment to the definition of recitation (*japa*):
at the end of one hundred single utterances, the state of *parā* is proclaimed.
It is declared that the Śatabheda consists of ten times its own quality;
the Sahasrabheda is said to be [ten times] that, and the Lakṣa is recorded as being one hundred times [the Sahasrabheda].
O woman of excellent complexion, a hundred times ten million and a hundred thousand [recitations] constitute this method of recitation that has been told to you, O beautiful one. (KubjT 5.105)
The *muktaka* is joined with a hundredfold variety through its hundred divisions;
by the division of the moving wheel (*calacakra*), it is declared to have one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) varieties.
O Goddess, O fair-faced one, when the *calacakra* has its ten million divisions, it has been described externally, O auspicious lady; now hear the internal [division]. *Kubjikātantra* 5.107.
They know that in the state of manifestation (udbhava) there are a hundred divisions, in separation (viśleṣaka) a thousand;
in dissolution (laya) there are indeed a hundred thousand divisions, but in the state beyond dissolution (layātīta) there are tens of millions.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Bindvī are thus proclaimed;
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, they are Icchā, Jñānī, Kriyā, and Śāntā in their respective order.
Having understood the movement and course of the self, the wise should always perform recitation with this very rosary,
which is characterized by the marks of a hundred thousand.
Indeed, the recitation (japa) must always be performed by those proficient in all the scriptures,
both in the [cakra] called Bhuvana and likewise in that called Śakti, O Varārohā.
Recitation is declared to be most excellent when distinguished by its movement and upward flow;
the rosary is said to consist of fifty beads, while the thread is Śakti whose essence is Śiva.
The stringing together is the Kuṇḍalinī power; at the end of dissolution, it is situated upon Meru.
This rosary, whose essence is Śiva, must be kept most secret.
One should never make it manifest, nor should one ever leap over Mount Meru.
O fair-faced one, conch, crystal, rudrākṣa, putrajīva, and brick—
these and others such as these are remembered as excellent gem-garlands.
Therein no deity exists, nor mantra, nor even consciousness.
O Dear One, wherever the garland is placed, no fault occurs;
O Goddess, once the ritual placement of the mantra has been performed, one must indeed ensure it remains secret.
O fair-faced one, where indeed should the body be concealed?
For when the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) has been performed, the self possesses a body that has been made complete (sakalīkṛtavigraha).
Just as that which is to be hidden should not be employed, so too is the rosary (akṣamālikā);
"akṣa" is said to be the sense organ (indriya), and the thread is remembered as Kuṇḍalinī. (KubjT 5.118)
That supreme, subtle digit (kalā), which carries nectar and brings about union in the void, is therefore celebrated as the "Thread" (sūtrā). 5.119.
And that [rosary] is said to be the *akṣamālikā* for the purpose of counting;
however, O lady of excellent hips, those made of conch-shell and other materials are recommended for the rite of recitation (*japa*).
One desiring prosperity should use a conch-shell rosary; for the sake of liberation, a crystal one;
and lotus seeds, O Dear One, are said to be born from the Lotus-born [Brahmā] and bestow both prosperity and nourishment.
Through rudrākṣas one attains siddhi, as well as that other state which is the station of the Khecarī;
O sinless one, the jīvakā plant should always be known as strung with cow-tail hair.
Coral is for rites of subjugation (*vaśya*), while pearls grant all desires;
as for the other gems that are remembered, O Supreme Goddess, they are born from jewels.
These have always been prescribed for you; there is no need for deliberation here.
A garland made from the bones of a raven or a crow is recommended for malevolent rites (abhicāra).
Nāgavaṅga, as well as other metals that are remembered as being mixed, are recommended for the purpose of killing, as well as for paralyzing and deluding. (Kubjikātantra 5.125)
O Goddess, it should be employed for shaking, destruction, and in malevolent rites (abhicāra);
likewise, among those others which have been mentioned, that born from the conch is the most excellent.

The channel that spirals like a conch shell (śaṅkhāvartā), which is situated at the end of the crest-lock (śikhā), is praised for all undertakings and is commended for the practice of recitation (japa). (Kubjika-tantra 5.127)
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, it is said that a rosary made of conch-shell should be used;
that which bursts forth on the head and spreads in two directions is likewise [to be used]. (Kubjikātantra 5.128)
Therefore, the crystal is taught as being established in the mouth of the Guru;
Rudra is known as the state of Raudrī, and he is situated at the tip of the palate.
Sound, touch, taste, form, and smell, conjoined with their subtle elements (tanmātras), proceed toward transformation and likewise toward cessation. 5.130.
Therefore, the recitation with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads is declared to be the best;
having placed the sleeping Amṛtakuṇḍalin within the belly like a son.
O future one, that living being is led by her both downward and upward;
for this reason, she is designated by the name "Putrañjīvakā" (the life-giver of the son).
O Goddess, they constantly experience many misfortunes consisting of both pleasure and pain, which are the wealth acquired by them in the past.
The garland known as Ariṣṭā is said to be immeasurable in other states of existence;
it resides eternally in the heart-lotus, awakening the imperishable syllables. (Kubjika-tantra 5.134)
O fair-faced one, that is declared in every scripture to be the lotus-seed rosary; these and others are remembered as synonyms for the *akṣamālā*. (Kubjika-tantra 5.135)
O Mistress of the Kula, all these have been described by me for myself and for those within my lineage;
thus is the rite of the rosary proclaimed for those who truly know the Kaulika tradition. *Kubjikātantra* 5.136.
Now I shall explain the nyāsa; listen to it in its true essence, O beautiful one:
it is natural, mobile, radiant, stable, and joined with the fluid and the ether.
The mere ritual placement (nyāsa) is declared to be of twelve kinds through its sixfold division.
The sixfold power (śakti) is declared to be supreme, imperishable, and auspicious.
Kuṇḍalī resides in the region of the navel; she is supreme, having the nature of space.
She is indeed one, supreme, subtle, imperishable, and of the nature of light.
That supreme goddess, the digit devoid of the six phonemes, situated in the abode of Brahmā, subtle, is declared to be the innate nature (svābhāvikī). 5.140.
In the station of Viṣṇu she is called Calā; in the place of Rudra she is known as Dīptā;
in Īśvara she has the name Sthirā; and in the one called Sadā she is born as Dravā.
Abiding as power (śakti) and having the nature of space, she is to be known by those who know the reality;
she is the support of the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā), possesses six attributes, and awakens the [three] qualities (guṇas).
Pervasive, having the nature of space, infinite, without protector, and without support;
she is both the uniter and the disuniter, established in the qualities of true being.
The one and only supreme power exists through the differentiation of her functions;
though she appears divided by the differentiation of functions, there is no division from the perspective of ultimate reality.
When the nyāsa has been performed in this way, O Goddess, it proceeds within the inner self;
externally, however, it takes the form of phonemes, being both one and manifold.
The ritual placement (nyāsa) for the coming and going [of breath] is said to be sixfold and twelvefold.

Thus, in the *Kulālikāmnāya*, according to the *Śrīkubjikāmata*, the fifth chapter, titled "The Extraction of the Great Rule (*bṛhatsamayoddhāra*) and the Determination of the Pervasion of the *Śabdarāśimālinī* and its Grasping," is concluded.
The venerable Kubjikā said:
"O God, you have indeed previously described the characteristics of recitation (*japa*)."
One hundred recitations, one thousand, and indeed one hundred thousand are to be known [as the measures]. // KubjT_6.1 //
"O Śambhu, leader of the gods, there are indeed millions [of mantras] characterized by distinct features;
yet, O Lord of the Suras, the measure of my recitation has not been known by me."
Therefore, I wish to hear this, for my intellect is dull and my mind is small.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
That Kuṇḍalinī Śakti, whose form is consciousness and who is the supreme digit, is the primordial power of Maheśa; subtle as an atom, she resides in the heart.
That [unit] is called an *aṇu* in the Tantra; two *aṇus* constitute a *truṭi*.
That goddess, who has become the *truṭi*, should be recited as the Parāparā. 6.5.
The supreme [goddess] is said to be devoid of color, while the inferior one possesses the form of color.
Having understood this, O lady of excellent hips, the wise should always perform the recitation (japa).
That goddess, whose form is the *truṭi*, is established in its support;
moving within the vital breath (*prāṇa*), she vibrates eternally through the ten locations in successive order.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva;
Kuṇḍalī, Vyāpinī, Praśāntā, and likewise Viṣuvat.
O Goddess of gods, these ten places are known as the seats of power (śaktisthāna), wherein Śiva, the supreme cause, moves about. (Kubjikātantra 6.9)
Whether upwards, or sideways, or in its own place, O Mistress of the Gods,
it should throb, joined with the ten great powers known as the *kalās*.
Therefore, O beautiful one, the tenfold reckoning has been explained to you;
it is to be performed with effort until the power (śakti) reaches dissolution.
O Goddess, it is said that there are one hundred [vowels] in the utterance of the phonemes; of this there is no doubt.
Without being uttered, the Lord of the World is the subtle support of the natural state.
O Supreme Goddess, for the yogin whose form is that of the *truṭi*, a division into a hundred parts is taught,
while a division into a thousand parts is likewise taught tenfold.
By the abandonment of both, Sadāśiva is the support of the *kalās*;
though devoid of vision, action, and knowledge, he manifests in a thousand ways.
There is no doubt that in the scripture it is taught that a hundred thousand repetitions constitute a *lakṣabhedha*;
indeed, such is the repetition prescribed for yogins who know reality. (Kubjika-tantra 6.15)
Beyond the hundred thousand, beyond the mind, liberated from the bonds of reality, he is eternally absorbed in the state of Unmanā; atomic in form, he is nothing at all.
O beloved, the embodied soul, established in pure existence as the awakener of the qualities and liberated from the perception of objects, manifests in hundreds of thousands of ways.
Indeed, it becomes ten millionfold in this way; this should be understood by those who speak the mantras:
that [recitation] which is whispered, that which has become silent, and that which is mental, being devoid of vocal utterance.
Japa has been previously described in various scriptures honored by the gods;
it is clearly stated that it is for the sake of purification through the practice of vocalizing the sounds. (Kubjikātantra 6.19)

For the sake of accomplishment, that which is free from dust is prescribed; it is self-activated, situated in the heart, mental, intended for the purpose of yoga, and devoid of both [external and internal] extremes.
O Goddess, he who has transcended the mind becomes the giver of liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, O Goddess, the recitation (japa), which is equal to the vital breath, has been fully explained to you.
Japa, which is equal to the vital breath, should be performed by those seeking both visible and invisible fruits; I have thus declared to you the unvoiced syllables and the combinations of letters.
Whatever radiance arises within the great void that is without support—one should constantly practice that within the womb [of the heart]; even one devoid of fortune attains accomplishment.
The root of yoga is purity, and that is oneness within the ocean;
O Dear One, the jewel of the Kula, established as one, is threefold in bliss. (Kubjikātantra 6.24)
Śrī Kubjikā said:
"O Lord, O Great Master, the mudrās have indeed been indicated, yet they are not understood by me.
Therefore, O Goddess of Gods, explain them to me so that my confusion may be destroyed. (KubjT 6.25)
The illustrious Bhairava said: O Goddess, that which is situated above Pātāla and within the center of Śṛṅgāṭapura is globular in shape; from there, O beloved, it extends upward through the aperture.
These two wheels are declared to be established as the primary ones;
they effect piercing, striking, and obstruction, as well as upward movement and extraction.
O you of excellent vows, stimulation, immobilization, possession, and movement are indeed found here;
a mantra-practitioner devoid of these will certainly become an object of ridicule.
O lady of beautiful hips, by the mere knowledge of this, one produces many effects; having placed the wheel in the center, it functions like a sovereign king.
Then, one who is devoid of worldly activity is undoubtedly a creator of poetry there;
having meditated upon the supreme-non-supreme (Parāparā), who is intensely white, in the center of the wheel.
With her hands occupied by a book and likewise bearing the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā),
she is adorned with all ornaments and holds a crystal rosary.
With a garland of flowers hanging from her neck, adorned with a halo of light,
she has two arms and one face, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons.
Vomiting forth many millions of scriptures by means of a great flood,
one who is thus absorbed in meditative concentration becomes Vāgīśvara himself.
He shall undoubtedly utter, both in words and in meaning, the refined Sanskrit and the Prakrit, as well as the depths of the Vedas and the Siddhāntas. (Kubjika-tantra 6.34)
O Dear One, by practicing either in the center of the seat or at the door of the seat,
one follows this Kaula tradition, which is Śākta and conforms to the state of Śakti.
O Goddess of the gods, one should perform the binding of the mudrās by means of the application of measure (mātrā);
here, that measure is said to be subject to the power of the upward breath (uccāra).
O Goddess, the innate [state] (sahaja) is situated in the center of the body;
it is emitted by means of a hundred-fold measure until the supreme is emitted.
As long as his body is possessed [by the deity], the wise one should explain the meaning of the scriptures;
he should meditate here upon that very [goddess] in her eternal form, possessing a luster like that of blood.
Resembling lac and red resin, she has four faces and four arms;
she is endowed with three forms and established through three divisions.
The Goddess who dwells in the three places, who moves along the three paths, who has attained the equilibrium of the three channels,
who is eternally moistened, O Mistress of the Gods, and likewise flowing with the intoxicating fluid.
All the goddesses assume a form with one face and two arms,
holding a noose and a goad, and their eyes are rolling with intoxication.
One should meditate upon the form of the Goddess as being in the prime of youth, intoxicated with passion, and delighted by the joy of wine, according to the established method of that practice.
She, the supreme one whose form is the Supreme, possesses the luster of a thousand flashes of lightning, bandhūka flowers, and pomegranate blossoms, and she is the support for the five śṛṅgāṭakas.
The Goddess, who is the playful manifestation of Mahāyoga, having pervaded the sphere from Śiva down to the earth, remains as the circle of the sun and the stars.
And the śṛṅgāṭaka is upward-facing, with its tip at the root and its base at the end of the horizontal lines;
it has the shape of a flame and an upward-pointing earring, presided over by Kāmaśakti.
O fair-faced one, one should meditate without doubt upon the Wheel seated there upon five lotuses, standing and assuming the form of the Goddess. (Kubjikātantra 6.46)

O Mistress of the Kula, this binding of the mudrā has been described to you; one should perform it with the mantra consisting of the three principles (tritattva), which will be stated hereafter. (Kubjikātantra 6.47)

O Goddess of the gods, O Goddess praised by heroes, [the rites of] causing flight, agitation, attraction, and subjugation, as well as the procedure for worship of the Goddess, [have been taught]. KubjT_6.48.
The venerable Kubjikā said:
"Tell me the characteristics of the three-pronged [mudrā], the lotus mudrā, and especially the yoni mudrā; explain them clearly and exactly as they are."
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Goddess, I shall describe the characteristics of the mudrās in brief.
First, one should form a hollowed cavity (*sampuṭa*) with both hands, facing upward.
One should interlace all the fingers, keeping both hands closely joined;
having bent the index and ring fingers so they are joined and positioned between the middle fingers.
O fair-faced one, the face should be formed at the base of those two;
the two index fingers are joined together facing each other, while the two middle fingers point upward.
O lady of excellent hips, by joining the thumbs and the little fingers together, it should be made like that; thus is the triple-pronged [mudrā] prescribed.
The two hands should be joined in the *sampuṭa* (cavity) gesture with the wrists pressed together;
the tips of the fingers should be extended, and the two thumbs should be positioned between them.
The lotus mudrā has been fully explained; now hear about the yoni mudrā:
one should form a hollowed cavity with both hands and join the little fingers with the middle fingers. (Kubjikātantra 6.55)
Having formed the hands into the shape of a hollowed bowl with the two thumbs placed together, the little finger of the left hand is extended outward. (Kubjikātantra 6.56)
O auspicious one, the *yonimudrā* is known as that which causes the agitation of all;
these mudrās have been fully described for the purposes of meditation, worship, and dismissal. (Kubjika-tantra 6.57)
Now, out of affection for you, O sky-traveler, I shall briefly describe the mudrā of the sky-farers (khecarīs), just as it pertains to the Lord of Birds.
The ring finger should be joined at the pericarp; one should press upon the sixteen spokes.
Through this pressing, O beautiful lady, it attains straightness on the path of the bird (the central channel).
When one hundred thousand [recitations] beginning with *pha* have been completed, there is no doubt that one gains the power of flight;
having formed a six-petaled lotus at the crown of the head, one should join it to the tip of the index finger.
Having become one whose mind is empty within emptiness, one should press [the petals] against each other;
then the six-petaled [lotus] should be caused to expand by the impulsion of the *udāna* wind.
One should meditate upon the [syllables] from *na* to *pha*; there is no doubt that one will attain flight through the sky.
One should place [the syllable *ha*] at the end of the uvula within the upper stalk of the twelve-spoked [wheel].

O Goddess worshipped by heroes, one should effect the piercing with the very same contracted [finger], and the bolt joined with the tortoise; one should meditate upon the sequence from *na* to *pha*, whereby the movement through the sky is attained.
The lotus-mudrā has been described as threefold; now hear about the yoni-mudrā:
having pressed the yoni against the yoni, one effects penetration with the mallet.
From the union of two visargas, one will certainly become a traveler through the sky;
one should meditate upon the supreme source called Amṛtā above the head.
Having traversed the path of fragrance, extending for a *yojana* from the letter *na* to the letter *pha*,
the wise one thus becomes capable of moving through the sky along the path of the womb.

One should worship the Lord Śikhin known as Lohita, situated on the right and left;

Shining like a jewel and filling the ten directions,
he is seen like the sun, resembling a sun-crystal gem.
One should approach the Lord who determines time, endowed with twelve digits (kalās),
the Lord of the Sacred Seat (pīṭhanātha) residing on the island, month by month in due order.
One should fill the succession of years, as well as the ages (*yuga*), the intermediate periods (*manvantara*),
the eon (*kalpa*), the great eon (*mahākalpa*), and even the interstitial voids (*khila*), with twelve jewels.
Because the Soul of the Universe fills [this center], it is therefore called Maṇipūraka;
for those who have entered the path of Śakti, it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should contemplate each wheel individually according to the instruction of the Lord’s command;
thus all accomplishments—superior, inferior, and middling—come to be.

When one practices for one month, [visualizing] Maṇipūraka situated at the feet, accompanied by the Lord of the Seat (Pīṭheśvara), and joined with the lords of the islands and sub-islands; KubjT_12.42.
The knower of yoga, established in worship, meditation, and samādhi, may through the path of power agitate the entire world of moving beings without hesitation. *Kubjikātantra* 12.43.
Within six months, indeed, by the end of the year there is no doubt;
moreover, a swift movement of that self proceeds for him.
By means of sandals or a foot-ointment, one attains the speed of thought;
likewise, through practice on the knee, one becomes a leader of spirits and vetālas.
He performs various wonders and shall remain for an eon;
he is self-possessed, possessed of great energy, and the lord of serpents from his thighs.
However, everything is accomplished gradually in twice that time starting from the first; one should distinguish between the beginning and the end.
By means of the practice of the buttocks, one becomes the lord of the Guhyakas,
as well as of the Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, Pretas, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas.
Having become the Leader and established in the method of the previous path, one who practices while the wheel has entered the path of the womb shall obtain prosperity. 12.49.
Together with the lords of the Kinnaras and the Gandharvas, he is worshipped throughout the worlds and the Lokaloka mountains;
indeed, like the wind, he wanders everywhere thus without hesitation.
When one practices at the wheel located in the middle of the navel, at the root, or in the secret organ,
[one attains] pacification, nourishment, subjugation, attraction, omniscience, and vast prosperity.
O Lord of Birds, those who practice thus by remembering [this] even once become masters of their own form at will and wander through the entirety of other cosmic eggs.
Having become a knower of Sāṅkhya wisdom, one should wander through one's own city once again.
Now, O Goddess, listen to me regarding the even more explicit abandonment of power (śaktityāga). KubjT_12.53.
This supreme seed-syllable called Haṃsa, which is situated in the heart—without it, one never knows perception at any time. (Kubjikātantra 12.54)
O blessed lady of beautiful hips, its three forms— namely sound (nāda), conjunction (saṃyoga), and disjunction (viyoga)— should be diligently characterized.
And here, the triad of consciousness consists of the Self (ātman), Power (śakti), and Śiva;
it exists as a triad of consciousness through their state of inseparable union.
By means of that, O auspicious lady, the god Haṃsa, who is both supreme and non-supreme, is worshipped.
When contracted, he is the Supreme Power (Parā Śakti); when expanded, he is remembered as Bhairava.
The Self should always abide in the center, accompanied by the eightfold group [of winds].
Expansion is proclaimed to be the upper channel, while contraction is the lower. (Kubjikātantra 12.58)
The center is called the navel; these three are very difficult to attain through the obstruction of the upper channel and the contraction of the lower channel. (Kubjikātantra 12.59)
Having concentrated the mind in the center, one should perform churning there;
the *liṅga* situated in the middle of the *yoni*, enclosed within the cavity of the womb. (Kubjika-tantra 12.60)
In the midst of that, one should repeatedly perceive the form of the Self;
for this is declared to be "churning," which destroys the impurity of ignorance.
Indeed, by means of the practice of churning the center, the fire of gnosis blazes forth;
when that fire has blazed, the light thus increases.
From the intensification of the great light, bliss arises;
just as bliss is produced from the churning of the female and male organs.
From the churning of Śiva and Śakti, bliss is thus produced;
O Goddess, certainty arises from the non-duality of Śiva and Śakti.
For this very churning has been described as that which produces the nectar of immortality, O beloved;
one should contemplate oneself being drenched by that nectar. (Kubjikātantra 12.65)
This is that supreme state; this is remembered as the supreme reality.
This is that supreme Brahman, characterized by supreme bliss.
That is known as the Śaktityāga, consisting of Ānanda and Parānanda;
this Maṇipūra has thus been revealed to you along with its secret.
That which was concealed in the earlier Tantras has been revealed to you, O Kubjā,
according to the division of the paths of the continents and the succession of the lords of the sacred seats (pīṭha).
For one who has attained the path of accomplishment, this is difficult to find; how much more so for others?
They will certainly achieve success within the stated time; my word is not false.
Listen, O Goddess, as I describe to you the Svādhiṣṭhāna exactly as it exists; it is explained according to its location for one whose body is composed of the *kalās*. (Kubjikātantra 12.70)
Formerly, when the three worlds had become a single, terrible ocean of darkness,
I assumed the form of a *liṅga*, subject to the will of the Supreme.
I am six-faced and the form of Time; established in the shape of a *liṅga*, eternally surrounded by the six *kalās*, I delight in the midst of the universe.
"Endowed with the six sheaths, I am the aggregate; I am the one whose splendor is beyond the senses.
From that, O beloved, the creation proceeded according to my will."
Worshipped, propitiated, and praised by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and other perfected beings (siddhas),
I then granted a boon to them, who were devoted to me.
The hexagon and the square are offered as one's own self;
by that, they are the Lords of Causes who perform creation through their causality.
"Those who take away, those who create, and those who are independent— whose forms, qualities, and minds are like mine"—
then those protectors began their praise once more, and I indeed spoke again.
"As long as he has been propitiated by you in manifold ways, so long has he been the granter of boons to you; now, being exceedingly gratified, ask for a most abundant boon. (Kubjika-tantra 12.77)
They said: "O Lord of the gods of gods, grant me this boon, O Master: that this linga, which faces in all directions, may be worshipped by me here. (Kubjika Tantra 12.78)
O Maheśāna, act in such a way that we may know with certainty the greatness of this *liṅga*, which is all-pervasive and exists exactly as it is.
Then, O Great Goddess, the path of pervasion was shown to them;
subsequently, the manifest sign (vyaktaliṅga), which is the sphere of the qualities of the six paths, was established.
Through the instruction on the sixfold path (ṣaḍadhva), their body was revealed;
Dviraṇḍa fashioned the torso, and the remaining [deities] formed the faces from above.
The wise know that these have arisen through the sequence beginning with Vāmā;
the face [of the deity] is above Chagalaṇḍa, situated above Mahākāla.
First, there should be the face of Vālin, a man in the form of a living being;
on the right is a cruel serpent in the form of a great and wondrous nāga.
The western one is named Pināka; it abides in Nivṛtti, acts as a restrainer, was previously called Avidyā, and is the destroyer that causes destruction in an instant.
Among these, the triad in the middle is supreme—indestructible, inexhaustible, and immutable; neither Māyā, nor Śambhu, nor Puruṣa ever perish. (Kubjikātantra 12.85)
Arising from the body of the Five-Faced One and born of the six families of the Kula,
their form has been revealed as the Path of Kalās, the leader of the Kula.
"I have been perfected by you, O Viṣṇu, through your unwavering inner self; by means of that yoga which is grounded in devotion, this has been shown to me. (KubjT 12.87)
"By entering completely into my supreme yoga of self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna), and by entering the *liṅga*, you, being wise, shall become worthy of worship. (Kubjika-tantra 12.88)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Ocean of the Authority of the Sixfold Modes," in the *Śrīkubjikāmata*, according to the tradition of the *Kulālika*.
The venerable Bhairava said:
"O Goddess, in this manner, that wise wielder of the wheel was formerly [established] by me."
Because it is well-established in the *liṅga*, it is indeed called *svādhiṣṭhāna*. (Kubjikātantra 13.1)
The abode of Māyā and Śambhu, the teaching that is the substratum of Kalā, joined with the atoms of Puruṣa—this is, in fact, the Svādhiṣṭhāna. (Kubjikāmatatantra 13.2)
One whose self is indeed colored by passion, who is constrained by destiny,
and impelled by ignorance, may go either to heaven or to his own downfall.
A triad has been declared auspicious, and likewise a triad inauspicious;
this station of the six sheaths has been explained by me to you as that which constitutes pervasion.
O Śakti, that which is proclaimed as the supreme and highest Śāmbhava has been described; O fair-hipped one, I shall now speak of the means of realization—listen! (Kubjika-tantra 13.5)
That means of accomplishment (sādhana) is renowned in the world and is presided over by the six Siddhas;
it is established in the self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna) and resides within the liṅga—listen now to how it is situated in its proper place.
His body [is formed] from Dviraṇḍa, and sequentially from Chagalaṇḍa and the others;
in that place where Māyā stands before the mouth of Mahākāla.
One should worship Vālīśvara, situated in the cavity, with a serpent upon his head;
and Pinākin, stationed at the sīmā-line, as the Restrainer (Niyāmaka).
In this regard, I shall proclaim the yoga that bestows auspiciousness upon yogis, by means of which they behold that aforementioned linga, endowed with excellent qualities. (Kubjikātantra 13.9)

By practicing for one month at a time, focusing on each [deity] individually— the Lord who is the sovereign of the island of islands and endowed with twelve rays— one shall obtain the [respective] qualities.
By practicing yoga, one attains prosperity and, in due order, the tasting of the six flavors:
pungent, bitter, astringent, sour, alkaline, and ending with the sweet. (Kubjikātantra 13.11)
The Lord is the island, the light of the island, joined with the sequence beginning with the islands;
through the application of the stages of meditation, there is nothing that he cannot accomplish.
One should contemplate oneself as the six-faced one and the Goddess, who is eager for union;
her mouth is joined to his mouth, and she is seated upon his own liṅga.
Rich with the essence of the nectar of the bliss of being, established by means of playful sways,
one should practice through that path which resides in the cavity of the *liṅga* located within the aperture.
One should indeed constantly practice that which issues from the circle of his face, having the form of a creeper of lightning-light, behind that very self.
O lady of excellent hips, within six months he can even split mountains;
in the second [six months], having the form of the bodiless god of love, he can agitate even the most beautiful women.
In that place, by looking horizontally with a blood-red gaze, one perceives those born as mortals,
sky-dwellers, yakṣas, and those within the domain of rākṣasas and piśācas.
The preeminent practitioner should agitate the city of Dhāṭakīśa by means of the yoga of Brahmā right there, with an eye that revolves like a wheel.
One should gradually extract all of them entirely, from their fruits and flowers onwards,
starting from the world of mortals and including those situated in the netherworlds and the heavens.
By the third yoga, however, one is capable of the fourth [application], namely immobilization;
but this is achieved through the eye of reality (tattvākṣa) when it is filled with the yellow [fluid], resulting in perfected intellect.
The great [practitioner] may arrest the wind of the celestial chariots with waters from the sky;
he may also stop the approach of elephants, horse-thieves, enemies, and serpents.
But by means of the fifth yoga, one who is stationed there within the black maṇḍala may kill whomever he is angry with; indeed, he whom he is angry with shall die.
Enraged, he is capable of destroying the three worlds— including gods and asuras— whether they be bipeds or quadrupeds, comprising all fourteen types of beings.
The sixth station, situated above, is celebrated as the "Gate of Brahmā" (brahmadvāra);
intent solely upon the rhythmic swing of play, one proceeds by means of the unmanifest path.
O Mistress of Yoga, one should practice repeatedly, again and again, until the expansion of the flash of the lightning-creeper occurs; then one shall attain the state of bliss. (Kubjikātantra 13.25)
One should abandon everything natural that falls within the sphere of the path of saṃsāra;
the yogi, devoid of perception, appears like a corpse or like a piece of wood. (Kubjikātantra 13.26)
When the state of being characterized by sattva, rajas, or tamas arises,
the yogi, having entered these three states, becomes identical with the previously mentioned signs.
He is worshipped by all the gods, both those who dwell in the sky and others;
he who knows this sixfold *liṅga* is a knower of reality. (Kubjikātantra 13.28)
All this has been told to you, along with its secrets and well-guarded mysteries;
this teaching must not be given to those of wicked intellect or to those who would steal knowledge.
As long as men are not able to endure bodily hardship with their whole being, this [gift] must not be given;
otherwise, one would go to hell through injustice. (KubjT 13.30)
O lady of excellent hips, he who knows this Kuleśvara Liṅga, which causes both dissolution and origination, is indeed a perfected one (siddha) in this teaching.
Therefore, one should not disparage the *liṅga* as long as it remains in the body;
for this exists in all [beings], and conceptualization is the cause in this matter. (Kubjika-tantra 13.32)
Having invoked the Lord of the Family, Mantramūrti, into this two-footed linga made of mortals— composed of silver, gold, and jewels— it is then established therein.
That is indeed his own self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna); by worshipping it, one may attain that state.
For no one attains omniscience all at once from the very beginning.
Therefore, one should not revile the *liṅga* which is endowed with the qualities of that form;
even when omniscience has been attained, one should strictly observe the rules of conduct (*samaya*).
For those who have entered into darkness and passion and follow the power of egoism, neither spiritual practice nor its accomplishment arises; instead, there is only a fall.
O beloved, hear now about the base of the *liṅga* of the illustrious Lord Kuleśvara;
it is proclaimed to be circular with a central aperture and square in shape. (Kubjikātantra 13.37)
O Great Mother, the source of the universe is the form of the Liṅga above the pedestal, having the shape of a three-holed ring and the splendor of a water-chestnut (śṛṅgāṭa).
Having understood that which is endowed with the four *kalaśas*, possessed of the four seats (*pīṭhas*), and joined with the four *siddhas*, it bestows the fruit of accomplishment. (KubjT 13.39)
Khaḍgīśa was placed upon the first layer of water,
and Baka was stationed at the junction of the crevices in the form of a sprout.
The white [element] is situated in the channel, established in the flow and existing in two places;
Bhṛgu exists all around in a circular form in the shape of a girdle.
One should recognize the seats at the crossroads (śṛṅgāṭaka) in front of the pit:
O, JĀ, PŪ, KĀ, and MATATVA, situated in the middle, on the right, and on the left.
In the region of the heart, however, there is the quadrangular *śṛṅgāṭa* situated at the peak;
thus, the support (*ādhāra*) is four finger-breadths [in size], according to the sequence of *kṛ*, *tre*, *dvā*, and *ka*. (KubjT 13.43)
There, one endowed with the qualities of initiation should practice;
being devoted and intent upon receiving the command, one shall obtain the fruit within four months.
When one meditates upon the deity situated on a water-cloth, endowed with the primary seat and white in color, one proceeds toward supreme pacification and nourishment.
When one abandons that [deity] known as Baknātha, who resides at Dakṣapīṭha, then one obtains nourishment, fortune, and health—the fruit of prior practice. (KubjT 13.46)

When one practices the white [seed-syllable] located at the opening of the channel and situated on the left seat through the yoga of sequential stages, it effects subjugation, attraction, and killing.

Through the conquest of disease and illness, nourishment, and gradually attaining the power of moving through the sky, one who practices the union with Bhṛgu and Kāma shall obtain these qualities. *Kubjikāmatatantra* 13.48.

Peace, nourishment, subjugation, and attraction; the agitation of cities and vast prosperity; the destruction of wrinkles and graying hair, and the attainment of mastery over speech—these proceed [from this].
It brings the dead back to life, draws forth trees, causes one to float upon water,
and acts as a paralyzer of wind, clouds, and rivers, as well as a stealer of speech.
There is success in speech and mastery, as well as the power to cause paralysis in mountains and other such places;
one whose mind is fixed on the support can paralyze all armies.
The support and the sequence have been described; indeed, without that, there is no means of accomplishment.
There is neither liberation nor enjoyment as long as the tradition has not been known.
This has been called the foundation; now hear the division of the commands (*ājñābheda*), by the mere knowledge of which one attains omniscience. *Kubjikātantra* 13.53.
They call the Śāmbhava the sequential [method], because from it everything arises;
for the attainment of speech, however, the Vācayājñā proceeds as its support.
But that which proceeds gradually through the mere practice of Śāmbhava is the state of Śāmbhava within all existing entities, established in the power of Aṇurudra.
For this [initiation], which consists of authority, bestows the quality of purity;
liberation does not exist for those who are devoid of faith and the command.
It is said that grace (prasāda) is the sequence (krama); from this sequence arises the Śāmbhava knowledge.
Through the Śāmbhava [knowledge], one knows and perceives all objects directly before oneself.
When the entire subject matter has been perceived from the teacher, from the scriptures, and by oneself,
then that [process] is said to be gradual, or indeed it is equivalent to the gradual method.
"Liberation does not come through the mere practice of the command as long as the lineage has not been known;
therefore, O auspicious lady, one should satisfy the guru with wealth, both external and internal. (Kubjikātantra 13.59)
But one who is endowed with devotion in every limb, with an inner self purified in three ways, should worship the Lord with devotion; he attains everything from him.
That which is devotion becomes power; through power, the sequence arises.
From the sequence, speech arises; through speech, the command proceeds.
With whatever disposition one should worship the Guru and the deity,
with that same disposition a portion of his command will be transmitted to some degree.
Due to the occurrence of obstacles, between the stated times,
there may arise some command for him that is crowded with the qualities of the waves of reality.
Just as a fully ripened fruit is endowed with the quality of excellent flavor,
so too the disciple, in due time, becomes a knower of all things.
Just as eating a sour fruit that is devoid of juice is not delicious,
so too is the labor of futile knowledge for disciples who are unripened.
Even by means of his power, having been granted permission, he may enter as a portion of the elements;
for the one possessed of ego is seized by the waves [of existence], and through that ego, he perishes.
One side has been fully described; now hear the further [explanation].
In this way, subtlety arises gradually through the gross path.
O illustrious lady, *bheda*, *randhra*, and *chidra* are one and the same designation;
likewise, there are those with seed (*sabīja*) and those without seed (*nirbīja*), and the distinction of their state (*sthitibheda*) exists in two ways.
Kūrmānanda, Paināka, and Mahākāla as the third;
Krodhīśa joined with Arghinī, and Vidyā as the second.
Joined with Jhaṇṭīśa, she is known as Kulavāgeśvarī;
having taken the Kaulika Praṇava immediately after Lakulīśa. (Kubjikāmata 13.70)
Then Śrīkaṇṭha joined with Ūṣman, followed by Lakulīśa and the others; endowed with the oral instructions, this bestows everything, beginning with Bhṛgu and ending with Āvadhika.
Having joined [the breath] within the hollow of the vajra, one should contemplate the end of the bow, accompanied by twelve verses and endowed with twelve wheels. (KubjT 13.72)
Having meditated upon [the deity] as united with the mouth of the Guru, one should accomplish the mastery of speech;
by the mere application of recollection, there is indeed no delay here.
Moreover, O beautiful one, if one should practice in this manner within the Vajrakodaṇḍaka [mandala],
omniscience known as *kriyā* shall arise for him.
From ritual action, the Word proceeds as the source of all things;
thereafter, the Lord of Speech, possessing the power of speech, creates everything.
Blazing with his own splendor, Lakulin comes from the left-hand path;
he is the eldest in the lineage of the Kula, surrounded by the powers of Rudra.
