In the thirty-third principle (tattva), indeed, there is authority and dissolution in the Supreme;
[therein resides] Saṃvarta alone, the Lord, who is both with seed and devoid of seed.
The state situated within its aperture is indeed the Śāmbhava meditation on the Command;
there is no recitation of mantra, no knowledge, no mudrā, and no mental visualization.
There is no exertion, nor cessation, no breaking of the knot, nor retention;
this is devoid of all means, but is rather the conceptualization of a location.

One should project the state of being there into the arrangement of the downward-pointing and upward-pointing hairs; the upper knot is below the bulb (kanda), and in the middle, nothing at all exists.
Know that place to be Śāmbhava, characterized by Śambhu and Andhra;
there, one should not think of anything at all, nor should there be even the slightest superimposition upon consciousness.
Thus, from mere recollection alone, the bliss of knowledge arises;
and by means of mere speech, it produces many convictions in others.
By recollecting [this] even once in this manner, one practicing it shall obtain prosperity;
and through the yoga of six months of practice, one shall attain all forms of higher knowledge.
If he indeed attains union with that [state], he obtains thirty-four abodes for eight years; that is his innate state.
O Dear One, by means of that mantra joined with the Lord who favors the serpents,
one who utters it shall destroy creation, acting as the bringer of the end for Lakulīśa.
For his enjoyment indeed consists in the dissolution of the sound (nāda) into the state of the Pervasive One (Vyāpinī);
for in reality, O Lord, this constitutes the two-fold division of the Command (ājñā). (Kubjikāmata 13.86)
Know that which pertains to the path of Śakti is the "remainder," while the other is again in the Upper [tradition].
This group of six is proclaimed as the supreme Śākta and the Dakṣiṇa.
Joined with the six yogis, it bestows immediate union:
"By you for me, by me for you; I am yours, and you are mine again. (Kubjikātantra 13.88)

O lady of beautiful hips, it has been told to you that for those other than yourself, even animals, birds, trees, grasses, shrubs, and reptiles, [this practice] bestows liberation. (Kubjika-tantra 13.89)
Wherever there is an exposition of the Path, those [beings] are inevitably liberated;
for by that [exposition], I have indeed been propitiated with devotion for thousands of years.

O beloved, in this final birth, this [state] which is very difficult for men to attain arises through association with those who are free from mental constructs— a state that bestows liberation upon those whose minds are devoid of thought.
How much more so for those possessed by the mind—does it not grant liberation precisely because of attachment?
For this reason, one should avoid association, eating and drinking together, and sitting on the same seat.
One should not cause another to give away garments, garlands, or offerings that one has personally enjoyed;
one should not associate with the wicked, nor should one abandon association with the virtuous. (Kubjikātantra 13.93)
One should worship him whose conduct is pure in intention and who is the support of knowledge;
for just as pure gold is ruined by contact with lead.
Thus, even one whose reality is purified perishes through association with the unworthy,
though he resides within the womb of the Yoginī-family and is born from the body of a Kula-vīra.
He is perfected within the lineage of the Siddhas; he attains the meaning of the six feet.
All this has been told to you, together with the characteristics of the right-hand path.
Ask about the sixfold yoga, the support of the Kula, or whatever else you desire.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Thorough Knowledge of the Right Sixfold Group," in the *Śrīkubjikāmata*, according to the tradition of the *Kulālika*.
The venerable Kubjikā said:
"Compassion is supreme for me; [it concerns] the Maṇḍalīśa and the Kulākula."
"The six categories have been known by me; [tell me of] the six Yoginīs, O Lord. (KubjT 14.1)
The venerable Lord Bhairava said: O Kubjīśānī, I, the Blessed One,
shall speak that which produces immediate conviction and bestows immediate union.
The goddesses Kam, Bam, Ālam, Vi, Kā, and Devī are, in sequence, the six [deities] in Kulākula;
these six leaders of the hexad are the bestowers of liberation and worldly enjoyment. (Kubjikātantra 14.3)
Arising from Ḍa, Ra, La, Ka, Sa, and Ha, they abide within the sphere of the Kulas;
dwelling in the six Kulas, they are engaged in both restraint and grace.
Each one bestows grace, while she who acts in conformity brings about restraint;
when worshipped on the six-petaled [lotus], they exist as the bestowers of the fruit of the six categories of reality. (Kubjika-tantra 14.5)
The venerable Kubjikā said:
"I shall ask you further; tell me about that which has begun—the arising of the fruits of the four pentads and the four [groups]."
The illustrious Bhairava said:
"By means of the instruction on the six categories, everything has been told by me; nevertheless, I shall further explain how the qualification [for practice] stands."
O Dear One, having seen the division determined by the syllables O-JĀ-PŪ-KĀMUKA,
which is endowed with the four mudrās, it has been explained according to the secret convention.

O Dear One, I shall explain according to the truth everything regarding the four ages (*caturyuga*), the four seats (*catuṣpīṭha*), and the four wombs (*yoni*) which exist both externally and internally.
In the navel, below the navel, the belly, the heart, the throat, the forehead, and the two eyes, respectively; Oṃ, Jā, Pū, and Kāmarūpiṇī—thus these four are established.
The group of four has been proclaimed as including both the external and the internal;
now I shall describe to you the group of five, conjoined with the Guru’s instruction.
The goddesses, the messengers, the Mothers, the Yoginīs, and the host of Khecarīs—
these indeed exercise their fivefold authority within the Kulākula.
The Svādhiṣṭhāna is the support for the four goddesses, resting upon six bases;
it extends from the aperture (randhra), the fire of desire (kāmaśikhi), and the sphere (gola) up to the limit at the end of the kanda of the banner (dhvaja).
The seventh reality has been indicated as the supreme state of Brahman;
here, creation arose, originating from the six families of the Kula.
Īśāna is presided over by the Goddess; he is the locus of the qualities of his own self-mastery, endowed with twelve apertures and possessed of the twelve desires.
Likewise, in Vahnīśvara there are twelve [syllables] for the Banner and the Root;
thus, accompanied by the twelve *piṇḍas*, there are eighty-four [mantras] in great number.
When yoga is presided over by Śambhu in the stainless Svādhiṣṭhāna,
one attains the state of consciousness characterized by the eighty-four qualities.
O Maheśānī, in this center is the cause of all causes;
one should understand how the *piṇḍa* is produced exactly as it is. 14.18.
First, the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti), and above that, the power of Brahmā;
this is called the Egg of Brahmā (brahmāṇḍa), endowed with the seven worlds.
The foundation is indeed Bhūrloka; Bhuvarloka is that which moves at will;
Svarloka is said to be Śikhi; and Maharloka is Golaka.
It is said that the people residing at the banner are in the Tapas-loka, while the Kandaga is in the Satya-loka;
the Satya-loka resides within the reality (tattva) and is situated up to the limit of the Brahma-knot.
Below Satyaloka, the creation consisting of the *kalās* and so forth arises from the physical body;
from the Ājñā [cakra] onwards, it proceeds until the end of the three, which is the mental creation.
Furthermore, the creation of the four [elements] below arises from the womb;
through the application of the middle churning-stick, it is the bond of the auspicious and inauspicious.
From the Bhuvarloka, a manifold creation proceeds in the lower world;
it should be known as the womb-born (jarāyuja), and it is filled with many sufferings.
From the *kanda* (the bulbous root) arises creation; indeed, the *kanda* consists of the seven worlds.
From the apertures up to the knots, it should be known as composed of the seven elements (*dhātu*). (Kubjikātantra 14.25)
From the bulb the sprout is born; from the sprout arises the root;
from the root come the leaves, tendrils, and branches; and from those, flowers, fruits, and so forth.
The body is said to be the fruit arising from the tree of the elements;
that physical mass arises from the bulb and is immersed in the waters of good and evil.
In the skin, blood, flesh, and the apertures, it is inauspicious when entered by the fire of desire;
it is auspicious when accompanied by the testicles, the bulb, the penis, and ending with the fat, bones, and marrow.
But the impure *rajas* is directly born from the mother and possesses the three powers;
the pure [sattva] is declared to be paternal, for semen is indeed the Lord, beginning with the Self.
O Kubjikā, the *piṇḍa* is everywhere common to both;
at the union of Śiva and Śakti, there then occurs the binding of the *piṇḍa*.
Whatever the mother may think, and whatever the father may think—
through the union of their states of being, that state becomes the innate (sahaja).
Just as a multicolored gem appears according to the nature of its adjuncts,
so too, when considering the adjuncts of that particular time, passion becomes innate.
Having reached this intermediate state, the *piṇḍa*, assuming the form of the cause,
binds itself fivefold through the [five] groups of five and so forth, in due order.
The Puruṣa and Prakṛti, the Guṇas, the Ahaṅkāra, the Dhī (Intellect), and the Manas—
these six surround the supreme Self on four sides.
The living being is led upward and downward like a silkworm;
it reveals itself and binds itself again and again.
Indeed, the individual soul (aṇu) wanders, armored by the fourfold group of Niyāmikās;
each one of these is proclaimed as the Wheel of the Goddess (devīcakra), consisting of four parts.
The Earth is the regulator; the Foundation is preceded by Sound;
Knowledge is filled with the Ear; and Peace is remembered as Vāgīśvarī. (Kubjikātantra 14.37)
The first should be known as Kṣoṇī, the second as Śabdadevī;
the third is named Śrotrikā, and the fourth is Vācādevī. (KubjT 14.38)
For this group of four goddesses is indeed fourfold individually;
O Goddess, this tetrad [resides] upon the path of the way of saṃsāra.
There is a tetrad of the elements, a tetrad of the subtle essences (tanmātras),
a tetrad of the sense organs of cognition, and a tetrad of those who perform sacrifices through action.
That pentad, however, should be known as being joined with the six qualities of the person;
thus the body (piṇḍa) is produced as twenty-five-fold in five ways.
This path of six sheaths consists of the four primordial goddesses;
it is taught with its secret core as the definitive determination of the city of the six Siddhas.
Kubjikā said to the Lord: "O Lord of the Kula, I have not understood the certainty regarding the city of the six Siddhas; tell it to me clearly. (KubjT 14.43)
The Blessed Lord said: "O Kubjīśānī, I have described to you the sevenfold creation; now I shall speak of the seven Siddhas."
The Lord is the master of the nine principles, the sovereign of the lords of the nine wheels;
he is the perfected Śiva of the cosmic egg, the destroyer, the creator, and the one who brings about descent.
That Lord, established in the sovereignty over all the Siddhas, is indeed the sprout whose root is the *kanda*; he is the sovereign master of the six cities.
Pumpura is the first city, and another is the Prākṛta city;
Guṇānanda is called Gola, while Garva consists of Jālandhara.
The city of wisdom (dhīpura) is called Kāmarūpa, while the city of the mind (manaḥpura) is the support (ādhāra).
In the city of the person (pumpura) resides the illustrious Khaḍgīśa, and in the city of nature (prākṛtapura) resides Khagīśa.
Viśvanātha is in Guṇānanda; I am Jhaṇṭīśa in Mahāpura;
Anugrahīśāna is in Dhīpura; and Mitreśāna is in Manaḥpura.
The lords of Ṣaṭpura, the Nāthas, the Kaulīśas,
and the leaders of the Kula are proclaimed as the Kula-siddhas, who reveal the flood of the sixfold transmission (ṣaṭkrama).
In a former kalpa, they will have come to the world of mortals;
O Ānanda, the Lord [will be] the one called Yoga, the final member of the lineage.
In another eon, there will arise those perfected through their lineage and born of noble families;
the god who is the sovereign of the perfected of the lineage is Ājñāmogha, the Lord of the Family.
He is the Lord of the six families; therefore, everything belongs to his lineage.
He is the sovereign Lord, the universal monarch of the nine universal monarchs.
Therefore, the creation beginning with Brahmā, which arises from the Kula, proceeds from him;
he is the support and the agent of the six Purāṇas according to the Kula-path.
The Teacher of all beings, the four goddesses, and whatever else exists in the entirety of speech regarding the creation of Brahmā—[all this was composed by him]. (Kubjika-tantra 14.55)
All that, from the foundation up to the end, is pervaded by you and the goddesses;
and within the Lord of the Four-Faced One is the bulbous root (kanda), which is sevenfold.
Therein, the entire world—including gods, asuras, and humans—is born;
this path of the four goddesses has been described in its entirety.
Now I shall describe the characteristics of the female messengers (dūtīs) as they are:
it is proclaimed that the support of Brahmā is endowed with seven supports.
This is the first supreme emission of Śambhu within the ritual of Kula;
it is the mandala situated below the navel of the Lord of the Lords of the Nine Principles.
Extremely vast with hundreds of millions [of parts], it is the refuge of the family of goddesses;
likewise, there is the triangle, the hexagon, and the sequence of trees and creepers.
This is the twofold authority regarding command with respect to restraint and favor.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Surrounding the shell of Brahmā’s egg on all sides,
there is the great city of Viṣṇu, a thousand crores [yojanas] in extent, situated within the waters.
It has the shape of the peak of a half-moon, crowded with small boats,
filled with many elements, and adorned with nine stalks.
There is a lotus petal, incomparable, with sixteen spokes and a pericarp,
wherein the messenger goddesses, possessing their own inherent natures, sport with various pleasures.
That place where that supreme Puruṣottama eternally delights is declared to be the highest state, where the female messengers born of nectar reside.
When those [energies], having been cultivated, are agitated at the proper time and release the nectar,
then the fourfold creation occurs in the Brahma-wheel, and not otherwise.
In the great sixteen-petalled lotus, overflowing with divine nectar,
situated there together with the messenger goddesses (dūtīs), one should nourish the state of Brahman.
Above the seed-syllables ending with the bulb of Brahmā (brahmakanda), there is a triad of sprouts at the upper aperture;
therein resides Ananta, the Lord of Knots, blazing with the rays of his own power.
Standing in the midst of the great waters, accompanied by nine female messengers,
the Lord Īśvara, the creator of emanation, dwells within the state of all objective entities.
Kapāla, Caṇḍalokeśa, Yogeśa, Manonmana,
Hāṭakeśvara, Kravyāda, Mudreśa, and Diṅmaheśvara.
These nine Bhāsvareśvaras, beginning with Śrī Anantīśanātha,
have fashioned the creation of the words by dividing their own self into nine parts.
Each one of them further creates itself ninefold;
thus there would be nine times nine steps, which constitute the causal nature of the dūtīs.
I shall now proclaim the individual names of the female messengers who have attained the state of the steps, and which specific body part each of them has originated from.
All those nine indeed who have arisen from the limbs of Śrī Ananta—
of them I shall now declare, without omission, their respective spheres of authority.
Bindukā, Bindugarbhā, Nādinī, and Nādagarbhajā; Śakti, Garbhiṇī, and another, Parā, who moves within the meaning of the womb.
Established in the state beyond conventional conduct, impartial and of infinite splendor,
those who rely upon the *kula* and *akula* traditions exercise their authority.
Caṇḍā, Caṇḍamukhī, Caṇḍavegā, Manojavā, Caṇḍākṣī, Caṇḍanirghoṣā, Bhṛkuṭī, and Caṇḍanāyikā. (Kubjika-tantra 14.77)
Accompanied by Caṇḍīśa as their leader, they abide in the station of Akuleśa;
from that station arises the supreme creation, originating from Manonmanī and the others.
She is swift as thought, presiding over the mind, mental, the mistress of reflection;
she captivates the mind, gladdens the mind, is the delight of the mind, and is the sovereign of the mind.
Joined with Manonmanī and having resorted to the state of Unmanā,
these nine supreme female messengers (dūtīs) bring about the state of Unmanā within the mind.
The goddesses of Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, Īśāna, and Kaulikeśvarī. (Kubjika-tantra 14.81)
Those situated at the end of the syllables of the flood of *samana*, established in the supreme space (*parākāśa*),
produce another creation in the state called Yoga, within the station of the Pervasive One (*vyāpinī*).
Hiraṇyā, Suvarṇā, Kāñcanī, Hāṭakā,
as well as Rukmiṇī, Manasvinī, Subhadrā, and Jambūhāṭakī.
Having attained the state of pervasiveness, the mighty Yogadūtīs pervade the moving and the unmoving through the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader.
Vāgvatī, Vāk, likewise Vāṇī, Bhīmā, Citrarathā, Sudhī, Devamātā, Hiraṇyā, and Yogeśī is remembered as the ninth. (Kubjika-tantra 14.85)
Residing within the state of Vāgīśvara and endowed with Vāgīśvarī,
they are born from the limbs of mantra and vidyā, and they bring about the realization of all goals.
Vajriṇī, Śaktinī, Daṇḍinī, Khaḍginī, Pāsinī, Dhvajinī,
Gadinī, Śūlinī, and Padminī arise from the station of the Lord of Mudrās.
The female messengers are tawny-hued, possessed of great heroism, and the ordainers of the divisions of time and its parts;
they are great goddesses whose form is splendor, born from infinite virtues.
Long-limbed, with pendulous breasts, emaciated, with a putrid mouth and a massive face;
elephant-faced, with a great nose, she is the mistress of lightning and of flesh-eaters.
Within the fire of time, the female messengers (dūtīs) abide in the state of withdrawal;
possessing infinite qualities and vigor, they withdraw all that is moving and unmoving.
Suprabuddhā, Prabuddhā, Caṇḍī, Muṇḍī, Kapālinī, Mṛtyuhantā, Virūpākṣī, Kapardī, and Kalanātmikā. (Kubjikātantra 14.91)
The Niyāmikās, situated at the end of the quarters, are the directors of good and evil;
through their division into eighty-one, these messengers (dūtīs) indeed possess great power.
This is proclaimed as the belly of the god Navakeśvara;
it is pervaded by eighty-one squares and filled with many wonders.
Endowed with the form of the word and joined with that which transcends form,
one who practices the method of the lotus path shall attain the state of the three principles.
Thus, in the Kulālikāmnāya, according to the Śrīkubjikāmata, the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Goddesses and Messengers," [is concluded].
Śrī Bhairava said:
O Kubjī, the doctrine of the goddesses and messengers has indeed been explained by you in great detail.
Now, listen to the definition of the pervasion of the Mothers as well.
Above the footprints is a lotus, consisting of radiant energy, exceedingly brilliant,
extending for hundreds of thousands and tens of millions of leagues, and as vast as the ocean in circumference.
Therein, in the center, is Maheśāna, Piṅgeśa, whose form is tawny,
situated in the middle of the triangular city, a mass of splendor, free from all ailment.
For when the time of dawn had arrived, having agitated his own body, he awakened eight individuals who were isolated consciousnesses (vijñānakevala). (Kubjika-tantra 15.4)
The eight Mudrās are the great ministers, O Great Mother, the source of the world;
from them is born the entire universe, everything that consists of speech in its totality.
The first is Khecarīmudrā; the second is named Ātmī;
the third should be known as Śaśinī; and the fourth is named Vahni. (Kubjikātantra 15.6)
The fifth is named Calanī; the sixth is remembered as Bhānumatī;
the seventh is named Mahimā; and the eighth is Sukṛtālayā.
These eight great ministers, born from the illustrious son of Mitra,
perform various creations— gross and subtle, supreme and inferior.
Each one divides herself eightfold;
among them, there are sixteen other channels that are very close to the sixty-four.
Born from the body of Khecarī, the eight Mothers, whose nature is the directions, reside starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna; they are the support of all, both supreme and non-supreme.
The portions of Rudrāṇī are declared to be the goddesses residing within Koṭānta;
joined with the heroes of Saṃvarta, they are the incarnations of the Śambhu-kalpa.
For all those who are both with parts and without parts arise solely from the self;
one should apply them to dharma and adharma until the dissolution of consciousness.
There, the eight Mātrīs born of Aṇu and Māyā reside in the center of Prayāga-pura, conjoined with Caṇḍakaulīśa.
The Brahmī-cakra is taught as being situated in the middle of the first kalpa;
it is said to consist of eight units of the size of the Self (ātma-mātrā), and one should state that there are eight units of the size of Indra (indra-mātrā).
Chāyā, Śīkarā, Jyotsnā, Ṛturatnā, Suśītalā, Payoghṛtavatī, and another; these are indeed the eight mothers of Indra belonging to Viṣṇu.
Residing within the city of Vārāṇasī, cool as the reservoir of nectar,
the Mothers of the World nourish and protect the entire universe.
Having reached the intermediate eon, joined with Krodha and Kaulīśa,
they perform various creations and liberate those [beings] from calamities.
Thirst, Passion, Delusion, Desire, Anger, Darkness, Envy, and Sorrow—these eight are proclaimed as the Mothers of Fire. (Kubjikāmatatantra 15.18)
United with Kaulīśa and Unmatta, they reside on Mount Kolla;
abiding within the midst of the Mahāntaka kalpa, they sport with immeasurable splendor.
The skin, the tactile sense, the sense of smell, the prāṇa, apāna, samāna,
udāna, vyāna, and kṛkarā— these are proclaimed as the eight winds (maruts) that sustain the body.
In a former divine kalpa, the Mothers, possessing immeasurable splendor, sported within the city of Aṭṭahāsa under the lordship of Asitāṅga.
Tamohantā, Prabhā, Mohā, Tejinī, Dahanī, Dinā, Jvalanī, and Śoṣaṇī—these eight are proclaimed as the forms of the Sun. (KubjT 15.22)
In the divine and non-divine aeon, those dwelling in the center of Jayantīpura,
united with the Lord of Rurukaula, take delight together with him.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti,
as well as Śāntātītā, Pṛthivī, Vajriṇī, and Kāmadhenavī.
The eight Mātṛs of the god Īśāna follow his conduct;
they abide in the midst of the non-divine kalpa, accompanied by Jhaṇṭhakauleśvara.
Seated upon the wheel presided over by Aindrī, they sport with immeasurable splendor;
stationed in the midst of the eight Pūrvas, they hold vajras in their hands and possess great strength.
Payoṣṇī, Vāruṇī, Śāntā, Amṛtā, Vyāpinī, Dravā, Plavanī, and Jalamātā—these are renowned as the eight Mothers of Milk (payomātṛ). 15.27.
In the present aeon, however, those residing within the Ekāmra forest are situated in the midst of the Cāmuṇḍā-cakra, [worshipping] Kapālīśa and Kuleśāna.
Residing in the eight-petaled heart-lotus of the venerable Lord Kuleśvara,
they follow the path of emanation according to the sequence of Īśāna.
The deity stands upon the pericarp, surrounded by a retinue of four,
accompanied by Raktā, Karālī, Caṇḍākṣī, and Mahocchuṣmā.

Standing within the interior of a great red forest, situated in the midst of a circle of light, he is the Lord of the Nine Principles, the God accompanied by the eight [perfections]. (Kubjika-tantra 15.31)
Because that which resides in the intermediate body fills the moving and the unmoving, it is therefore called the "Eightfold Filler" (pūryaṣṭaka), which fills in eight ways. (Kubjikātantra 15.32)
That Śiva, the Supreme Lord, dwelling in the hearts of all sentient beings,
causes the entire world to revolve through his illusory power (*māyā*), as if it were mounted upon a machine.
Situated above the seventy-two thousand [nerves] and dwelling within the interval, he is mounted upon the axle and accessible through the axle; yet to those who lack wisdom, he is like a Piśāca.
That is said to be the mouth of the Guru, and it is obtained from the mouth of the Guru;
that yogi who relies upon the mouth of the Guru attains the state of being a Guru himself.
O Goddess, that fire-principle (tejastattva), however, is surrounded by the powers of Rudra;
above this, the station of the Yoginīs, known as Ghaṭa, is proclaimed.
The mouth of the Guru is within the mouth of the Guru; it is indeed established in the mouth of the Guru.
It is obtained from the mouth of the Guru; therefore, one should satisfy the Guru. (Kubjikātantra 15.37)
Having offered praise, Kubjikā said this to the Supreme Lord:
"O Lord, I ask you with diligence about the very extensive location of the jar."
The Blessed Lord said: "O sinless one, free from your inquiry, O Kubjā, I shall tell you everything exactly as it is, with your mind focused. (KubjT 15.39)
Extending for many millions of leagues, with its base shaped like a jar, it is divine, marked with vajras and lotuses, and extends upward as far as the Lord Piṅga.
To him who bestows infinite virtues and accomplishes all goals, everything—both pertaining to this world and the next—is attained. (Kubjika-tantra 15.41)
Where all vessels are obtained in a thousandfold way and again go to dissolution there, that is called the place of the jar (ghaṭasthāna).
Because everything proceeds in such a manner, because things go forth and break apart,
and because they reach a state of indestructibility therein— that place consists of the *ghaṭikā*.
The vessel of the one hundred and eight worlds is indeed located there as the vessel of the [eight] steps;
situated therein is the vessel of the phonemes, which consists of the principles (tattva), the mantras, and the kalās.
The cessation and other states of these [elements], including the treasurer, are proclaimed;
that state, moreover, exists at the end of enjoyment by means of its support.
Within the heart of the god Śrīkuleśvara, inside the upper jar,
is that great sixfold city of Kuleśvaradeva, which is difficult to pierce.
Having divided his own body into the six categories of reality,
the God of great splendor established the six Yoginīs within the six cities.
Ḍāmarī, Rāmaṇī, Lambakarṇī, Kākinī,
Sākinī, Yakṣiṇī, and another born from the Kusumbha ocean.
Seated upon vajra-lotus thrones, endowed with the qualities of saffron,
they are firmly established in the sovereignty over the lords of the six cities.
"By means of the division of O-JĀ-PŪ-KĀMA and the transposition of KĀ-PŪ-JĀ-O, this sequence is fully explained within the scope of emanation and withdrawal. (KubjT 15.50)
Listen now to how the lordship of the Yoginīs is attained, according to the division of superior and inferior, reaching from the gross and the subtle to the ultimate. KubjT_15.51
Duḥśīlā is the fierce Ḍāmarī residing at the base;
Rāmaṇī, whose nature is delight, resides within the city of Svādhiṣṭhāna. *Kubjikātantra* 15.52.
Residing within the city of Maṇipūra, she is Lambakarṇī, the Great Wonder;
in the city of Dhvanideva she is Kākī, and in Viśuddha she is remembered as Sākinī.
The one situated in the center of Ājñāpura is called Yakṣiṇī;
the six Yoginīs, both supreme and non-supreme, are born from the belly of Kubjikā.
All this world, born from Brahmā down to Rudra as its limit,
they again dissolve by means of reverse order when they have been duly worshipped.
These [teachings] are indeed accessible through oral instruction by way of a traditional succession;
one must learn the sixfold path in its six aspects from the mouth of the Guru.
Indeed, [the marks] in the ears, eyes, nose, and likewise in the mouth,
as well as in the chin and the region of the throat, are obtained from the mouth of the Guru.
With her mind overcome by affection, Kujeśvarī said this:
"What is the place of pervasion for them? Who is the follower of which path? (Kubjikātantra 15.58)
Thinking that she had asked out of devotion, the Supreme Lord smiled and said:
"O Kubjikā, I shall tell it to you in due order."
O fair-faced one, that upon whose limb all things are joined is called the "place of the jar" (ghaṭasthāna), characterized by the quality of the gathering (sandoha).
It consists of fifty Rudras, is endowed with fifty Śaktis,
includes eight Cakravartins, and comprises one hundred and eight worlds.
It is filled with pleasing regions and crowded with support-houses;
it stands in the center of the petal of the syllable Oṃ, joined with the heart of Aghorī. *Kubjikātantra* 15.62.
There, that goddess Ḍāmarī has blazing, fierce, tawny eyes;
she abides as the sovereign of the heart-mantra, difficult to master, and is the very soul of the universe.

Furthermore, situated in the midst of the repetition [of mantras], encircled by eighty-one words, the yogin is presided over by the head and is filled with the abode of his own empowerment (svādhiṣṭhāna). 15.64.
One might find pleasure on the path of the footprints, crowded with the people of the Buddha;
yet it is difficult to behold, unbearable, and terrifying, its form agitated by the blood of the intellect.
Residing within the palace of Maṇipūra, she has gone to the interior of the petals of desire;
possessing the luster of a thousand flashes of lightning, the Great Goddess is in the form of a flame.
The Great Goddess Varṇeśvarī, who brings joy to those born of ego, resembles a garland of frost; she is the embodiment of action, both supreme and non-supreme.
The mantras arising from its limbs are proclaimed to be omniscient;
that [organ] is known as Lambikā, the meat-eater and the lecherous one.
In the midst of a full plantain leaf, she has a luster like blue collyrium;
she displays the pride of one clad in armor and is adorned with the path of mantras.
Residing in the center of the unstruck sound (anāhata), surrounded by many qualities and people,
the solitary female crow, greedy for fat and marrow, destroys those very qualities in an instant.
She is eternally wrathful toward him, fierce, violent, and terrifying;
she has entered the path of mantra, is a yoginī, and is the presiding deity over dissolution and enjoyment.
Furthermore, she stands in the center of the *puṃḍala*, situated within the house of purity;
she resembles the fire of universal destruction (*saṃvarta-anala*) and is radiant, empowered by her eyes.
It is crowded with ordinary people, encompassed by the path of the arts (kalā),
permeated by the power of Rudra, and bestowing a fierce state of being.
Always fond of breaking bones and destroying common objects,
this Sākinī is most terrible, pervading the gross, the subtle, and that which is beyond.
On the right, on the petal of Kāmeśvarī, she resembles a mass of snow;
at times she appears in many forms, her range being the qualities of limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
Situated in the midst of the city of the path of reality, adorned with the temple of the Command (ājñā),
filled with a multitude of people, and surrounded by a great flood of missiles.
Majjabījāśinī, Yoginī, Yakṣiṇī, Śakti, and Śāmbhavī—these six Yoginīs reside in the support of the jar (ghaṭādhāra) and establish the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan). 15.77.
There, situated in the center, is the maiden Viśvarūpā, both transcendent and immanent;
she is the consort of all yogīs, the Mistress of Yoga (Yogeśī), whose form is infinite.
Surrounded by those who are radiant with the splendor of the *kam-ba-mā-la* [mantra], she stands in the center;
furthermore, they bestow grace through the application of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*).
These [energies] bestow grace in succession— namely, the Bhūta, Bhāva, Śākta, Āṇava, Raudra, and Śāmbhava— with respect to the principles (tattva) and so forth, beginning from the worlds (bhuvana).
Those great Mothers situated on the southern path cut away [impurities],
while those situated in the north bring about the welfare born of immortality.
Seated upon vajra-lotus thrones in the midst of an ocean of water-pots,
they flood the world of moving and non-moving beings with surging waves of streams of nectar.
I shall describe her form, her majesty, her practice, and the signs of accomplishment hereafter; for now, listen to Khecarī. (Kubjikātantra 15.83)
Thus, in the Kulālikāmnāya, according to the venerable Kubjikāmata, the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Yoginīs" in its sixfold form, [ends].
The venerable Bhairava said:
[That which is] conjoined with the sprouts of the worlds and adorned with the petals of the words...
It is strewn with the thorns of [wrong] colors and endowed with the vulnerabilities of mantras.
Woven with threads of artistic design, divine, situated above the knots of the principles (tattvas),
it is hundreds of millions of millions of leagues in extent and twenty-four finger-widths in length.
Situated in the midst of the vast ocean of the sky, with a luster like black collyrium,
resembling a thousand suns, and possessing a brilliance like the fire of cosmic destruction.
There, they say there are twenty-four mandalas above, in sequence:
the fields (kṣetra), sub-fields (upakṣetra), and meeting-places (sandoha), starting from the east and beginning with the earth element.
O Knower, two fields and two sub-fields, as well as two sandohas, shine upon the petals; there is a group of four and six starting from the directions.
Starting from Aṭṭahāsa and ending with Rājagṛha,
the conjunctions of all things from the king down to the common subjects form a maṇḍala.
Beginning with Saumyā and ending with Bhagnanāsā, these Kulanāyikās, the Sky-farers (Khecaryas), reside within the solar orb; some are situated individually within the circles of the wheels.
In the center of the moon-maṇḍala, however, are thirty-two others of great power,
born from the limbs of Kubjikā, fierce, formidable, and preeminent in their qualities.
Caṇḍā, Ghaṇṭā, Mahānāsā, Sumukhī, Durmukhī, Balā, Revatī, Prathamā, Ghorā, Saumyā, Bhīmā, and Mahābalā. (Kubjika-tantra 16.9)
Jayā and Vijayā, as well as Ajitā and Aparājitā,
Mahotkaṭā, Virūpākṣī, Śuṣkā, and Ākāśamātṛkā.
Sehārī, Jātahārī, Daṃṣṭrālī, Śuṣkarevatī, Pipīlikā, Puṣpahārī, Aśanī, and Sasyahārikā. (Kubjika Tantra 16.11)
Bhadrakālī, Subhadrā, Bhadrabhīmā, and Subhadrikā—
these great Mothers (Mahāmbikās) of Cakreśvarī are endowed with thirty-two qualities.
Now hear about those situated in fire, who abide in the center of the lunar mandala;
here reside the Mothers, the mistresses of the lords of the sky-goers.
Arising from the body of Asitāṅga, these powers— both supreme and subordinate, consisting of action and form—
swiftly effect various creations, abiding in agility.
Śrī Kubjikā said:
O Lord, why is the word "tvaritā" used, and what is meant by the word "khañjī"?
Why is the word "kubjā" proclaimed, and how is that maṇḍala-gaṇa?
How is the form of Maheśānī? Tell me all this in due order with effort, so that delusion may be destroyed.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
"Excellent, O Goddess Mahādurgā! O Pārvatī, do you not understand?
Is it not known to you why you have come here?"
Just as you move with such speed through this division of time that is split a thousandfold from the hundredth part of the tip of a hair.
Likewise, you are named Tvaritā, the destroyer of all suffering;
you have been described to me as Khañjinī again and again, over and over.
She within whose center the universe resides, and who resides in the center of the universe—
she is called Khañjikā, for she moves subtly within the subtle reality.
This one has been described to you as Khañjikā; now hear of Kubjinī. She is known by a name that accords with her meaning, O Kuleśvarī, while you are indeed [the other].
In the gross, the subtle, and the supreme reality—the manifest, the unmanifest, and the stainless—all this is pervaded by the Goddess; and she is you—do you not realize it?
Just as someone with a large body must enter a small house by contracting their limbs, so too does this Maheśvarī. 16.23.
Having four and twelve supports, endowed with sixteen knots at the joint, it is called Vaḍava; above the trident, it consists of three principles and extends to the end of the Kalās.
This body of Kauleśvara, which is to be meditated upon and taught, has been heard;
for him in whose belly that resides, what else remains that is higher? (Kubjikātantra 16.25)
Because she has become the peak (kūṭa) in the midst of that, and because she has gone forth crookedly (kuṭilī), having burst forth from many lineages— this is the will of the Supreme Lord.
Therefore, you are called Kubjikā, the supreme among all things.
In this regard, O Goddess, that which is difficult to obtain and highly secret has been revealed.
Established by the Vedas, the animal (paśu) is above; or rather, the state of being an animal is above on the left.
The left is the right-hand path, while the right is [the path] in the Kula teaching.
But that [Tantra] is dissolved in the ocean of the womb; according to the Kubjikāmata, the womb is the female principle (strī).
For this reason, the Tantra has been kept secret by me and has not been revealed to anyone. (KubjT 16.29)
Today, by means of a state possessed by impetuosity, this has been manifested by you.
Śrī Kubjikā said:
The abiding of the sun and moon has been declared, as well as the determination of the station of fire.
How does she perform creation? Who is Asitāṅga, the Lord of Kula? (Kubjikātantra 16.31)
The illustrious Bhairava said: O Kubjeśī, listen to how the creation proceeds according to its state;
Maheśāna is Asitāṅga, situated above that upon the mandala.
In the center of the moon is the position of the sun; in the center of the sun resides the Fire-god (Śikhin).
In that center is the divine sprout arising from Asitāṅga.
From that, there arises a manifold creation of diverse forms:
the principles (tattvas), the powers (kalās), the phonemes (varṇas), and the ancient words of mantra and vidyā.
They emit the great bliss of the mandala of Śakti and Bhairava;
from among the twenty-five, sixteen are at the beginning and eight are at the end.
[He beheld] Asitāṅga, the Lord of the Kula, abiding in the power of Bhairavānanda,
situated in the center of the primordial maṇḍala, surrounded by sixteen perfected ones (siddhas).
The mandala, which is of the nature of the sky-farer (khecarī), resides at the source of the beginning;
by means of its method of worship, one obtains the fruit of the source of the command (ājñā). (Kubjikātantra 16.37)
For this is the primordial maṇḍala, the most excellent, the highest of the high;
indeed, all the various kinds of maṇḍalas have arisen from within it.
Among the mandalas, that which consists of twenty-five is the first;
each one of them should be understood as being endowed with four siddhas, thus making twenty-five.
O Goddess, from hair to sword, within each and every mandala,
this other pentad is the Kula-vidyā in the Kula-sacrifice.
Joined with the cruel serpent, she bears the qualities of the three forms;
she is common to all the Siddhas in the twenty-fifth mandala.
Bearing a body arisen from the maṇḍala, she who is supreme in the qualities of ritual action and time—
the Goddess, accompanied by the four— creates the ocean of phonemes.
Beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with *ma*, and beginning with *ya* and ending with *ha*:
herein the mantras have arisen, along with the great multitude of vidyās and mudrās. (KubjT 16.43)
Born from the body of the Goddess, that Goddess arises from the mandala;
she stands in the midst of the twenty-four, adorned by the four groups of six.
She resides in the center of the circle of fire; she possesses many forms yet is formless;
her hair grows like that of a barbarian, her eyes are tawny, and she is hunchbacked with protruding teeth and a large belly.
She has the radiance of a dark blue cloud, she is formidable, and she shines with deep-set ornaments;
she has fashioned a garland for her head from the Vedas along with their six ancillaries and the methods of word-order.
She has the Brahma-sūtra as her sacred thread, the Purāṇas as her girdle,
the science of astrology as her adorned eyes, and the Dhvani-śāstra as her ear-ornament.
With a mass of necklaces hanging from her waist, radiant with the bracelets of consciousness,
and emerging from the nectar of the mud of sound, she adorns the circle of her face.
Wearing various garments, soft with many silk cloths and fine fabrics,
she sits upon a couch draped in cloth, established on a seat of immeasurable proportions.
The Goddess who assumes such a form, situated in the midst of the twenty-five principles, is another creator of emanation; she is the supreme one, the primordial twenty-sixth principle.
Seated in the center of the first maṇḍala, she rests upon the lap of the Black One;
she has two arms, is adorned with ornaments, possesses one face, and has three eyes.
With a face possessing lovely bimba-like lips, endowed with manifold virtues,
she was formless yet perfected in beauty, the source of beauty appearing in her presence.
The Goddess, who assumes forms at will, is attained through the Navātman mantra.
Śrī Kubjikā said:
"The Navātman is all this; it is his supreme, highest [energy]. O Lord, tell me: by what means is that supreme [energy] attained, which is the Navātman?"
The venerable Bhairava said: "Excellent, O Bhairavī! You have inquired with effort for the sake of the stainless meaning.
There is nothing whatsoever devoid of that; this is the truth from the perspective of the supreme reality."
Wherever [a teaching] is worshipped by force, there the lineage of the Siddhas does not exist;
but where the lineage of the Siddhas exists, O auspicious lady, it is here that this has been concealed by me.
Those who have tasted the flavor obtained through [the Guru's] command abandon this [world], which is so difficult to attain;
yet they do not abandon that mandala which is the upper part of the pure mandala.
Previously, the Vidyā of the twenty-five-fold division was extracted;
now, having omitted its first pair, the remaining syllables are the pure letters.
These three, Bhṛgu, Lākula, and Saṃvarta, follow in succession;
among them, the abode of Lākula and Bhṛgu is situated upon a serpent-throne.
He is the great time of universal destruction (saṃvartaka-mahākāla), endowed with the qualities of the wielder of the Pināka bow (Śiva),
seated upon a sword-blade throne above the joy of Arghīśa.
This Kūṭa, the Lord of the Maṇḍala, stands at the summit of the bliss of grace, is endowed with the bliss of cruelty, and is joined with supreme bliss.
O Goddess, this is the means for that Great Soul, the goal to be attained, within whose womb resides the entirety of all speech and all things moving and unmoving.
This is the Lord of Kula, named Kauleśvara, whose form is the Peak (kūṭa).
Without this, there is no accomplishment or means to attain the state of Khecarī. (Kubjikātantra 16.63)
Having worshipped that which is within the mandala, the mandala is known as the granter of desires;
by merely worshipping it, one attains the state of all-pervasiveness. (Kubjika-tantra 16.64)
The great tree of the lineage has twenty-five branches;
it is enriched by the beauty of the flowers of command and garlanded with the fruit of higher knowledge.
That maṇḍala by which, through sacrifice, one effortlessly attains the fruit that brings the bliss of matured rasa and the satisfaction of liberation— [that indeed is the maṇḍala].
Situated in the center of the wheel of Khecarī, endowed with the qualities of the three principles,
blazing forth from the maṇḍala, that maṇḍala is the mouth of the submarine fire (vaḍavāmukha).
Each of the twenty-five [tattvas] is endowed with four powers—
Ambikā, Raudrī, Jyeṣṭhā, and Vāmā— at the beginning of the ocean of emanation.
Within these four resides the nine-faced Lord of Kula (Kuleśvara),
the all-pervasive master seated upon the submarine fire, bearing the trident of command.
The venerable Kubjikā said: "O Lord of Sādhakas, for the sake of attaining success, tell me how the individual worship of the maṇḍalas is performed,
and how everything exists as pervasion, O Bhairava."
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O lady of excellent hips, I shall describe how the Goddess resides within the body,
according to its pervasiveness, names, and divisions, so that the wise may understand it.
The maṇḍala of Kāma is on the shoulder, and that of Khecara is situated below it;
the maṇḍala of the Guru is at the joint, intensely radiant in the center of the palm.
The Rudra-maṇḍala is on the right hand, specifically at the tips of the nails;
the Candra-maṇḍala is on the left, while the Chāyā-maṇḍala is below.
At the junction [of the fingers], the Jayantamaṇḍala is produced as a humming sound from the middle of the hand;
the Jñānamaṇḍalaka is situated on the tip of the finger on the left.
Above the buttocks and below the navel on the right is the Amṛtamaṇḍala;
at the junction of the two thighs is the Somamaṇḍala, and at the junction of the thighs is the Ḍāmaramaṇḍala.
The maṇḍala of Kanyā is at the two feet; the maṇḍala of Umā is on the nails;
the maṇḍala of Tārā is on the left [thigh]; and the divine maṇḍala of the family is between the thighs.
The infinite mandala is at the joint, the Mitra-mandala is at the end of the foot;
the mandala preceded by Meru is declared to be at the tip of the toe.
The blood-maṇḍala is in the right side of the belly, and the fire [maṇḍala] is on the left;
the family-maṇḍala is at the back, and that which is reckoned as the vajra is situated in the center.
That Lord of the Family is surrounded by twenty-one mandalas:
the sixth mandala is at the navel, and the Kāla-mandala is at the heart.
Starting from the venerable Nātha and so forth, these three in sequence are the lords of each of the twenty-one maṇḍalas.
The fourfold group of the twenty-five-fold yoga has a personified lord;
and of the collective lords, there is one lord, the sovereign of purity.
The circle of apertures is situated above the millions of pores on her rounded body;
the goddess’s entire body, beautiful in every limb, has arisen from the maṇḍala.
The supreme form of Śāmbhavī is the mandala spontaneously manifested by herself;
her body is produced from the mandala, and she resides in the center of the mandala.
She is the self-acting creator and the self-withdrawing destroyer, the Mistress of the Kula of mandalas;
she is established upon the seat of the trident in the form of the submarine fire.
Seated upon the summit of Kaṅkāleśvara, abiding above the six categories of existence,
she has four arms and one face, holding a rosary and displaying the gesture of fearlessness.
Through the awakening of all-knowledge, she is the bestower of boons from the books;
she is the fifth goddess in the upward sequence, whose form arises from the mandala.
The body of the Lord of Śrīkula measures eighty-four crores from its base to its summit; his cranial vessel [is located] within the lotus-maṇḍala.
Abiding there, she brings forth everything; therefore she is the supreme Kubjeśvarī.
Her body is produced from the maṇḍala, and she is situated above the maṇḍala.
Having meditated upon the goddess within the mandala who bestows the mandala, one should contemplate that very tree of glorious great bliss as being composed of many *ḍālas*. *Kubjikātantra* 16.89.
Joined with the sprouts of the scriptures, adorned with the buds of discernment,
rich with the flowers of unbroken knowledge, and endowed with the fruit that is the arising of accomplishment.

This is the tree of the mandala, from which everything is obtained: it is rich with the ripe juice of bliss and bears the excellent fruits of liberation, contentment, and so forth. (Kubjika-tantra 16.91)
One should always worship that in every way; what is the use of this distracted [practice]?
One should not worship with a yoga devoid of conduct, but rather with one possessed of proper conduct.
Therefore, having realized the state of pervasion and having experienced the body born of a Cāṇḍāla,
he beholds the supreme tree, moving through the sky, which arises from the maṇḍala.
Having cultivated the meditation on that state and regarding him as the Guru, one should comprehend that whatever is before him, all that is known as the maṇḍala. (Kubjika-tantra 16.94)
If the body were a mandala, one should worship it with mandalas and other offerings,
according to the yoga of the submarine fire (vaḍavānala), for the duration of each month.
It is conjoined with the Kula-vidyā, endowed with the four kalās,
united with Kauleśa and Īśāna, and it conveys the instruction situated in its own place.
Having reflected thus with his mind, endowed with devotion and having conquered his senses,
he acquires the material qualities within twenty-five months.
But with double that time, one becomes a creator of the qualities of a Piśāca;
and with triple that time, he partakes of the state of a deity.
Through the fourfold quality, one attains the state of being desired in the abode of the gods due to its universality;
by union with the fifth state, one proceeds as far as Satyaloka.
By the sixth yoga, however, the state of Viṣṇu is certainly attained;
by the seventh yoga, one may travel to the very end of the cosmic egg.
In the eighth [state], he is Piṅga; at the end of the ninth, he is the Lord Īśvara;
in the tenth state, he is Maṇḍalīśa, the sky-farer (khecara), the sovereign of sky-farers.
Through the yoga of practicing the maṇḍala, the yogin, being without external conduct,
is filled with the submarine fire (vaḍavānala) within the midst of the submarine fire.
In the form of the submarine fire (vaḍavānala), one should observe the vow of non-conduct;
having ascended the submarine fire, one shall attain the state of Vāḍava.
For this entire world is composed of that [Command], like the belly of the submarine fire;
it is the Command of all the Goddesses, and its origin is from the Divine Command (divyājñā).
And for the other six categories of existence, he is the primary reality, like the submarine fire;
as the great banyan tree is contained within its subtle seed.
Thus, within the belly of this heart, the entire world exists;
there, the Lord of the Sky-goers is with the Goddess, who is draped in a garland of banyan leaves.
This Mālā, the submarine fire, which is the employer of the Ājñāsūtra and resplendent with eighty-four qualities,
is obtained from the mouth of the Guru.
Even those who perceive otherwise through their own imagination do not truly see;
this has been declared to you as the Pentad, the belly of the All-pervasive Sustainer.
Now hear again of the divine state at the end of Khecarī, which is another group of four.
Thus, in the *Kulālikāmnāya*, according to the venerable *Kubjikāmata*, within the sixfold system and the fivefold Great Bliss (*mahānanda*), this is the sixteenth chapter.
The venerable Kubjikā said:
"O Lord, there is a group of four, a group of five, a group of six, and likewise a group of five."
All that is pervaded by gnosis has been understood; what, then, is the nature of the tetrad?
I ask you, for I am unable [to know it] by my own power alone;
O Lord, speak of the bliss of qualities (guṇānanda) so that we may understand everything. (Kubjika Tantra 17.2)
Śrī Bhairava said:
O Kubjikā, you who possess supreme wisdom, why do you not understand, you of deluded intellect?
If all that has been spoken thus is so, I shall tell you the remainder.

Just as the state of pervasion through worship resides within stability, enjoyment, and dissolution, so shall I declare to you all that entire [teaching], both what has been stated and what remains unstated. 17.4.
The four seats of the Goddess and the four clusters of Siddhas are pervaded by the four ages, according to their division into the higher (para) and lower (apara).
O Maheśānī, listen to how the state beyond conventional conduct exists within the body of the god Akuleśvara.
One should worship the entire sequence of O-JĀ-PŪ-KĀ from the center, to the left, right, front, and upward, as the pervading reality; below the navel, one should first worship the Siddhas.

One should know the Śāmbhava [krama] from the mouth of the Guru through oral instruction: according to the sequence of O-JĀ-PŪ-KĀ, it resides on the heart starting from the right [side], and reaches the navel on the left. KubjT_17.8.
In this manner, one should worship the ear, the mouth, and the nose, as well as the area above the nose, as before,
together with the previously mentioned flames and the hosts of Siddhas along with their protectors.
Abiding in the states of childhood, youth, and old age, established in the three purities, and reaching the three principles—
[one attains this] from the abyss through the instruction on the yoga of the submarine fire.
In the supreme station, which is both the lineage and beyond the lineage, one should worship the omniscient Śāmbhava sequence,
endowed with universal pervasion, using the flowers of the Command (ājñā).

Through the yoga of that which transcends form and so forth, she whose body is produced from the mandala is the supreme goddess abiding therein; she who abides in the center possesses the supreme form.
Abiding at the summit of Time, she is peaceful, beyond all parts, yet the source of all parts;
she is the destroyer of Time, transcendent of parts, the Kambalīyā, the Mistress of the Kula.
Having crossed the submarine fire, Kuleśvarī blazes with intensely radiant qualities; she resembles a thousand suns and transcends all forms.
The form of the Goddess according to the *Pīṭhakrama* is like the luster of a dark cloud or collyrium;
she is endowed with twelve arms, has six faces, and her locks of hair are curly.
Bṛhodarā, Lamboṣṭhī, Stabdhākṣī, Virāladvijā, Bālakramamadhyasthā, Rūpasthā, Nagnā, and Kubjikā. (Kubjika-tantra 17.16)
Blazing like the submarine fire (vaḍavānala), exceedingly fierce and most terrifying,
she is accessible through the teacher’s instruction and bestows the meaning of the divine command.
Standing in the midst of the Youthful Transmission (kaumārakrama), she has one face and four arms;
she holds a book and a maṇḍala, and bestows the boon with her rosary.
Situated within the submarine fire (vaḍavānala), she possesses a gentle form and is intensely longing;
filled with great bliss, she causes the three worlds to enter into a state of spiritual possession.
Established as one who ferries beings across the great ocean of saṃsāra,
she is indeed Mahāntārikā, yet here she has attained the state of the Great Ones in her maidenhood.

She is the one who brings about the destruction of the flood of bonds, relying upon the scriptures of Vidyā; by the utterance of whom even mountains, though struck by thunderbolts and maces, are instantly shattered.
She is indeed the great Arī, the weapon of knowledge consisting of five times five;
perfected by the flood of syllables, she is the supreme one who possesses the power of utterance.

Whether it be one who is not a devotee, or one who is hostile, or one established in debate, or anyone else—whomever this [mantra] dwells in their heart, the enraged [deity] shall cause all of them to fall. (Kubjika-tantra 17.23)

When that Supreme Goddess has been perfected through the yoga established on the *pada*, she quickly causes the *piṇḍa* to enter; listen, O Kubjinī, to [the teaching on] her who is established in the *piṇḍa*. (KubjT 17.24)
She stands in the center of the lineage of the elders, possessing a subtle form and great splendor;
she has two arms and one face, abiding as a mass of light in the form of the Lord.
The Goddess who takes away the life-force of beasts, who cuts through the snare of bonds,
who subdues all sins, and who is the supreme cause of higher knowledge.

And that which was previously described as being at the end of the form, endowed with qualities and adorned with the ornaments of the limbs of knowledge—know that to be the state of being established in the body (piṇḍasthā). KubjT_17.27.
Endowed with thirty-two syllables and encircled by the six limbs,
that which was described as the continuum of karma yields its fruit here in due sequence.
The Goddess who brings about the perfection of mantras and the supreme perfection of the *piṇḍa*,
by means of the yoga of the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*), he shall indeed attain omniscience.
Residing in the crooked place of the submarine fire (vaḍavānala), she utters cries while assuming the form of bliss;
therefore, she is named Kubjikā, whose form is like a jewel and who is slightly hunched.
The state and form of this Goddess proceed beyond all form; she is the Supreme Mother, the mistress of the body, radiant with eighty-four qualities. (Kubjikātantra 17.31)
Having worshipped in due order with mental flowers, honey, sugar, and so forth,
[one should worship] the lineage of the four Siddhas and the venerable master (svāmipāda) in succession.

One who practices should remember the Command (ājñā) situated in the union of the *piṇḍa*, moving transversely through the center, mounted upon the family of Kubjinī; such a person shall obtain prosperity. (KubjT 17.33)

It effects pacification, nourishment, subjugation, and attraction; it is the play of speech, the remover of fever, the destroyer of death, the agitator of cities, and the paralyzer of armies and the drying up of waters.
The paralyzing of the bonds that bind the individual soul (paśu-pāśa), the tooth-stick, the añjali-gesture, and the water-jar;
the rendering seedless (nirbījīkaraṇa) and so forth, the shattering of trees, and floating upon water. (Kubjikā-tantra 17.35)
The rending of seals, the splitting of rocks, the uprooting of great trees, and the causing of rivers to flow or their stopping, as well as that of boats and carts; KubjT_17.36.
Causing fire not to blaze, causing the army to fall, paralyzing the army,
making it rise upward, creating a pillar of flames, creating a pillar of water, and rendering a mountain immobile by the mere sound of a jar or a weapon.
One may paralyze the fall of a thunderbolt and ward off the torrent of lightning;
one may slay, shatter, and split mountains, and rend the surface of the earth.
The increase of hands, perfection of mind, hearing and seeing from afar, knowledge of the present, the past, and the future, and lightness of body.
The perfection of speech, the Mahendra [mantra] which sets in motion the net of Indra,
meditation on the interior of the form at will, and the knowledge of the Mother-families.
Stretching out the tongue, gradually increasing the size of each individual limb,
cracking dry wood, and snapping fruits and flowers.
The quick resurrection of the dead, the great restoration of the burnt to life,
the ripening of tree fruits out of season, and the growth of flowers and grain.
Entering another’s body, awakening to other births, bringing back the dead who are out of sight, and the spreading forth of the blaze of vision; KubjT_17.43.
Knowledge that causes the growth of the teeth, the supreme cognition of the flame,
fruits and flowers within the body, as well as the manifestation of images, speech, and attraction.
The conversing with maidens, invisibility, seeing what is above, rising upward without support, and the extraction of another's form. (Kubjikātantra 17.45)
The battle between the enemies was like a theater of variegated dancing;
the seizing of their sounds and sights increased with every effortless stroke.
The supreme means for subduing beings consists in robbing others of their power, employing men and women as instruments,
and bringing about the contraction of the limbs of living beings.
In the worship of the sequence of the *piṇḍa*, one obtains the fruit of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*).
Through the yoga of the hunched fire (*kubjānala*), there is the fourfold *kubjapiṇḍa*.
One is curved like an aśvattha leaf, another is like the beak of a parrot;
there is another, Maṇikubja, and yet another beyond that, Randhrakubja.

All this has been clearly explained to you: the fourfold group of the Kubjāmbīs, consisting of the aggregate (piṇḍa), the word (pada), the form (rūpa), and that which transcends form (rūpātīta), in their respective order.
