ha da hsauṃ / kṣa pha aiṃ // KubjT_18.55 //
For these three powers of Rudra are established in the state of bliss;
they are mutually encircling in form and adorned with fifty stations.
That which stands at the end of Vāma and Raudra on the right, and goes to the end of Dakṣa and Raudra on the left—
joined with Raudra and A-raudra— that is the "Triple-Raudra," and this is its extraction.
Vāgeśvarī, Māyā, Mohanī as the third, Jñānadevī, and Gāyatrī—these are remembered as the five jewels. (KubjT 18.59)
Through mere placement [of the mantra], penetration occurs clearly through its utterance;
for this is the binding of the body, which destroys even a wicked lion. (Kubjika-tantra 18.60)
Its roots are firmly bound by those planets, and it is adorned with five jewels;
its limbs are jewels and its body is jewels—now hear the determination of these jewels. (Kubjikātantra 18.61)
The jewels are said to be the nectar; yet, O beloved, the nectar is fivefold.
Without the binding of the *piṇḍa*, life itself does not exist.
The five jewels are the jewel of the nectar of space, likewise the jewel of the nectar of heaven, the jewel of the underworld and of the mortal world, and the jewel of hell.
Born from the body of the Goddess and emerged from the body of the Goddess, he possesses the vigor of knowledge; yet, being devoid of vigor, he causes the loss of vigor when [the truth] is unknown.
The third tooth of the Goddess is situated in her own heart, located on the hip;
indeed, this is joined with the end of the crest-lock and resides above the left breast.
With the ear-ornament situated on the left and the head struck by the seed-syllable—
this is proclaimed as the extraction of the words for the conjunction of the five jewels and so forth.
The vital breath (prāṇa) mounted upon fire, adorned by the secret power (guhyaśakti),
with the bindu at its head and pervading it, is the differentiator of the five jewels.
O auspicious one, listen to how each individual jewel is protected by the yoginīs, and how the distinction of their pervasion is established. KubjT_18.68.
Sixty-four groups [of deities] pervade the sky, thirty-two roam the heavens,
the netherworld (pātāla) is filled by sixteen, and the mortal realm is endowed with eight.
But those residing in hell are the presiding deities of the four jewels;
they are known as the illuminators of its radiance, and when unknown, they are the stealers of that radiance.
The power of the jewel is incomparable, blazing with intensely radiant flames;
by its power, O lady of beautiful hips, the yoginīs become exceedingly powerful.
For this reason, these women, possessing superior strength and virtue, conceal their wealth;
they protect what is entrusted to them by their masters, yet they seize what is not so entrusted.
Through seeing these, through touching them, and through the application of the words of the objects, one attains a divine body; through their utterance, one becomes a creator of agitation.
The divine mass consists of sixteen parts, well-restrained by the sixfold nyāsa,
accompanied by a garland of verses, and adorned with a series of planetary deities.

Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) which possesses the majesty of the five jewels, has a face turned away, and is endowed with the *akula*, one should maintain a body that bears the maṇḍala within the physical frame.
This supreme body of the Goddess is indeed the state of Śambhu preceded by the planes;
it abides in the yoga of the submarine fire, being the body of the planes and born from the planes.
Through the instruction on the placement of the feet and the body, the yogin is devoted to the ritual placement (nyāsa);
having performed the nyāsa in its entirety, he who remains well-concentrated [attains success].
For him, many wicked obstacles do not arise—
neither *śākinīs*, *bhūtas*, *vetālas*, *piśācas*, *uragas*, nor *rākṣasas*.
Lions, tigers, elephants, and bears with various wicked minds who may harm one when they have not been provoked— against them, Praty-aṅgirā shall be effective.
One should protect oneself and others from all calamities,
lest one be seized by a fierce Yoginī or led away to the command of Yama.
Having performed this sixteen-fold placement, O Goddess, he shall not die;
once the placement has been performed, he is freed from the sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.
Even in contact with them, he is not defiled; rather, he brings others to perfection.
This is the truth, the truth, and again the truth: this is directly perceived as the supreme sacrifice.
He upon whose feet one who has performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) falls will certainly die;
however, one should not fall at the feet of the Guru as long as this body remains.
If he should revile him, he would suffer the pain of disease, or he might even die;
therefore, once [the fault] is known, one must not act [upon it] as long as one remains in the teacher's household.
O beloved, a disciple who causes harm to his guru does not rejoice, being rendered helpless;
yet one who is devoted to the command, preeminent in virtue, and expert in the multitude of traditions of the lineage [does]. 18.85.
Indeed, no one else has authority over him; even one who is senior by birth should salute him.
This applies regarding pre-established lingas and well-consecrated images.
O beautiful lady, he who has performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) will fall at [the teacher's] feet; his foot will quickly burst open, there is no doubt.
Furthermore, he who always practices the placement of the body...
Without its performance, there would be an upward departure [of the soul];
likewise, by means of the yoga of the nyāsa of the three times at midnight.
O Great Mother, they pass their time according to this method;
and there is another supreme [method], O Goddess, which is the "Unknotting" (granthibheda), very difficult to obtain. (KubjT 18.89)

I shall describe the rare ritual placement (nyāsa) through the application of the "division of the swan" (haṃsabhedaprayoga), situated between *o*, *jā*, *pū*, and *kāma*, located in the heart, the navel, and the middle of the generative organ. (Kubjika-tantra 18.90)
Or the seat (pīṭha) joined with the words, consisting of the first four knots:
Oghānanda, Jayānanda, and Purānanda as the third.
The first four divisions are conjoined with Kamalānanda;
likewise [the others are] Ḍikkariyāṇa, Lampārṇa, and Mahānandapura.
Having placed the two ears upon the mouth, one should place the seat (pīṭha) or the feet;
this is proclaimed as the second placement of the knots of the feet (padagranthi). // KubjT 18.93 //
It is eighty million leagues in total extent; hear now from me of its three and a half crores:
Āmardaka, Dharāpīṭha, Giryaṅka, and Rūpiṇīpura.
One should place two conch-shells rising upwards, meeting at their central tips;
[this forms] a pedestal joined with a lotus, situated in three places and having four knots.
Situated in the center of the cessation of Māyā are four other knots:
the peak of Jñāna, the peak of Ramā, and the third, the peak of the Sage (Ṛṣi).
The seat (pīṭha) should be provided with a full horn, or joined with a foot [symbol], endowed with the lineage of the Siddhas, and accompanied by the row of Gurus. // KubjT_18.97 //
One should deposit that Kulākula within this fourfold [mandala] by means of the vision of knowledge;
this divine Kulākula is supreme and common to all.
And for those possessing the enjoyment of the [spiritual] stations (*padabhukti*), this station is proclaimed;
another, even higher body, resides in the twelve million [sacred sites].
The path of the word *akulīna* is supportless and has its abode in the sky;
this is the pervasion of *akula*, which is filled with sacred fields (*kṣetra*) and seats (*pīṭha*). (Kubjika-tantra 18.100)
For yogis who practice within the family of right conduct, there are ninety-six topics;
the pervasion [of these] by eighty-four topics has been elucidated elsewhere.
But those for whom it turns back again and again there are known as the *haṃsa* consisting of ninety-six steps by those who know the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). (Kubjikātantra 18.102)
This has not been revealed to others who have not attained the Siddhakaula state;
therein, the divine sequence (divyakrama) is to be worshipped by the yogi through the movement of the feet.
Listen to that supreme state where one goes beyond all conduct:
it stands upon the twelve supports at the crown of the head, elevated above the four seats. *Kubjikātantra* 18.104.
Below that is the octad of fields (*kṣetrāṣṭaka*), and below that again are the sixteen *sandohas* in measurement; below that, moreover, is the [mandala] with four gates.
Accompanied by the prefix *upa*, devoid of side-entrances,
this body of the non-noble lineage consists of sixty-four parts.
From that everything is born; everything dissolves back into that very place.
In that [place] are meditation, recitation, yoga, worship, ritual action, and sacrifice.
Established in this, he is not obstructed by any object whatsoever;
for it is the supreme Self, the supreme knowledge, the eternal and supreme Śaiva reality.
One whose body is not of noble lineage, yet is bound by the triad of supreme principles,
should constantly practice yoga upon the aggregate situated within the principle of the self (ātmatattva).
The mantras residing in the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) are endowed with the application of words;
one should practice the yoga residing in the principle of Śiva, which is the repeated cultivation of form.
In that state, the yoga pertaining to the Śiva-principle is indeed beyond form;
there, the *piṇḍa* is proclaimed to be the power Kuṇḍalinī, and the *pada* is Haṃsa.
Form is declared to be the drop (bindu); that which transcends form is the stainless.
Having abandoned the body of the family (kuladeha), one abides in the body of the non-family (akulīna).
And that entire mass indeed belongs to the Kaulikas in the Kujīmata;
everything else is pertaining to the fettered (pāśava), characterized by the three principles and qualities.
Those Śaivas who are devoid of the Śaiva path and follow other doctrines worship [the deity] by means of well-known paths for the sake of attaining worldly success. (Kubjikātantra 18.114)
Those who have abandoned what is unestablished do not perceive the body that is beyond the *kula*;
for without the *akula*, there is no accomplishment (*siddhi*) in this life, whether it be for a worthy vessel or otherwise. *Kubjikātantra* 18.115.
In this path established as well-known, liberation is certain;
it is the straight path leading to the unmanifest, reaching the pool of nectar at the end of the sixteen.
Having filled [the breath], she, whose form is life-force, should fill everything up to the end of life;
she is well-known as the constituent of the senses and the one who determines the count of time.
In this cycle of existence, however, its movement is that which leads one to the certainty of the path to liberation;
it consists of twenty-one thousand and six hundred [verses].
The transmigrating being indeed calculates [time] by means of the instruction on days and nights;
however, by another path, one perceives the characteristics of the way of transmigration.
He calculates the duration of time as one hundred thousand [breaths] per day and night;
however, in a full day and night, there are seventeen hundred thousand and one crore.
In every way, time thus calculates by means of eighty-four *pada*s;
but for those who know the path of the *pada*s, it is entirely free from old age and death.
Now hear otherwise regarding the path of the Siddhas for those who know the path of Śiva:
it consists of twelve crores and four hundred thousand crores.
Indeed, the count of the rosary of days and nights is within the body of Akula;
it extends as far as the body of Akuleśa, which is the conduct of the Kula-yogins.
The bliss that sustains that body shall proceed to the state beyond conduct;
the state of the Kula-sacrifice resides in the heart, and therein lies the supreme sequence.
One should worship Dhṛtstanau, Nābhi, Siddhāvāpī, Ṭhapāduka, the illustrious Barbaram, Oḍḍīśa, and Padasthaughamahārṇava. 18.125.
Having worshipped her, one should meditate upon her; by doing so for one year, one obtains the stated fruit.
With two years, however, there is inferior accomplishment (*siddhi*), and with three years, one attains the middling state. *Kubjikātantra* 18.126.
O Khecarī, through twelve years of practice with the six [methods], the [attainment] is superior;
the inferior is the terrestrial (bhūcara) rite, and the middling is the accomplishment of the subterranean (bilasādhana). (Kubjika-tantra 18.127)
Through the most excellent of supreme accomplishments, one becomes a sky-farer, moving through the sky and ascending above it;
thus, O Goddess, is this entire sacrifice of the ritual of the yoga of the planes.
The path of the stages, together with its secret, has been told; it is very difficult to attain.
For there is indeed a form even of the stage, but the transition is beyond form.
The state of the knowledge of the Haṃsa has been proclaimed; now hear concerning that which abides in form.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, concerning the division of the words of the Tetrad, in the *Śrīkubjikāmata*, the tradition of the Kulālikas.
The venerable Bhairava said:
Form is said to be of two kinds; it is proclaimed as gross (*sthūla*) and subtle (*sūkṣma*).
The gross form is of one kind, O blessed lady, while the subtle form is infinite in its reach.
Starting from the pit of the throat and blocking the final end,
it is the locus for the perception of form, filled with the bliss of consciousness.
The measure of the path of form is established as twenty crores;
however, the limit of illusion (māyā) is in places such as wells, where consciousness arises here.
This is pervaded by words of form and endowed with the wheel of forms;
in each and every wheel, there are four wheels by the millions upon millions.
O lady of noble descent, cultivate the power of these consciousnesses,
eighty-four in number, individually and sequentially, both collectively and separately.
I shall describe them to you in due order, O beloved, beginning with Citrabhānu;
the second is the form of Varuṇa, and the third is Daṇḍapāṇi.
The fourth is the form of the vital breath (prāṇa), while the fifth is the form of the *haṃsa*.
The sixth is the form of the self-possessed (*ātmavat*), and the seventh is preceded by power (*śakti*).
The eighth is the form of Brahmā, the ninth consists of Keśava,
the tenth is Rudra, and the eleventh is the Moon, Vidhu.
The twelfth form is Bhāskara, and the thirteenth is called Īśvara;
it stands between two bows, intensely radiant and full of splendor.
Two [channels] are curved like a bow, consisting of Vāmana and Kubjikā;
two others are situated within the bow, located between Karṇa and Kubja.
Two [deities] bearing the form of conchs are the bestowers of Sāṅkhya and Yoga;
the eighteenth is named Ananta, and the nineteenth is Piṅgala.
The twentieth is Sakalīśāna and the twenty-first is Nirodhī;
each one is seated as Vaḍavānala in the form of a wheel.
Contemplating by way of its own nature, one who has taken recourse in the state of non-existence shall become the source of consciousness in the form of Akuleśvara.
Whatever form belongs to anyone, that very form he assumes—
whether he stands at an intermediate stage or has transcended the succession.
And through the yoga of its repeated practice, one does not attain the state of omniscience;
rather, established in whatever pervasion one possesses, one obtains that specific result.
At the end of the causal process, Mahādeva shines forth, radiant with rays;
through the yoga of constant practice, one shall reach that state within three years.
Abiding in the state of the Great Knot, she brings about the cessation of all things;
when known, she delivers one across, but if unrecognized, she causes one to fall.
When she is known, she enables one to cross the terrible ocean of Mahāmāyā;
therefore she is called Mahātārī, standing above all forms.
Not knowing her form, which resides in the gross, the subtle, and the most subtle,
they do not perceive its quality or form as long as it has not entered into them.
The Mother, worshipped and meditated upon in the previously described Krama-maṇḍala, which is eight crores in extent and resplendent with qualities exceeding three crores; (Kubjikā-tantra 19.20).
When recited while situated there, meditated upon, and worshipped, she bestows the fruit;
she accomplishes all forms when honored with *vaṭa* and blue lotus flowers.
The form of the Goddess has been described as possessing all qualities without exception;
however, her gross body, as it actually exists, has not been mentioned.
And by its utterance, O Goddess, she who blazes with awakened rays shall cause [the target] to fall through her glance,
like a female serpent struck by a staff.
In the same way, this [goddess], who is of great heroism, great movement, and great power,
exists in many ways within the wheel of emanation, struck by the staff of knowledge.
Situated above the sixfold [worlds], she has six faces and a large belly;
endowed with twelve arms, she has sunken eyes and is most terrifying.
Vajrahastā, however, stands upon a vajra; she resides in the midst of the six families of yoga, is joined with the Lord of the Sixth [family], and is placed in the row of the Siddhas.
Listen to me regarding the pronunciation of that which is joined with the staff of knowledge;
she is the Mistress of the Family of Yoginīs, hidden elsewhere in this teaching.
Hā svāyai is the first step; ṇḍā ka ḍu ku is the second;
ḍu ku ṭī ṅga is the third; and pi ṭī ṅga ri is the fourth. (Kubjikātantra 19.28)
Five, five, and likewise five—this is the garland of syllables in their essential form;
it is declared to be the conventional [teaching], made perfectly clear in the mouth of the Guru.
O great noble ones, this method, which is difficult to obtain, has been revealed;
by its mere utterance, the entire host of Ḍāmarīs trembles. (KubjT 19.30)
This is proclaimed as the Vṛddhājñā of the sixfold sequence of withdrawal;
this command descends upon devotees, but it does not transfer to those who are not devotees.
But she, having been propitiated and having come down through a certain lineage of transmission, would shatter mountains by her mere utterance;
what need is there to mention others when she is enraged?
One who is intent upon the worship, meditation, recitation, and fire-offerings of this Goddess shall accomplish everything gross, up to the end of Mahāmāyā. (Kubjikātantra 19.33)
Whatever form he contemplates, all that shall come into being by his will;
through great illusion, the yogi becomes the creator of qualities, being illusion itself.

The Lord of the Earth possesses the qualities of earth on the path moving upon the earth; the Lord of Waters is of the nature of water on the path of water; the Radiant One is on the path of fire; and the Lord of the Bearer of Wind is on the path of wind.
In the sky, the yogi becomes the lord of the sky through the union with the five internal qualities;
and after fifteen years, he becomes omniscient, the Lord of Qualities.
Worshipping the continuous stream [of deities] with garlands of *vaṭa* and blue lotuses, one shall accomplish every form—gross, subtle, and beyond the senses. (Kubjika-tantra 19.37)
By His grace, one should pierce through Māyā and proceed to the three powers;
there indeed is that Mahāmāyā, whose form is subtle and who moves in the most subtle state. (Kubjikātantra 19.38)
Moving through the void, she possesses manifold forms; subtler than the subtlest, supreme, she is perceived like a mirage through the instruction of the Guru’s command.
Following the feet of the god Akuleśvara, she is indeed Viśuddhamālinī; through practice of that, one becomes all-knowing.
One should also practice this by placing the sun on one's back,
standing during the intervals between the twilights near palaces, houses, or trees.
Furthermore, if at the time of midday, while standing at the foot of a tree, one beholds the entire lake down to its most subtle atoms, then one possesses form. (Kubjika-tantra 19.42)
O lady of excellent hips, listen to the other form which consists of the instruments (karaṇa),
by means of which one accomplishes the forms of the Khecarīs and so forth in due order.
O Goddess, that which is common to all does not bear fruit unless one proceeds by its grace and through the command of the Guru. (Kubjikātantra 19.44)

On an auspicious day or at an auspicious moment, having given the command and performed worship, and having prepared the mandala and so forth, one should lead the disciple to a solitary place. (Kubjika-tantra 19.45)
And having placed it above that, in the stainless expanse of the sky,
one should observe its reflection according to the instruction regarding the well of the throat.
Then one should gaze into the sky as a form possessing the appearance of matter;
there one beholds the solar orb, which is the form of Śiva, Sadāśiva.
Upon seeing him, there will be an end to all sins;
through the practice of yoga for six months, one shall become the lord of the earth-dwelling goddesses.
Within three years, however, the lord of the earth— the master who is himself both the destroyer and the creator—
abandons all states and proceeds to that which is beyond the five states.
By means of yoga that is beyond conventional conduct, there is nothing that it cannot accomplish;
O Mistress of the Gods, by this one shall achieve everything, both what has been mentioned and what has not been mentioned.
By the practice of even a single repetition, whether in a month or in a year,
one indeed finds that the time of calamity has arrived for oneself or for others.
If one dies for six months due to a deity of black complexion, death is certain;
if [the deity] is on the face or the head, one should know there is danger, and if it falls upon the head, death is certain.
If it is red, there is the sin of killing a Brahmin; if yellow, there will be fear of disease;
where the two feet are not visible, there will be travel to a foreign land.
If it occurs on the path of the thighs, there will be disease; if in the private parts, one's beloved perishes.
If it is on the belly, there is loss of wealth; but if in the heart, one shall meet with death. (Kubjikātantra 19.54)
If [the mark] is missing from the right arm, a kinsman will perish; if on the left, there will be danger from one's wife.
One should observe all these signs for oneself or for another within six months. (Kubjika-tantra 19.55)
O Goddess of the gods, the remainder [of the teaching] is obtained through instruction from the mouth of the Guru;
one who dwells within the lake of the full form stands in that form with a mind free of expectations.
By means of the most subtle form within the subtle, one should go to the state beyond form;
O Great Goddess, those perfected in yoga are seen as hosts moving through the sky.
All of them, in the form of the *bindu*, are seen in some places and not in others;
one should press the vital breath (*prāṇa*) situated within the vessel of the jar by means of the tortoise-machine (*kūrmayantra*).
"One should not breathe for one month; Bhairava spoke this truth," said Bhairava:
"O auspicious lady, the form of the Kula has been revealed. (Kubjikā-tantra 19.59)
Now listen to the nature of Akula, which is all-pervasive and extremely subtle;
Vyomamālinī is established through the division of the one and the many.
Abiding in the midst of the ocean of nectar, moving about and carrying out her movements,
the Goddess who assumes forms at will is Kubjinī, the Mother Kujā.
The Goddess has two arms and one face, or many arms and faces;
she stands in movement, she is situated in the midst of movement, her body is movement, and she is the Mistress of Movement.
This is the practice of Candragarbha; she is fierce and extremely wrathful.
Seated in the center of the sacred seat (pīṭha), she should be worshipped together with Candragarbha.
Situated in the center of the sixteen spokes, she is the source of the arising of the fruits of the four aims;
joined with the sacred seats and the lords of the seats, she is the all-knowing one who bestows everything.
O fair-faced one, she generates the realization of supreme knowledge and reveals her divine form;
yet her true nature remains hidden from her by the yoginīs.
Therefore, for those who possess form, the pervasion by form is not established;
she is intensely radiant, the Great Bliss, with the splendor of a thousand suns.
The divine garland, throbbing, proceeds from the Command;
it is ever-arisen, eternally blissful, and bestows supreme bliss. (Kubjikātantra 19.67)
But that which transcends time, the end of time, radiant with the form of the Command, supreme,
infinite, and all-encompassing knowledge, is brilliantly illuminated by the highest divine command.
And this form of the northern hexad arises from another;
it has also been described for the southern hexad as being endowed with power.
O lady of beautiful hips, the gross form is revealed everywhere;
however, the supreme, hidden form is that which bestows perfect accomplishment, guarded by the deities.
Why is this accomplished so swiftly elsewhere, while in other places it is crowded with obstacles? One should achieve the state of Bhairava by means of the form of Bhairava.
For this [mantra] is indeed free from the web of obstacles; therefore, it bestows swift accomplishment.
One who has grasped its form here obtains the fruit previously described.
By means of the path of the lineageless transmission (akulakrama) and through the yoga of the command (ājñāyoga) in every respect,
he stands within the sequence of the lineageless and has taken refuge in the state of Kubjīśa.
"The bliss of Bhairava, preceded by all forms of bliss, is attained;
O Goddess, since I have been gratified by you, this has been made manifest by me. (Kubjikātantra 19.74)
O auspicious one, this method for the accomplishment of form, which is most secret, has been proclaimed to you;
it has vanished from all tantras, yet it is now clearly revealed to those who possess the yoga.
The similarity to a string of pearls is white and red, while the yellow one pertains to the neck; that [neck] is coiled, and from it there shall then be separation.
If it stretches out its beak, there will be rain; if it closes its beak, there will be famine.
If it is black in color, death will occur within six months; of this there is no doubt.
O Mahāmati, one should not see anything at all, for it perishes immediately;
one should perceive the Self situated between the eyebrows by means of the six limbs.
The orb is seen like the sun, standing directly before one's eyes;
if it is short and blue, one should know there is danger, but if it is long and thick, there is indeed freedom from disease.
O fair-faced one, it is said that with smoke-colored [flames] there is eradication; with red, disease;
and with black, either the destruction of one's Vedic knowledge or even death occurs.
Likewise, there is loss when it is spotted; similarly, there is misfortune when it is dark blue.
But when the knower of yoga sees a smoky garland in the northwest, KubjT_19.81.
Then, O Goddess, there is eradication; in the southwest, there is fear of fanged creatures.
But when the knower of yoga sees a broken garland in the southeast, KubjT_19.82.

When the practitioner of yoga perceives a vulnerability in the midst of that [enemy's] army, there will be the loss of the country, destruction by fire, and the king himself will perish. (Kubjika-tantra 19.83)
O lady of excellent limbs, his death shall occur within ten days;
in the northeast there is danger from stationary objects, while in the north it bestows the attainment of wealth.

In the eastern quarter, O Goddess, there is indeed the attainment of one's station; in the western quarter, one prospers in happiness; in the southern quarter, one dies—of this there is no need for further deliberation. (Kubjika-tantra 19.85)
O fair-faced one, that which is complete, perfectly even, yellow, smooth, and free from dryness, along with the *sāmala*, is declared to bestow success; it is the *Jīvāditya*.
In the illustrious Kubjikāmata, everything has been clearly explained to you:
Mālinī is situated in the void, and the Bindu is likewise in the void.
Now hear about the person called *Kula*, who is space and transcends form. 19.88.
The illustrious Bhairava said: "O auspicious lady, they spoke thus once more regarding the determination of that which transcends form;
listen with your whole being, being free from contempt."
It is mindless, beyond the mind, devoid of existence and non-existence,
liberated from both dissolution and upward emission, and free from causes and logical reasoning.
Free from both what is to be abandoned and the means [of abandonment], devoid of scriptural authority and illustrative examples,
endowed with a state of nihilism, it is the void, free from affliction.
They know that which is beyond the objects of knowledge, the union, the past, the Lord of Causes, beyond the senses, and beyond speech— that indeed is the Supreme Space (parākāśa).
This entire ritual of the path of yoga is the means for that;
listen now to that path by which the formless is accomplished. *Kubjikātantra* 19.93.
Having made the sky into the all-pervading space, he should dissolve that [object] by recollecting it within this very space of consciousness,
for that is indeed the external space itself.
In the supreme space, in the highest station, is the space of the vehicle;
above that is the formless, and further above that is the station of the supreme, free from doubt.
O Goddess, what is the use of much speaking? This has been described by me before:
by the grace of this Guru, the supreme state is attained.
The characteristics of the qualities of the Unseen have been previously described to you;
all this has been fully explained as the locus of the qualities of Śambhu.
One should practice the Śāmbhava [state] by means of the path that is beyond formal conduct.
But what is the need for practice for one for whom everything is already present before him?
He who has realized Śambhu, the bestower of infinite qualities,
is indeed honored everywhere within the assembly of yoginīs as one whose self is yoga.
If he is a devotee of the ordinance of Śambhu, with a mind detached from worldly existence,
that omniscient and omnipresent one accomplishes [his goal] even with this very body.
O Bhairavī, there is no meditation, no recitation, no worship, nor the performance of offerings in mandalas and the like; by this very body, through the practice of non-observance of rules.
One who subsists on whatever is obtained should always worship oneself;
like fire among all castes, such a person shall quickly partake of the fruit.
Whether it be the lowest, middling, or highest ordinary accomplishment,
they attain the state of the supreme among the supreme in six months, step by step.

One established in a position of authority must perform [the rites] according to the prescribed rules, beginning with the worship of the mandala of gurus and the rest, in accordance with the ancient tradition. (Kubjikātantra 19.104)
Śrī Kubjikā said:
"O Lord of Gods, I have heard everything regarding the determination of the categories of reality;
now tell me this, O Bhairava: what is the tradition (āmnāya) and how is the worship performed?"
Having heard the words spoken by the Goddess, Bhairava, with a smiling face, said:
"You do not understand this entire traditional teaching on worship as it is being told."

The first is the tradition of the continents (dvīpāmnāya), the second is the tradition of the goddesses (devyāmnāya), the third is the tradition of the sacred seats (pīṭhāmnāya), and the fourth is the tradition of the perfected ones (siddhāmnāya).
Its extraction and worship in a single place is thus proclaimed:
in a secret location, rich with fragrance, secluded and free from disturbances. (Kubjikātantra 19.108)
The sacred seats (pīṭhas), the lords of the seats, the Siddhas, and the Mothers of the seats are in their vicinity;
[one should meditate on] the Goddess situated in the center of the seat, accompanied by the four Siddhas.
One should worship the lineage of gurus in the northern sector of the mandala;
this is declared to be the oral tradition, provided it is accompanied by the mandala. (Kubjika-tantra 19.110)
With the measure of a palm’s breadth, one should draw a mandala and so forth at the tip of the womb;
there, I am to be worshipped within the mandala by means of the syllables of the Navātman mantra.
Joined with the word "Ānanda," preceded by "Śakti" and "Bhairava," followed by the word "Bhairava" and then "Vīrādhipate. (Kubjikātantra 19.112)
Endowed with sixteen parts, he is to be worshipped here in this mandala;
for this is the Mandala of the Tradition (Āmnāya), possessing four girdles and four kalās.
All this sequence of transmission—the mandala upon the mandala—becomes quickly accomplished through worship; all that has been declared by me.
A vessel filled with honey, separately provided with water according to the rule, should be prepared at the time of the ritual; it is to be offered as the *argha* at the conclusion of the worship.
One should offer sandalwood paste, incense, and food offerings, and separately provide water for sipping;
therefore, one should perform the rite of propitiation through this entire sequence of ritual acts.

One should indeed perform the ritual for the worship of the wheel in this manner during the rite of propitiation: with a festival of lamps, accompanied by food offerings, vessels of honey, and betel leaves. *Kubjikāmatatantra* 19.117.

Alternatively, one should worship with one's whole being the Tradition (āmnāya), which is the foundation and the path of the scriptures of the Divine Current (divyaugha); he shall protect the entire Tradition.
Then, for one who daily performs that same first circle of the womb,
there occurs a supreme pervasion, and the flood of the sequence proceeds.
Whoever recites this divine scripture, which is the support for crossing the flood, after having worshipped the sandals on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days; KubjT_19.120.
In a divine enclosure of flowers, adorned with garments and garlands,
rich with the fragrance of celestial scents, and beautified by rows of lamps.
With gold, silver, and so forth, or with copper, iron, stone, or clay,
one should worship the God with devotion according to one's capacity, as well as flour-lamps mixed with ghee.
Having thus performed [the worship] in many ways with food offerings, fruits, incense, and flowers,
one may thereafter engage in exposition or recitation.
One should perform the maṇḍala of the Guru three times a day before the book;
for I am indeed his gurus wherever the scripture itself resides.
The Guru who is intent upon the awakening of knowledge must be honored like a god;
for there is no knowledge without the Guru, nor is there a Guru devoid of knowledge.
As is the teacher, so is the knowledge; as is the knowledge, so is the teacher.
Having acquired knowledge from the side of the teacher, once that knowledge is attained, the status of being a teacher is realized.
Thus, he who knows the traditional path in every respect, both in its textual form and its meaning, is a Siddha equal to me; for there is no one common [to all] who is his equal.
This is your Kaulika path according to the instruction on the ultimate reality (paramārtha):
the Kula, the Kula-vidyā, the Kula-path, and the Kula-lineage.
He who understands this tetrad shall be a delighter of his lineage;
the quartet has been fully explained—now ask another according to your preference.
Thus, in the *Kulālikāmnāya*, according to the *Śrīkubjikāmata*, the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Fourfold [System]," is concluded.
The venerable Kubjikā said:
"O God, formerly you imparted to me the *Dvīpāmnāya*."
O Lord, please speak thus according to the instruction on the ultimate truth.
The illustrious Bhairava said: "O Goddess of gods, this which you have asked is true and excellent;
I shall reveal to you the descent of the Dvīpāmnāya, which is most secret."
But at the descent of the first kalpa, from the midst of the ocean of gardens,
[there arose] a place crowded with people who were black and red, possessing a radiance like intensely blazing flames.
The configuration of the creation of Oghasṛṣṭi is the supreme Mātaṅgadvīpa;
here, in the second subsequent kalpa, it possesses a luster as red as vermilion.
It is crowded with people who are yellow and red, the leader of the island who has slain a Brahmin;
it is the locus of the creation of splendor, possessing a radiance like that of a terrifying fire.
In the third Dvāpara Kalpa, the island was radiant with dust resembling safflower-water, and it was crowded with people who were yellowish-red in hue.
The configuration of this playful creation possesses a radiance equal to fierce and terrible eyes;
it is filled with the waters of the Bhairava-gardens and agitated by rows of surging waves.
In the fourth great aeon, however, [the world] will have a radiance like that of a ruby;
it will be crowded with people who are white and red, and will possess pure and unfailing prosperity.
The arrangement of this creation of will is here an orchard and a great forest,
rich with fragrances, garlands, and beautiful flowers, and adorned by Mahocchuṣma.
In the fifth divine eon, however, [he was] possessed of a splendor equal to ten million moons,
divine and consisting of lunar radiance, situated in the midst of the pure ocean.
It is crowded with people who experience the bliss of desire, the source of the fourfold creation,
endowed with manifold joys, and enveloped by the virtues of the Island of the Moon.
It is the bliss of the qualities of the four castes, the source of the fruit of the four aims of life;
it transcends the four types of illusory births and consists of the immortal essence at the end of the fourth state.
The foundation of knowledge and action, whose form is both unmanifest and manifest,
the mass of emanation, bliss, and the locus of the qualities of the Moon-island.
This is the ritual service consisting of the five continents; now hear of the sub-continents, four of which, possessing seeds, manifest in the sacrifice of the Kula.
The first is Upadvīpāruṇa, the second is Vāruṇa,
the third is Narasiṃha, and the fourth is Lokāloka.
Since all this— consisting of the continents and sub-continents, all that is moving and unmoving,
and both the manifest and the unmanifest— has originated from Him, He is therefore called the Cause.
Beyond [these] are four continents, and likewise four others;
beyond them is the Moon-Continent (Candradvīpa), situated in the center, which is the cause of manifestation.
The supreme bliss of the creation of the islands, situated in the midst of the ocean of gardens, is to be perceived through instruction; the rest has been extensively explained previously.
The venerable Kubjikā said:
"O God, how was the Bliss of the Island (Dvīpānanda) described? Although I have heard it from you, there is still a weariness in my mind; explain it clearly."
O Lord, tell me how all this— the origin and the abiding state— exists within those [principles] situated in their respective places through the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! Excellent in every way, O Mālinī!
Listen to what you have asked, O auspicious lady; I shall speak to you that which is faultless."
First, there are sixteen seats; within each seat, the islands arise.
Know that these are twelvefold, and each one is distinct from the others.

One should discern the threefold [mandala] joined with the family wheel (kulacakra), endowed with the seats (pīṭha) and secondary seats (upapīṭha), and characterized by the fields (kṣetra) and clusters (saṃdoha). KubjT_20.23 //
O Dear One, having served the Guru, one should diligently identify the two Upakṣetras and the two Upasaṃdohas, which are surrounded by the Pīṭhas. KubjT_20.24.
O lady of excellent hips, thirty-four islands and the fourfold group residing on those islands are each established within one [of the Mothers].
One should discern those [objects] situated at a distance, those standing before one, and those residing within the body;
without them, accomplishment does not arise even through effort.

For the other [type of practitioner], they are situated outside; for the adept, however, they are situated within the field (kṣetra); and for that very person, they are situated within the body. Indeed, in this way, he becomes a partaker of liberation.
Wherever an eminent practitioner establishes his residence,
whether for the practice of mantra-yoga or for the installation of a *liṅga*, [that place becomes sacred].
Having understood that the image is for the sake of authority, one should take recourse in its location;
otherwise, there will certainly be no enjoyment, but rather hostility toward dualities accompanied by affliction.

Having understood the island, the lord of the island, the goddess, and the lord of the island according to the sequence of the *pīṭhas*, one indeed attains success without hesitation. *Kubjikāmatatantra* 20.30.
Having ascertained the configuration within the five [elements] of a field, village, town, sacred seat (pīṭha), or city, one should then establish the layout accordingly.
Five, five, and likewise five, ending with the fifth, reaching the limit of the families;
in the moving and gentle [directions] there are four, and one for Īśvara, starting from the directions.

One should take recourse in that direction where there is what is called a city, wherein an excellent array of seats is in the center and an array of islands is situated on the outside. (Kubjika-tantra 20.33)
Just as one might loathe a body covered with bones and excrement due to its defects,
yet still experience enjoyment from it through the application of placing one's mind upon that very spot.
A mantra does not become endowed with yoga merely through the syllable;
rather, even for a mantra, it is through the application of its specific location [within the body] that it becomes so.
O illustrious lady, the liṅgas installed by means of mantras are seen to be motionless and devoid of a physical base, yet they were established by the perfected ones (siddhas). 20.36.
O Mistress of the Kula, due to the absence of a suitable place, that which is a marvel is seen in some instances as the motionless Śambhu, illuminated by his own splendor.
The mantra is all-knowing, the giver of everything, eternal, preceded by meditative absorption;
it bestows all things, abides at all times, and is of the nature of the nectar that is the form of time.
It is concealed in all tantras, concealed by the tradition of the islands;
likewise, it consists of the syllables of the islands, combined with the days of the week, lunar dates, and constellations.
This mantra, worshipped by the gods, is conjoined with the syllables of the practitioner;
it is joined with the sacred seats (pīṭha) according to the object of cognition, and otherwise distinguished by the sacred seat.
Whether by the tenth or the eleventh [letter], or together with the immovable [letter],
or even the first letter of the city [of vowels], it becomes a disturber in its own place.
For upon entering any sacred field whatsoever, one should begin the recitation;
with the mantra consisting of one's own name, one should enter the city by means of that very name.
O beloved, having looked toward the directions, one should recite [the mantra] for up to seven times;
by that much, even children, the elderly, and the young are agitated within that sacred field.
One should perform the ritual procedure precisely where stability is to be maintained;
elsewhere, one should enter the city while reciting the mantra once during the repetition.
In that regard, no suffering whatsoever arises concerning food, drink, or bedding for one who practices with devotion through his entire being. (Kubjikātantra 20.45)
Having established oneself on a site for a dvīpa, one should accomplish the mantra of one's own choice;
there too, O Dear One, his eightfold accomplishments arise.
Even if they remain for a full hundred years without knowing the Lord of the Island,
the practitioners of mantra will not achieve success through yoga or meditation.
O fair-faced one, these sixteen are declared to be the lords of the seats (pīṭhādhipatayaḥ);
by them all this [universe], extending to the end of the thirty-four [tattvas], is pervaded. (Kubjikātantra 20.48)
The lords of the continents are said to be thirty-four in total;
when joined with the lords of the sacred seats (pīṭha), they are fifty lords.
O auspicious one, one should observe that which is situated at the beginning and end in the middle of the liṅga;
having observed it without confusion, one should likewise observe the seat, the village, and the city.

Wherever there is this syllable of Pālaka, it is not the first one. Why? Because the lords reside in the sacred seats (pīṭhas); one should not worship that which is separate from the sacred seats. (Kubjika-tantra 20.51)
Neither the Guru, nor the beginning, nor the end, nor the middle joined with the sacred seats (pīṭha) [should be used];
if it is obtained as a whole alone, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, then that is indeed the primordial [mantra].
The designation of gender, however, is entirely concealed by the name;
therefore, one should grasp whichever single syllable constitutes the root of that gender.
Having grasped that [reality], one should abandon the middle and extremes through conceptualization, O Beloved;
having understood this, accomplishment then arises from non-conceptuality. (Kubjikātantra 20.54)
One who performs the sādhana without understanding these two [deities] should not be honored;
for even the guardians, O beloved, create obstacles for those who act as my equals.
"O Goddess, you have heard all that has been declared here as the most essential certainty regarding the sovereign lords, even within the fifty names."
Although its definitive conclusion was indicated even in the *Aghorīyāḍāmara-tantra*,
it has been determined with complete clarity and in its full essence in the *Kubjikāmata*.
Śrī Kubjikā said:
O God, how is the abode of the lords of the seats and continents situated within the body?
In what location, O God, is it established? Tell me this with certainty.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, to how the head within the body is surrounded by sixteen sacred seats (*pīṭhas*),
extending from the backbone to the private parts, and reaching as far as the bow [the forehead] by means of the islands (*dvīpas*).
O Goddess of the Gods, from below the neck along the path of the bamboo-pipe up to the top of the *kanda*,
the five continents are presided over by Brahmā.
O blessed lady, those five [faces] of Māheśī are adorned and located at the navel;
those of Vaiṣṇavī are indeed in the belly, while Kaumāry is situated in the heart.
Kālī, endowed with the five islands, is situated at the end of the throat;
Aindrī, however, stands in the space of the sky, surrounded by a retinue of four.
Cāmuṇḍā, joined with the four continents, is above the eyebrows;
Mahākālī, however, abides in wrath and moves along the path of withdrawal.
On the islands presided over by the Goddess, he who is stationed at each respective boundary is Daṇḍadhārin,
Pracaṇḍa, Daṃṣṭrālin, and Vajratuṇḍaka.
Trijatī, Śaṅkhatuṇḍa, Kapālī, and Triśiras—
these are declared to be the eight lords of the divisions, possessed of great strength and wealth.
In whichever direction they are situated, one should worship facing that very direction;
considering [the deity] as being both outside and inside, one thereby becomes a recipient of siddhi.
O Goddess, this tradition of the islands has been revealed to you in brief;
I shall now speak of its remaining details at length in the *Kulasāra*.
Consciousness, endowed with supernatural power and filled with the mandala of gnosis—
by that [consciousness] this Śrīmata was proclaimed, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Dear One, even without ritual practice, one becomes a vessel for enjoyment and liberation through this known essence of the Tantra; if this is so, the wise man should keep it secret.
Deprived of the illustrious [teaching], those joined with partial knowledge and deluded—since they are devoid of vision—are divided like the blind men and the elephant. (Kubjika-tantra 20.70)
Hearing that the elephant had arrived, he was surrounded by a crowd of blind men, who clung to him with their tails, ears, feet, and trunks, as well as to his back, flanks, and belly.
"By whomsoever and wherever the elephant was touched, he was transformed into that very being's nature.
Thus spoke the Puccha and Hasta: "This elephant has the form of a chowrie. (KubjT 20.72)
Those situated on the ears are like winnowing baskets;
those on the feet are like mortars; those in the belly have the form of a wall; and those on the back have the form of a house.
Both pillars have clubs attached to their hands, while the two tusks of the elephant are fixed to them;
thus, those blind women, being deluded, vie with one another.
But others, possessing eyes, while fighting with one another in this manner, began to laugh upon seeing them; and hearing that, they were struck with amazement.
Then, having heard that great laughter, they asked, "For what reason are we laughing? But they were told by Akṣimukha: "Do not fight me, for you are thus deluded."
"Alas, those devoid of vision [perceive you] to you as having the form of an elephant, though you abide otherwise;
for they have touched all the limbs of the elephant with their intent focus."
When one's vision is obstructed by a cataract,
one should consult a physician so that one may see the entire body of the great elephant Śrīkubjaugha.
Just as an elephant [leads] a blind multitude, so does knowledge proceed;
without the sequence of the Command, the world follows that sequence—thus it is in the *Kubjikāmata*.
That which has been told to you is faultless,
according to the principle of the limbs of an elephant, wherein the right, left, and upper [parts] belong to the Kaulika.
Everything has been prepared for you, O ocean of the lineage of the bliss of command;
now listen, O auspicious one, to the Kālacakra as it truly exists. (KubjT 20.81)
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Descent of Candradvīpa," in the *Śrīkubjikāmata*, according to the tradition of the Kulālikas.
The venerable Bhairava said: "The Śaktis, whose forms consist of the conduct of a hundred thousand [mantras], abide within the vital potency (*vīrya*)."
Through the immersion into the power of Rudra, one's own self is nourished by them.
Through union with the consciousness of Śiva, there is the expansion of the consciousness of Śakti;
through union with the consciousness of Śakti, there is the expansion of the consciousness of the individual soul (jīva).
Through the union with the consciousness of the living being (jīva), there is the nourishment of the consciousness of the mantra;
through the union with the consciousness of the mantra, there is the nourishment of the consciousness of the body (piṇḍa).
Through the union with the consciousness of the *piṇḍa*, there is the nourishment of external conduct;
without consciousness, everything is insentient, like a stone or similar object. (Kubjikātantra 21.4)
O beloved, [the body] is inactive and devoid of consciousness, like a dead corpse;
yet, through the union with fire and consciousness, even water here becomes a burner.

Therefore, with every effort, one should worship within the interior of the circle of the earth, in another region of the continent, that which consists of the power of knowledge, vigor, and consciousness.
One should worship exactly twelve Yoginīs here in the twelve-spoked [cakra];
one should worship the deity Śabdarāśi, together with his characteristics, in the pericarp.
Kumārī, Siṃhaladvīpa, Suvarṇa as the third,
Karṇaprāvaraṇa, and another, the excellent region of Svāmukha.
A wise person should worship with these lands: Kulūta and Oḍḍiyāna, as well as the renowned Jālandhara and the other, Ekapāda. (Kubjikātantra 21.9)
Kuśadvīpa, renowned as Pārasaukula, and Śālmalī;
Parṇadvīpa, called Kumāra, and likewise another, Yavadvīpa.
The land known as Kāmarūpa, as well as Puṣkaradvīpa, and another, Kaṭāhadvīpa; beyond that is the land of Cīna.
Candradvīpa, Janadvīpa, the most beautiful Ratnadvīpa,
Rasadvīpa, Gomeda, Garbhoda, and Sūryadvīpaka.
The island of Āsava is renowned, as is the one endowed with the Maru region;
there also dwell the great island of Saradvīpa and Amṛtadvīpa itself.
Ānanda, the two Gandharva islands, Agnidvīpa, Mahāvana,
extending as far as Aṅgāradvīpa and ending at Nagnadvīpa.
I shall now state the names of these lords of the continents; listen to them.
These extremely fierce guardians of the fields provide protection for the practitioner.
Vidruma, Gastina, Caṇḍa, and likewise the Yakṣa Gaṇādhipa;
Mahābhṛgu, named Jaya, and Vikrama with the great tongue.
Dhvāṅkṣa and Jayabhadra reside in each and every seat (pīṭha),
as do Mahādivya, Dadhīci, and another, Kumārīśa.
Mahādhanuṣṭra, Karālīśa, and Śrutidhara are proclaimed;
as well as Mahādhvāṅkṣa, Mahānandin, Sugandhin, and Gopālaka.
Puṣpadanta, Dhanāḍhya, Vipula, Nandakāraka,
Śukra, and Viḍāla— these two have faces as beautiful as a parrot and a rooster.
Ratipriya, Surapriya, Citrāṅga, Sudurjaya,
Rasana, Viḍāla, and Pradyumna are the Kṣetrapālas in the lineage of the family.
Manoharā, Rūpiṇī, Devī, Citrā, Citrarathā,
Citrāṅgī, Citrarekhā, Vicitrā, and the auspicious Citranāśubhā.
Citrākṣī, Citrarūpā, Subhadrā, Kāmadā, and Śubhā—these are the goddesses of the letter Ka, who preside over the Kanyādvīpa. (Kubjika-tantra 21.22)
The field-protector is Mahāviṣṇu, mighty-armed and holding a discus;
and there are Krūrā, Piṅgalā, Khaḍgikā, Lampaṭā, and Satī.
Daṃṣṭrālī, Rākṣasī, Dhvāṅkṣī, Lolupā, Lohitāmukhī, Bahvāśī, Virūpā, Lampaṭā, and Āmiṣapriyā. (KubjT 21.24)
These goddesses of the letter *kha* reside on the island of Siṃhala;
there is also the great yogin Kṣetrapāla and the great ṛṣi Agasti.
Suprakīrṇā, Prakīrṇā, Lambā, Lambamukhī,
Lamboṣṭhī, Dīrghadaṃṣṭrā, Lambajā, and Prāṇahāmukhī.
Gajakarṇā, Sukarṇā, Mahākālī, Subhīṣaṇā,
Vātavegā, Ravā, and Ghorā— these deities reside in the letter Ga.
And [the goddesses] presiding over Svarṇadvīpa are Caṇḍanāthā, Mahābalā,
Ghanaravā, Ghoraghoṣā, Mahāghoṣā, and Atighoṣikā.
Ghaṇṭā, Ghaṇṭeśvarī, Ghorā, Mahāghaṇṭā, Sughaṇṭikā, Atighaṇṭā, Atighorā, and Kalakalāravā. (Kubjikātantra 21.29)
In the syllable *gha*, these deities indeed reside within the circle covering the tip of the ear:
the great god Yakṣarāja and the mighty Kṣetrapāla.
Vibhūti, Bhogadā, Kānti, Khaḍginī, Padminī, Gāndhārī, Yogamātā, Sudhārā, and Paramojjvalā. (Kubjikātantra 21.31)
Sehārī, Māṃsahārī, Prāṇahārī, Balāpahā, Ṛcchikā, Gṛdhratuṇḍī, Revatī, and the one known as Raṅgiṇī. (Kubjikātantra 21.32)
Indeed, these deities reside within their own mouths in the maṇḍala;
they protect the kingdom in the land of the Ka-group in the northern region.
Kṣetrapāla and Gaṇapati provide protection for the practitioner;
as do Caṇḍā, Caṇḍamukhī, Caṇḍā, Caṇḍavegā, and Mahāravā.
Bhṛkuṭī, Caṇḍavīryā, Caṇḍabhrū, Caṇḍanāyikā,
Cañcalā, Calavegā, Calajihvā, and Caleśvarī.
Indeed, these deities— Kṣetrapāla and Mahājaya—
and those dwelling in the land of Kulūta, provide protection for the practitioner.
Kālarātrī, Vetālī, Kaṅkālī, Karaṅkiṇī, Kiṅkiṇī, Caṇḍaghoṣā, Aṭṭahāsā, and Mahāravā. (Kubjikātantra 21.37)
Caṇḍamātaṅgī, Caṇḍālī, Sūkarī, Kukkuṭī, Gandhārī, Ḍombī, and Campākṣī are remembered as the deities of the syllable *cha*. (Kubjika-tantra 21.38)
The heroine is in Oḍḍiyāna; the field-protector is Mahābhṛgu;
and [the goddesses] are Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Mahājvālāvatī, and Prabhā.
Tejas, Tejavatī, Vahni, Sutejas, Nirmalojjvalā, Jvālāvatī, Karālī, Visphuliṅgā, Śikhā, and Śikhin. (Kubjikātantra 21.40)
In the syllable Ja is the deity of the king who brings all beings under control;

[one should worship] the Goddess together with her weapons and accompanied by the Kṣetrapālas.
