however, O Dear One, if one is incapable or negligent, [one attains purity] by reciting the names of the *pīṭhas*.
I shall fully explain that which one who recites upon rising in the morning attains as perfect purity, for the sake of the purification of the observances (samaya). (Kubjika-tantra 22.22)
I bow to the one who brings about auspiciousness, who resides at Aṭṭahāsa upon a Kadamba tree, whose face is gentle, who holds a vajra,
and who is accompanied by Mahāghaṇṭā.
I bow to the one named Kṛṣṇā, who dwells in Karañja on Caritrā, who wields a spear, who is endowed with great strength, and who bestows excellent accomplishment. (KubjT 22.24)
I bow to Mahālakṣmī, who dwells on Mount Kolāgiri, who is accompanied by Agnikā, who holds a staff in her hand, and who increases prosperity for the forest-dwellers.
I bow to Jvālāmukhī, who dwells at Śrījayaṃtī beneath a nimba tree, bearing a sword, accompanied by a great preta, and bestowing the accomplishment of all aims. (Kubjika Tantra 22.26)
I bow to Mahāmāyā, who resides in the Aśvattha tree at Ujjayinī, holding a noose,
accompanied by Mahākāla, and bestowing the accomplishment of all aims.
I bow to her who stands beneath an udumbara tree, who possesses the speed of the wind, whose weapon is a banner,
who is accompanied by Pavana at Prayāga, and who destroys all enemies.
In Vārāṇasī, having bowed one's head to the goddess Śāṅkarī— who stands upon a palm tree, has upward-pointing hair, wields a mace as her weapon, and is accompanied by Śaṅkara— KubjT_22.29.
I bow to Karṇamoṭī, who dwells at Vaṭa, who is accompanied by Śūla and Hetukā; and to Śrīpadā at Śrīkoṭe, the bestower of royal prosperity. (KubjT 22.30)
I bow to the goddess Ambikā, who is free from passion, who holds a mudrā and a paṭṭiśa,
who is accompanied by Anala, and who brings victory.
I bow to the auspicious Airūḍyā, whose face is fire, who holds a vajra and a spear, who is accompanied by Ghaṇṭārava, and who destroys enemies. (KubjT 22.32)
I bow to her who has a pestle in her hand, who possesses great shanks,
and who has tawny eyes, for the sake of the destruction of enemies in Hastināpura.
In Elāpura, at Kharāsyā, I bow to the one of great strength who holds a noose in her hand, who is accompanied by Gajakarṇa, and who crushes the wicked.
I bow to the crusher of enemies, who holds a kāśmarya fruit and a gokarṇa, who bears the mudrā and the lakuṭa, and whose shanks are like lightning. KubjT_22.35 //
I bow to her who is joined with Karālā, who holds a goad,
who traverses the Maru desert, and who effects the attraction of the three worlds.
I bow to Halāyudhā, who possesses thighs like the trunk of a plantain tree, who dwells in the city and resides at Caitrakaccha, for the attainment of wealth. (Kubjikātantra 22.37)
I bow to Cāmuṇḍā at Puṇḍravardhana, who is endowed with the *kumbhaka* breath-retention and adorned with a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) in her hand, for the sake of purifying my sins.
I bow to her who stands on the far shore with a serene countenance, bearing a vajra-chain, endowed with three matted locks, and who effects both division and paralysis. (Kubjikātantra 22.39)
In Pṛṣṭhāpura, I bow to Vidyunmukhī, who brandishes the staff and the spear as weapons,
who possesses a thunderous roar, and who effects the expansion of differentiation.
I bow to the one of great power who is accompanied by Ulkāmukha, who possesses a goad and a club,
and who breaks the limbs of the wicked.
I bow to her who is accompanied by flesh-eaters, who brandishes a cleaver,
whose face is fire upon the shore, and who tears apart the sacrificial animal that is the enemy.
I bow to Kṣīrikā, the Mother of the World, who holds a sword in her hand,
who is equal to the great Mount Meru, and who cuts away great suffering.

The goddess who wields the vajra weapon, who is gentle yet possesses a fearsome countenance, who performs the rites of immobilization and attraction, and who causes Māyāpurī to tremble. (Kubjikātantra 22.44)
I bow to her who is endowed with great wrath at Pūtanāmrātikeśvara,
who holds a mace as her weapon in hand, and who performs striking and drawing [toward herself].
I bow to her who has a broken nose in Rājagṛha, who is endowed with large ears, who wields a thunderbolt and a spear, and who bestows all fruits.

Whoever, with a concentrated mind, recites the names of the Mothers who abide upon the circle of the earth in the fields, sub-fields, and junctions, together with the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas), [attains success].
Having risen in the morning— or even at the time of sleep— the wise knower of mantras,
though joined with even the most terrible sins, shall become esteemed by the Mothers.
A killer of a mother, a killer of a father, a slayer of a Brahmin, a slayer of a cow, a thief of a hero’s property, and one who has fallen from his vow through negligence; KubjT_22.49.
O Dear One, even one who has fallen away from the practice of mantra by reciting the names of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) casts off the cloak of sin and never beholds an evil rebirth.
Furthermore, one whose nature is pure who recites this three times a day attains all desired objects and becomes beloved by women.
Whether in a sacrificial pit or a mandala, in an image or even on a cloth painting, in a linga or the Dakṣiṇāmūrti, or even having gone into the midst of water— KubjT_22.52.
Whoever, being purified in mind, recites this three times a day or even once a day,
shall be protected from poison, weapons, fire, as well as from diseases, spirits, and planetary afflictions.
One who is undefeated remains free from affliction for a very long time;
even when great danger has arisen, [one is protected] by means of the dung of a tawny cow.
One should cause twenty-four mandalas to be made in the four directions: in the east, the north, the west, and the south. (Kubjika-tantra 22.55)
A group of six should indeed be formed there, and they should be worshipped in sequence;
likewise, the Yoginīs and the Kṣetrapālas [are to be worshipped] at the Kalpavṛkṣa of the cremation ground.
In the east, however, with white flowers; in the south, with yellow flowers;
in the west, with red flowers; and in the north, with black flowers.
Having placed weapons [around them] with white flowers, and with delightful perfumes and incenses,
one should place a water-pot filled with divine water in the center.
One should cause twenty-four lamps to be offered at various locations,
and one should rotate the twenty-four seats in due order.
Having fasted for a day and a night and remaining well-restrained for one night,
the practitioner of mantra should, at the clear dawn, provide a feast for the heroes.
I bow to her who dwells in Rājagṛha, whose nose is broken, who possesses large ears, who holds a thunderbolt and a spear, and who bestows all fruits.

Whoever, with a concentrated mind, recites the names of the Mothers who abide upon the wheel of the earth within the collection of fields (*kṣetra*) and sub-fields (*upakṣetra*), together with the guardians of the fields (*kṣetrapāla*).
Having risen in the morning— or even at the time of sleep— the wise knower of mantras,
though joined with terrible sins, shall become esteemed by the Mothers.
A killer of a mother, a killer of a father, a slayer of a Brahmin, a slayer of a cow, a thief of the hero’s substance, and one who has fallen from his vow through negligence; KubjT_22.49.
O Dear One, even one who has fallen away from the practice of mantra by reciting the names of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) casts off the cloak of sin and shall never behold an evil rebirth.
Furthermore, one whose nature is pure, who recites this three times a day,
attains his desired wishes and becomes beloved by women.
Whether in a sacrificial pit or a mandala, or in an image, or even on a cloth painting; or in a linga, or in the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, or even while standing in the midst of water—KubjT_22.52.
Whoever, being purified in mind, recites this three times a day or even once a day,
shall be protected from poison, weapons, fire, as well as from diseases, spirits, and planetary afflictions.
One who is undefeated remains free from affliction for a very long time;
even when great danger has arisen, [one is protected] by means of the dung of a tawny cow.
One should cause twenty-four mandalas to be made in the four directions: in the east, the north, the west, and the south. (Kubjika-tantra 22.55)
One should perform six groups of six there, worshipping them in sequence;
likewise, the Yoginīs and the Kṣetrapālas are to be worshipped at the Kalpavṛkṣa of the cremation ground.
In the east, however, with white flowers; in the south, with yellow flowers;
in the west, with red flowers; and in the north, with black flowers.
Having placed weapons [around them] with white flowers, and with delightful perfumes and incenses,
one should place a water-pot filled with divine water in the center.
One should cause twenty-four lamps to be offered at various locations and should rotate twenty-four seats in due order.
Having fasted for a day and a night and remaining well-restrained for one night,
the practitioner of mantra should, at the clear dawn, provide a feast for the heroes.
Then, having prostrated again and again, he should ask the presiding deities for forgiveness;
thereafter, the mantra-practitioner swiftly becomes free from obstacles and a possessor of spiritual accomplishments.
Through [the practice of] upasargas, grahas, and so forth, as well as by means of [mantras for] kṣaya, kuṣṭha, jvara, and the like,
one is liberated from all diseases and even becomes wealthy.
Through this consecration, a maiden obtains the desires she wishes for;
one seeking sons obtains sons, and a lustful man becomes fortunate.
The seeker of knowledge obtains knowledge, the merchant indeed enjoys profit,
and one who is devoted to the propitiation of mantras becomes free from affliction.
Constantly devoted to the practice of yoga, he attained perfection and went to the supreme state;
all of this has been revealed through the context of the Dvīpāmnāya.

O Mistress of Kujā, this entire knowledge of time— which you have asked about— is characterized by the pervasion of all things collectively and individually, as well as the combination of the fields (kṣetra) and sub-fields (upakṣetra).
Therefore, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, I shall fully proclaim to you this entire ocean of the sequence of the bliss of command, which has been accomplished for you.
Now listen, O auspicious lady, to how the Kālacakra is situated. KubjT_22.68 //
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Pervasion in its Totality and Particularity," in the *Śrīkubjikāmata*, the tradition of the *Kulālika*.
The venerable Bhairava said:
O lady of excellent hips, [I shall explain] the wheel of time (*kālacakra*) of both oneself and the other.
Having recognized [the signs], one should either dispel the [obstructing] time or [perform] the transference of consciousness according to its specific characteristics.
O Goddess of the Gods, listen as I reveal to you that supreme bliss which is most secret, by means of which the resolute practitioner gains certain knowledge. (Kubjikātantra 23.2)

Time is said to be threefold: the supreme (para), the intermediate (parāpara), and the inferior (apara). The inferior time is the support of the creative energies (kalā) and is subject to the power of time itself.
Time beyond the *truṭi* and *lava* is the "beyond" (*para*); time from the opening of the eyes (*unmeṣa*) onwards is both "beyond" and "not-beyond" (*parāpara*).
From the *manvantara* down to the smallest unit (*kāṣṭhā*), that time fashions its own body.
Having remained through the time of successive and non-successive kalpas, one effects the deception of time;
by remaining through time that is further beyond the furthest, one becomes the maker of time.
Having thus understood from the mouth of the guru that supreme time is the source of honor,
they thereafter engage everywhere in the fearless play of knowledge.
But beyond ninety-six [units], that which is both supreme and non-supreme consists of ninety-six;
while that which is non-supreme and consists of conceptualization is measured by eighty-four.
Bound by a group of five, one quickly goes to the state of the five;
through the conjunctions of Nandā, Bhadrā, and so forth, [the lunar days] Jayā, Riktā, and the others extend to the full moon.
Five, five, and likewise five months constitute the limits of the seasons and the solstices;
[these] form the year, the yuga, the manvantara, and the kalpa.
Thus they calculate that time, with five times five as its limit;
the wise know that the continents situated within the temporal limits are [subdivided] by the continents and the seats (pīṭhas).
The principles (tattvas) situated within the seats (pīṭhas) are indeed the five elements;
each one of them is surrounded by a pentad, according to the procedure ending with the twenty-fifth.
Endowed with the five vowels, they wander in the ocean of *kalās*,
bound by the lotus channels and situated upon the machine of time.
This [wind] quickly carries away living beings and dries them up moment by moment;
having acted through the rays of the moon and sun, it is capable of being the vehicle for Kṛtānta (the God of Death).
Having repeatedly drawn up this entire ocean of living beings,
one should irrigate the trees of decay that bear the fruit of old age and death.
Thus, these three kinds of time have been explained to you in great detail; now listen as I describe that which is perceived by means of their cries. KubjT_23.15 //
Having understood the external and internal [obstacles], he deceives them;
he who cannot be deceived goes into the presence of the Guru.
Or if, through the power of meditative concentration, one sees one's own shadow as discolored in a dream or while awake, such a person shall live for three years.
Facing north, one sees the southern direction; it appears discolored as previously described, for one month minus three days. (Kubjika-tantra 23.18)
If one sees the sun as pure, stainless, and devoid of rays,
it should be understood that within two years he will find death for himself.
O Goddess of the Gods, he who does not see Arundhatī, Dhruva, the shadow of the moon (Soma-chāyā), and the Great Path (Mahāpatha) shall not live beyond a year.
O beautiful lady, whoever sees a hole in the center of the moon,
one should know that his death will occur in the eleventh month.
If he sees a tree with broken branches, or likewise a city of Gandharvas,
or sees Pretas and Piśācas, he shall live for ten months.
If, immediately after bathing, the heart and feet of a person become parched,
or if there is smoke at the crown of his head, he lives for eight months.
If one's footprint should have a missing portion either in the front or at the back,
whether on dust or in mud, that person lives for seven months.
One who, through the occurrence of such a dream, obtains red garlands, red ointments, and red or black clothing, shall live for six months.
He upon whose head a chameleon climbs and remains steady shall live for five months, maintaining his life through three forms.
If a man sees himself with a black iron staff as his only possession through the occurrence of a dream, he lives for four months.
If one sees the sun rising like the orb of the moon,
devoid of its circle of rays, he shall live for three months.
If one sees a lamp with a reddish-copper luster, the solar disc in the sky,
or the earth as crimson, he shall live for two months.
If one does not see oneself in water or in a mirror,
or if one sees one's reflection as headless, one lives for only one month.
If one eye should flow with tears, the region of the throat becomes parched,
his speech falters at the outset, and his own body possesses a radiance like fire.
He experiences intense pain and lives for only one year, he whose forehead throbs and whose face becomes discolored. (Kubjika-tantra 23.32)
If perspiration constantly arises in the *dhruva* location, one lives for eleven months; of this there is no doubt.
He whose heart feels such anguish that he no longer regards his own body, whose speech falters, and whose teeth grow parched; KubjT_23.34.
He whose mind is constantly forgetful lives for ten months;
he whose heart withers does not recognize his own duty.
The private parts wither quickly, and he lives for nine months;
the right limb withers, and likewise the left limb withers.
If he reels constantly with great intensity, he lives for eight months;
if one who was suddenly stout becomes thin, or one who was thin becomes stout—Kubjaka 23.37.
If he is greyish or smoky in color, he lives for seven months;
if, when the sun has risen in the east, he sees his shadow facing south.
O delight of the family, he whose nose is crooked lives for only a moment; indeed, this is the truth, and after a month he shall no longer live.
If the body smells like goat, the teeth chatter,
and one sees the reflection of one's own self as deformed, he shall live for seven nights.
He whose tongue becomes black, whose face becomes the color of a lotus,
and whose cheeks and back of the neck become intensely red-colored, lives for three nights.
He whose face appears naturally darkened in its teeth and whose collection of sense organs functions in a contrary manner, lives for only a day and a night.
He who does not hear sounds, nor sees the wick of a lamp,
and sees his shadow without a head, lives for only a single moment.
Moreover, O lady of excellent complexion, listen to another supreme method,
by the mere knowledge of which one knows time according to its true nature.
One should observe the light within that blazing fire by means of the movements of the sun and the moon through their sixteen and twelve spokes.
One who knows time should understand the characteristics of time in the center of that which was previously described as being within the sixteen and possessing four petals. *Kubjikātantra* 23.46.
If the petal below the moon is destroyed, one will certainly die within six months;
likewise, if it is above, death occurs in three months, and if it is near the sound, in two months. (Kubjikātantra 23.47)
For one month, [the breath] is near the wind; that they know as the rising of Pūṣan.
This has been declared as the lunar wheel (somacakra); now hear concerning the solar [wheel]. (Kubjikātantra 23.48)
O Goddess of the gods, when the light is no longer seen in the twelve-spoked and four-petaled [lotuses], his life lasts for one fortnight— that is, fifteen days.
When the light is no longer seen by him along that very path—
whether for fifteen days, or three, or one day— that is his remaining lifespan.
Now I shall describe another supreme and definitive characteristic of time:
they live through the practice of that, and they die in its absence.
O lady of excellent limbs, that indeed is certainly the conjunction of time;
for she who forgets it is a day that desires her death.
Everything situated within the body dies when impelled by Time;
having distinguished [the self] through both supreme and non-supreme time, one should practice.
By means of the yoga of counter-clockwise rotation and so forth, proceeding in sequence from the right to the end,
through the application of the white and black [paths], one reaches the end of *ka* and *ha*, not the last.
One should practice the Wheel of Time situated in the midst of the full moon;
five, five, and likewise five [days] from the beginning of the white fortnight, starting with the first lunar day (pratipad).
Relying upon the individual self, one should practice day after day the conjunction of vowels and consonants, beginning with the white [syllables] and ending with the black [syllables]. 23.56.
For the sake of destroying old age and death, the great vidyās quickly proclaim this piṇḍasādhana, which is the characteristic of the time of Time itself.
If, despite some means, this person intent upon that does not attain accomplishment,
then the "inducer of forgetfulness" is drawn forth by the circle of Yoginīs.

Or if the lunar day (tithi) is forgotten while practicing again and again, O Goddess, that very weekday and that very lunar day [are to be used]; this has been declared by me with certainty. (Kubjika-tantra 23.59)
O Goddess, this supreme time and ultimate reality has been proclaimed to you;
it is a source of wonder and has been revealed as indivisible.
O Goddess, if you desire life for a long time in the ultimate sense, then,
having abandoned the interior of the body, remain elsewhere, fully realized.
The supreme yoga, which is the nectar of the body, must not be given to one who has not been tested,
for as long as the body is not indeed filled with knowledge and dispassion.
O future one, just as the knowledge of past and future time arises through the application of writing and other such means, so too does it arise through the application of the ritual method.
On the fifth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
one who has prepared the necessary materials should perform a night vigil.
One should take flawless birch bark together with yellow pigment, blood, and saffron;
facing the east, one should write the twelve auspicious vowels.
Having repeatedly protected those who are fully endowed with the measures and the bindu, one who has recited the vidyā should restrain them with a white thread and anoint them. KubjT_23.66.
Having worshipped the lineage tradition (kramāmnāya) with offerings of white sandalwood and beautiful jasmine flowers, well-conjoined with the lamp-mantra, [one should proceed].
Having placed it inside a casket of two shallow bowls in the midst of *jātī* flowers,
one should recite the mantra until the end of the night has arrived.
Then, at the time of dawn, having again performed the sequence of worship, one should indeed satisfy the maidens; hear now how the vidyā is obtained.
"Hrīṃ hūṃ svleṃ svāhāpataye rakṣa rakṣāmṛtodbhave svleṃ hūṃ hrīṃ"—having thus encased [the mantra] by reciting it again, one should consecrate it. (KubjT 23.70)
When the mantras have been recited, the goddesses praise him and declare what is auspicious and inauspicious;
however, when the goddesses do not praise him, it is because his mantra has not been encapsulated.
They show great loss and a fall from the family of Yoginīs;
yet, by virtue of their power, there shall be no death, nor will one go to a fallen state of accomplishment.
Having done this, one should thereafter examine the syllables situated on the birch bark while reciting them, [determining whether they are] equal, deficient, or bestowing great prosperity.
Where there is an excess of syllables, one should predict sovereignty;
where there is an excess of morae (mātrā), there will be gain; and where they are equal, there is health and well-being.
When one sees [a letter] devoid of its bindu (vowel dot), there is indeed a loss of wealth in that case;
if it lacks a mātrā (vowel length), there will be disease; and if it is without the syllable (the consonant), there would be death.
One should observe [the ritual] according to the instruction by means of the sequence beginning with the left;
at that time, the Vidyā-vase together with the vardhanī, which has been worshipped, [is to be used].
Then, having again been anointed with the paste of the village and the city, one should cause it to be whirled sixteen times; it will not burn when touched by water.
This has been told to you, O Goddess, which distinguishes between the auspicious and the inauspicious;
it must not be given to those of wicked intellect, and one should always guard this scripture.
O Goddess, the understanding of time is characterized by the period of the sun;
when the sun has reached the seventh sign, and the moon is in the lunar mansion of one's birth.
O Kubjikā, at the time of the rising of Makara, the period of Pūṣan occurs;
the appearance of ill omens toward the Lord is pacified through recitation and fire-offerings.
Listen clearly to that [method] through the yoga of Mṛtyuñjaya:
one should first place the name enclosed by *juṃ* and *saḥ*, and then apply *saḥ* and *juṃ* at the end. (KubjT 23.81)

The individual soul (pudgalātman) should contemplate the nectar situated within the rising moon; O Goddess, remaining within the body of the supreme and the non-supreme, one should recite the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra.
It is praised when performed with a divine rosary, and not with any other.
The illustrious Kubjikā said:
"This speech is full of wonder, most marvelous, and without apparent cause.
You previously spoke of the rosary; now tell me of the divine rosary. (Kubjikātantra 23.84)
The illustrious Bhairava said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the determination regarding the divine rosary,
which has not been told to anyone and is the supreme state that bestows perfection.
That which cannot be pierced by a wheel, nor burned by fire, nor threaded upon another string, whether made of silk or cotton; (KubjT 23.86)
Meru stands in its center, yet there are no knots therein;
for from that thread of fifty letters, all that is moving and unmoving [proceeds].
When mantras are broken or split, when they are greedy or angry, or when one is asleep—
by reciting this mantra over the thread, one will certainly accomplish that which has not yet been accomplished.
This perfected rosary awakens all paths;
O Supreme Goddess, it should be practiced in secret upon all paths.
The definitive conclusion of the Sūtra has been described by means of the path introduced [previously].
Śrī Kubjikā said:
"O Lord of the Gods, tell me the mantra of the Ḍākinī, Rākṣasī, Lāmā, Kākinī, Śākinī, as well as Yakṣiṇī and Bhrāmaṇī."
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Having taken the letter situated between *ū* and *ḍha*, and likewise that situated between *ṇa* and *ṭa*;
having extracted the two preceding *va* and *kha*, and again that situated between *dha* and *ha*.
Having taken that which is situated between *ya* and *sa*, this group of six is extracted; then, having extracted the last of the *ña*-series, make it joined with a long vowel.
By means of the sixfold procedure, one should apply each group of six;
she is indeed declared to be the Sovereign Bhrāmaṇī, presided over by the six vowels.
They should be employed in all matters concerning restraint and favor;
O illustrious one, I shall indeed tell you another secret regarding the Śākinīs.
Having extracted the one following Ū, it should be placed on the seat preceded by Ha;
it should be conjoined with Repha (Ra) and likewise joined with the one following Da (Na).
The peak-syllable (kūṭa) joined with the letter preceding jha and endowed with the bindu,
extracted according to the path of the prastāra, is the determination of the group of six.
Listen, O auspicious lady, to what is being told as it is presented;
for if one practices otherwise than by observing the signs of death (ariṣṭa) and so forth, [the result is different].
When the region of the uvula becomes parched, one should then abandon meditation;
for tranquility does not arise merely from recitation, meditation, and worship.
Then, it becomes certain that the signs of death will appear within five days;
at that time, one should certainly take refuge in the Guru-deva.
Having spoken of his sons, wife, and other kinsmen, he should say this:
"Within five days, I shall perform the rite for my departure. (Kubjika-tantra 23.101)
But he who acts otherwise is indeed a sinner, a destroyer of his own self;
neither out of distress nor out of anger should one perform the rite of the soul's departure.
If one is unable to protect the body for the sake of fame,
then even a heavy [penalty] must be given by the teacher, having recognized the disciple as possessing the proper characteristics.
But he who bestows [the teaching] otherwise is a guru who violates the [sacred] signs;
for he by whom the fivefold Self has been known within his own body [is a true guru].
For he consists of all sacred fords; indeed, even those fords created by men who have attained perfect success have all established their foundation somewhere within him.

By its power, a place becomes a sacred ford (tīrtha); it is not a sacred ford merely because it is filled with water. Those who are endowed with the awakening of knowledge are capable of accomplishing true knowledge.
Wherever they reside, that place is a sacred site (tīrtha) in the ultimate sense;
such as Vārāṇasī, Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, and likewise Bhairava.
Wherever the Guru is present, there indeed are all sacred fords;
the sacred fords are filled with water, and the gods are made of stone and clay.
Those who know the Self do not consider that to be a sacred ford, even when it has been overrun by the powerful and has come under the influence of a teacher; so do other people.
Even for a knower, no fault exists if the killing of one's own self is performed,
because the Tīrthaṅkara is the Guru when life has been abandoned for the sake of that task.
For he goes to the womb of an animal and experiences the fruit that ends in suffering;
O beloved, at no other time should the transgression of the ritual ascent be performed.

and Jayantī is in the great field (*mahākṣetra*) together with *ḷ*, *ṣā*, and Bhaṭṭārikā.
Vārāhī is thus adorned in the western direction by Tādin;
and in the Mahākṣetra of Caritra, she is accompanied by Aiśā and Kilakilā.
Aindrī, situated in the northwestern corner, is to be worshipped with water for the feet;
and in the great field of Ekāmra, she is Au-vakā together with Kālarātri.
Cāmuṇḍā, established in the northern direction, is to be worshipped with the syllable *yā* and others;
she resides in the great field of Devikoṭṭa, conjoined with *aḥ*, *hlā*, and Bhīṣaṇa.
Lakṣmī and the others, adorned with ornaments, are to be worshipped starting from the northeast;
one should worship Kubjinīśāna, situated in the center, at the letter *kṣa*. (KubjT 24.78)
In the syllable *ḍa*, the Ḍākinī is to be worshipped; likewise, in the syllable *ra*, the Rākṣasī;
in the syllable *la*, the Lākinī; and similarly, in the syllable *ka*, the Kusumālikā.
Know that Śākinī resides in the letter Śa, and Yakṣiṇī is considered to be in the letter Ya;
Bhrāmaṇī is to be worshipped in the center. This is proclaimed as the group of six on the right.
I shall now proclaim the subsequent [teachings] correctly and in due order:
Guhyākhyā, Mahākhyā, Balākhyā, and Maṇicandrikā.
Together with the Mālinī-vidyā, the group of six is known as the "Northern" (uttara);
above that is the lineage of the Siddhas, extending from Mitra onwards to the gurus.
Ādhārīśa is in Oṃkāra; Kuraṅgīśa is in Jālaka;
Cakrīśa is in Pūrṇagiri; and Mathana is in Kāmarūpa.
One should worship the Yoginīs and the Yugas in their proper sequence:
Caṇḍā, Ghaṇṭā, Mahānāsā, Sumukhī, Durmukhī, and Balā.
Revatī is the first, followed by Ghorā, Bhaumyā, Bhīmā, Mahābalā,
Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā.
Mahotkaṭā, Virūpākṣī, Śuṣkā, Ākāśamātṛkā,
Sehārī, Jātahārī, Daṃṣṭrālī, and Śuṣkarevatī.
Pipīlikā, Puṣpahārī, Aśanī, Śaṣpahārikā, Bhadrakālī, Subhadrā, Bhadrabhīmā, and Subhadrikā. (Kubjika Tantra 24.87)
Having worshipped these with the letters beginning with *ka* and likewise the lords of the seats (*pīṭhādhipa*) with the vowels,
O Goddess, one should worship this Siddha-lineage of the Mothers of the Siddhas.
"If one desires long life, this must be guarded with great effort;
it should not be given to those of wicked intellect—such is the command of the Supreme Lord. (Kubjikātantra 24.89)
One should worship with constant effort; of this there is no doubt.
A yogi equal to a practitioner of yoga (yogācāra) should thoroughly worship the mind. (KubjT 24.90)
O Goddess, one should worship this sixfold [rite] three times a day, or once a day, preceded by the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa). KubjT_24.91.
One should worship the goddesses and the Siddhas with the sixteen vowels.

One should worship the seat (pīṭha), the Mistress of the Seat (pīṭheśvarī), the Lord (īśa), along with the Protector of the Seat (pīṭhādhipa-sapālaka), joined with the Goddess Nātha and accompanied by the Goddess Siddha. (KubjT 24.93)
One should worship the fifth seat, situated in the center and accompanied by the four goddesses, joined with the four Siddhas, in due order. (Kubjikātantra 24.94)
The six-limbed arrangement of enjoyments, the row, the five jewels, the secret sixfold [set], as well as the [mantras] beginning with *ḍa*, and thereafter the six locations. (Kubjikāmata 24.95)
This indeed is the Six Yoginīs, and then again the Pentad;
likewise the eightfold group of fields, and the fourfold octad.
Beyond that, another group of six should be worshipped with great effort;
he who knows this possesses fitness, otherwise he is merely a bearer of the name. (Kubjikātantra 24.97)
After that, one should diligently recite the sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa):
namely, Svabhrā, Nirabhrā, Bhūcarī, and likewise Khecarī.
Gocarī and Gaṇamukhī, and the six Yoginīs established in the Kula;
Sūkṣmā, Susūkṣmā, Antimāmṛtā, and Antimā. (Kubjikātantra 24.99)
Starting from Kāmarūpa and the other sites, there are the Yoginīs joined with the Siddhas:
Kamalā, Barbarā, and Mahāntārī as the third.
Laghvinī is the fourth; then there is the one called Bimbā, the group of five elders (vṛddhapañcaka), and those known as Raktā, Karālā, Caṇḍā, and Ucchuṣmā.
The fifth should be known as Khaṇḍikā; these five goddesses have been proclaimed:
Mātaṅgī, Pulindā, Śabarī, and likewise Campakā.
In the middle, however, is the one named Kubjā, adorned with jewel ornaments;
she is indeed the pure [center] of Anāhata as well as Maṇipūraka.
One who knows the reality of the sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa) should worship Svādhiṣṭhāna, Ādhāra, and Pañcaratna; otherwise, one acts in reverse order. (Kubjikātantra 24.104)

In the direction of the worshiper and the object of worship, according to the sequence of the purification of the stages, he is a worthy disciple belonging to the lineage; otherwise, he is a mere bearer of the name.
With various perfumes and flowers—jāva, bandhūka, and pāṭala;
karavīra, kubjakuṇḍa, jāti, mallikā, and campaka.
With *saivala*, blue lotuses, *yūthī* flowers, *sindūra*, and *kiṃśuka* blossoms,
as well as with these and many other fragrant incenses and *guggulu* resins.
With substances such as the left-hand nectar (vāmāmṛta) and so forth, as well as those produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*,
with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and likewise with others combined with wine (*ali*) and grain-liquor (*phalgu*).
With great incenses of flesh, along with parched grain and lamps,
one should thus perform the worship according to the ritual procedure and in accordance with the rules.
Having offered the *argha* in due order with a large conch as the *argha*-vessel,
O Goddess, there is likewise a quartet of mandalas to the east of that.
Having worshipped each one in sequence with yellow flowers,
O Goddess, one should again worship four [deities] to the south with black flowers.
One should worship the four in the north with red flowers;
O Goddess, one should worship the four in the west with white flowers.
Afterwards, a prostration with eight limbs is performed mentally;
thereafter, one should offer a hymn of praise, O Goddess, and that I shall now declare.
Homage be to you, O Mahāmāyā, whose body is subtle, both transcendent and immanent;
who are solitary, the pure self, known as Nāda, and garlanded with Bindus.
And when she has arisen bodilessly within the immovable sustainer of the universe—
Mahākuṇḍalinī, the eternal one, established in the midst of the Haṃsa.
O you who abide in the midst of the moon, sun, and fire; you who pervade the void, both supreme and non-supreme;
you who reside in the form of the syllable Oṃ; you who bear the half of the half of the letter Ha.
Subtler than a hundredth part of a hair-tip, infinite, inexhaustible, and immutable,
resting upon the filament of the lotus at the base of the half-measure of the letter *ha*.
O Great Illusion named Sakala, giver of boons, worshipped by the world,
you who abide within each individual channel and pierce each individual vital point!
O Goddess, when the thirty-eight kalās have been differentiated and have reached the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
[the five faces are] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
These five great pretas stand at your feet;
O Goddess, mother of the three worlds, salutations to you who are the embodiment of Śakti.
O Goddess, you who reside between the iḍā and piṅgalā, whose form is like a lotus fiber, who abide in the center of the bindu, who are curved and possess the luster of a half-moon.
O Gaurī, who appears like a drop of frost, who rests at the *dvādaśānta*,
who is known as Umā, who has entered the heart, and who possesses the splendor of twelve suns.
O Supreme Goddess, you who abide within the void, in that which is called Haṃsa, the sustainer of breath; you who are known as Lambā, moving between the south and the north.
When the *hṛllekhā* has emerged at the tip of the nose, flowing along the central channel, and is established at the root of the palate in supreme bliss; (KubjT 24.124)
When the two sacs of dharma and adharma—gross and subtle—are thoroughly agitated and joined by the friction of the *nāda* and *ghaṇṭikā*, they become endowed with the eight qualities. 24.125.
In the state of the agency of cause and effect, which is triple-void and consists of the form of Nāda;
in that which is both supreme and non-supreme, pure, consciousness, eternal, and firm.
O Goddess who bears all colors, renowned as the secret reality, bodiless one, highly fortunate one, you who carry [beings] across the ocean of saṃsāra! KubjT_24.127
O Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Aparājitā,
who abide in the midst of the seeds of Tumburu— homage to you, the liberator from evil!
O Goddess, she who effects bondage and liberation is established at the end of the sixteen;
she is the one who causes whirling by means of the trident of power, endowed with the great array.
O Bhramaṇī, Bhrāmaṇī, Gaurī, you who set in motion the machine of illusion;
O Goddess Svacchandabhairavī, Krodha-unmattabhairavī!
The Rudras have been proclaimed by you as residing within the form of the fifty phonemes;
O Ruru in the one called Amṛtā, O Caṇḍā, salutations to you, Jñānabhairavī!
I bow to you, O Goddess of the lords of gods, who are fierce with tusks, whose tongue is like lightning, whose eyes are like stars, and who are terrifying yet not terrible in form. KubjT_24.132.
O Jvālāmukhī, O Vegavatī, O Goddess Umā, O Sarasvatī!
O Goddess who possesses the voice of a swan, O Gomukhī, O Śaktimālinī!
O Goddess Kroṣṭukī, Subhagā, Durgā, and likewise Kātyāyanī; those known as Nityaklinnā, Raktā, Ekākṣarā, and Parā. (Kubjikātantra 24.134)
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, as well as Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā, whose face is fearless. (KubjT 24.135)
O Goddess of the gods, you are indeed the Mistress of Yoga, adorned by the eight Kulas;
you are Aindrī, Āgneyī, Yāmyā, Nairṛtyā, and Vāruṇī.
Vāyavyā, Kauberī, and Īśānī are thus proclaimed;
[the sites] Prayāgā, Varuṇā, Kollā, Aṭṭahāsā, and Jayantikā.
In Caritra, Ekāmra, and Devikoṭṭa—thus [the goddess] is eightfold.
Likewise, O Kālī, O Goddess Umā, O Devadūtī, homage be to you!
O Bhadrakālī, Great Goddess, you who hold the skin and the severed head, O terrifying one,
O Mahocchuṣmā, O Great Peaceful One, salutations to you, whose form is Śakti!
"O Great Illusion, at the end of the *svāhā* [utterance]—*bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*—show compassion toward me, your servant, who seeks knowledge; O Mahāmāyā, I desire to know this."
The person who recites this hymn at the three junctions of the day obtains all desired objects and becomes beloved by women.
Thus ends the *Śivaśaktisamarasamahāmāyāstava*.
The venerable Kubjikā said: O Maheśāna, how is the *pavitrārohaṇa* (the rite of ascending the sacred thread) performed for those born of the *Kula*?
"At what time, how, and for what purpose should it be performed? Tell me, O Lord. (KubjT 24.142)
The illustrious Bhairava said:
"O Goddess, O highly fortunate one, in former times when the Ocean of Milk was churned by the gods and the asuras,
there [arose] the powerful Netro, the son of Kaśyapa."
O auspicious lady, when he has been cast into the churning pit and is unconscious from the sleep of poison,
he is unable to dwell at the bottom of that pit during the rainy season.
Therefore, O Goddess, I was gratified by that pure-souled one;
for a thousand divine years, I, possessed of great strength, subsisted on air alone.
"I am pleased with him, O Goddess of Gods; what should be done as previously stated?
Then he stood before my feet on the ground like a staff.
"O Hara, during the rainy season I am unable to dwell at the base of that tree.
Then, O Goddess, he too was lifted from the ground by me with both hands.
O Goddess of beautiful countenance, he was worn upon my matted locks on my head;
thereafter, O Queen of the Gods, he was worn pure upon the heads of all.
Ten billion acts of worship are equal to the performance of the Pavitrārohaṇa rite;
otherwise, initiation is in vain, knowledge is in vain, and even the propitiation of the Guru is in vain.
"O Goddess, the King of Serpents indeed seizes [the merit] from one who does not perform the *pavitraka* rite; the exertion of such a person is in vain. (Kubjika-tantra 24.150)
Therefore, O beloved, those born of noble family should perform this with every effort during the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, when the sun is situated in Gemini.
If that is not obtained, it should be performed when the sun is situated in Cancer;
it should be carried out without conflict until the full moon of Tula.
A golden thread, fine and tripled, is prescribed there;
it is said to consist of one hundred strands, with a knot at every fourth part, according to the teacher’s view.
For the one worthy of worship, two more [mudrās] are to be performed; for the one who returns the worship, four more;
for Śiva, seven more are taught; and for the Yogīśīs, six more.
One should perform that for every seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) as being six more;
O Dear One, one hundred and eight sandals (pādukās) should be fashioned.
There are indeed thirty-eight knots or fifty conceptualizations;
that which was taught for the Guru by eight more shall likewise apply to the Vaṭuka.
Alternatively, in the absence [of silver], the thread may be made of cloth;
having taken a white thread, it should be tripled and then tripled again.
With that [thread], one should prepare one hundred and eight strands for the Great Penance (mahātapa);
twenty-four [strands] for those beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha, and sixteen for those beginning with Ajeśa.
The four Vidyāmātṛs are with the eight Mahākālas;
the six-thread [mantra] belongs to the group of the six beginning with Ḍā, and the eight-thread [mantra] belongs to the eight Kulas.
The knots should be made according to the beauty [of the occasion] and according to one's capacity;
the *pavitraka* should be prepared with *gorocanā* or else with saffron.
Having thus accomplished it and performed the sacrifice, O fair-faced one,
the *pavitraka* should be offered at the conclusion of the worship by one endowed with devotion.
O fair-faced one, singing and dancing should be performed here;
or rather, the *hindola* [swing] should be performed with a slow tempo (*mandatāra*).
Those who have attained the state of *samayin* should be honored with great effort;
all of that [practice] must be performed during the four-month period (*cāturmāsya*), O fair-faced one.
O Goddess, O Beloved, by performing this for seven days, or three, or even just one day for the sake of heroic play, it becomes fully accomplished.
O lady of excellent hips, having performed that purification, one should ask for forgiveness;
O Goddess, [this yields] the fruit of many sacrifices as well as the fruit of many sacred fords.
O Goddess of the gods, they do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of the dharma of giving;
it is supremely purifying, meritorious, and free from all defects.
Therefore, O Goddess of beautiful countenance, this task must be performed by those born of noble families;
for the transgression of the rules is an act devoid of the prescribed ritual.
O fair-faced one, those defects come to an end through this purifying rite;
it should be performed every year according to the extent of one's means.
O Bhairavī, it should be fashioned with *kāśa* and *kuśa* grass by one endowed with devotion;
one must not practice stinginess regarding wealth here in this Kula tradition.
An action performed with deceit shall not lead to the state of accomplishment;
knowing this, O lady of excellent limbs, one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth.
The grasping of that [mantra], as well as worship and the supreme investiture with the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa)—all this has been fully explained; what else do you ask?
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Installation of the Purification Thread and the Worship of the Planets," in the *Śrīkubjikāmata*, according to the tradition of the *Kulālika*. [Next:
