The Goddess said:
O Bhairava, please grant me the favor [of explaining] the ritual procedure for the mandalas.
"By what means, O Lord, may I know this? Please explain it according to the prescribed method."
The illustrious Bhairava said:
The mandala has been declared to be the essence; its fruit is the supreme and the non-supreme.
Because it takes up that which transcends restraint (yama), it is therefore celebrated as the mandala.
In the syllable *ma* are all the Mothers; in the syllable *ḍa*, the host of Ḍāmarīs;
and in the syllable *la*, the group of Lākīnīs; by these, the Maṇḍala is thus described.
In the syllable *ma* is the self, and in the syllable *ḍa* is the host of *khecarīs*;
in the syllable *la* is the group of *bhūcarīs*: by these, the maṇḍala is proclaimed.
The deity who resides in the syllable *ma* is held to be Śakti in the syllable *ḍa*;
in the syllable *la* is the sixfold emanation; therefore, it is celebrated as the maṇḍala.
One should know that the letter *ma* is the Śiva-principle (*śivatattva*) and the letter *ḍa* is the Knowledge-principle (*vidyātattva*);
the letter *la*, however, is proclaimed as the Self-principle (*ātmatattva*), and by it the mandala is formed.
One should know Śiva to be in the syllable *ma*, the Supreme Goddess (*parameśvarī*) in the syllable *ḍa*,
and it is proclaimed that the seven crores of mantras reside in the syllable *la*.
In the syllable *ma* there are five causes; in *ḍa*, however, are the *parāparā*;
in *la* are the five *aparā*; therefore, it is proclaimed as the maṇḍala.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—these are said to be the maṇḍala; therefore, it is called a maṇḍala.
All the planets, the guardians of the directions, the nāgas, and indeed Bhairava and the others, remain merged within the maṇḍala; therefore, it possesses supreme excellence.
The path, beginning with Ananta and ending with Śiva, is proclaimed to be sixfold;
for that [path] resides within the maṇḍala, and therefore the maṇḍala is all-pervasive.
Since there is nothing superior to the mandala because of its all-pervasive nature,
therefore the mandala should be worshipped by those who seek the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
Thus has the chapter on the mandala been taught in the Kubjikāmata;
O Goddess, one should perform the circumambulation clockwise and the dismissal counter-clockwise.
O Goddess, in the presence of the illustrious one, and likewise in the presence of the Guru,
one should then carefully examine the well-known Jyeṣṭhā with great effort.
This question, which has come down in due order, consists of twenty-seven divisions;
it is the intense vision of those whose ignorance is of three kinds and six types.
One should construct the mandala for those who are devoted, affectionate, peaceful, and free from hypocrisy and deceit; otherwise, it will produce contrary results.
And this is the sequence for his worship: having placed one's knee upon the ground, one should perform the sweeping on a pure and sprinkled surface.
Having rotated the palm of the right hand over the mandala created with water,
one should smear it with sandalwood and other substances, provided with a profusion of beautiful flowers.
Having offered that threefold arghya, combined with ritual substances, according to the procedure for sacrifice,
the disciple should perform worship of his own primordial self (purātman) with perfumes, incense, and other offerings.
Having worshipped that [mandala] on all sides, provided with the sixfold ritual arrangement,
one should then praise the lotus-feet of the Guru with devotion through hymns and other such means in due order.
Thereafter, having prostrated with devotion purified threefold, and having risen by his permission,
one who desires the fruits of enjoyment and liberation should bear [the teaching] upon his head.
The disciple should respectfully offer flowers at the feet of the Guru,
perform the lustration ceremony with great devotion, and then present auspicious articles.
From afar, by way of circumambulation, or indeed standing at the side on the festival days, one should bow to the Lord with devotion; such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Having smelled the flowers, one should release them; having taken them away, there is no lack of flowers.
Thus has the procedure for the mandala been taught, as well as the sequence for the ritual of worshiping the Lord.
The disciple who performs this sequence with devotion according to the Kubjikā-mata shall,
by the grace of the feet of the Master, further obtain the divine command (divyājñā).
This maṇḍala has been explained by me to you exactly as it is.
Now speak, O Goddess of Gods; what else shall I tell you?
Śrī Kubjikā said:
O Lord, how are the fivefold selves situated, and which one is Śiva?
O Lord, what are their duties, and what is their established measure?
The illustrious Bhairava said:
"O Goddess, you ask most skillfully about the expansion of qualities;
O auspicious one, I shall relate that which causes wonder, in due order."

The Supreme, the Both-Supreme-and-Non-supreme, the Accomplished, the Well-known, whose nature is the *pudgala*—I shall describe him according to the indication of his stations; listen, O lady of excellent complexion! (Kubjika-tantra 25.3)
The Supreme Self is established at a distance of one hundred crores;
however, that which is both supreme and non-supreme (parāpara) is to be known at ninety-six crores.
Established by the measure of eighty-four [crores], the Self indeed abides;
situated in the midst of thirty-six crores, he is renowned as the Lord of Causes (Kāraṇeśvara).
Established as a person consisting of forty-eight [units],
he should be understood as being playful, according to the distinction between the higher and the lower.
Mounted upon the well-known neck and struck by the perfected charioteer,
he goes and is led wherever [he desires] through the vision of the higher and the lower.
Designated as an atom and constrained within the activity of karma,
he is sluggish in bearing the burden of his own nature along the path of the left and other routes.
The cart, overcome by its own nature, breaks apart and perishes upon the ox;
there the driver weeps, while the one who sees both the higher and the lower looks on.
Having ascended the path beginning with the left, he travels through the rivers, oceans, streams, and lakes;
indeed, he beholds their central regions, such as Varṣaṇa and the rest.
If one whose burden is overcome by phlegm should see the game of vehicles,
the person-self (pudgalātman) shall go there, impelled by the charioteer who has attained perfection.
Overwhelmed by the burden of the bile-humors and directed onto the path of Jyeṣṭhā,
he is situated either in the midst of a mass of flames or within a single blazing city.
But when overcome by hunger and thirst, thieves seize them on that path;
they experience the fury of battle and the embrace and kisses of women. (Kubjaka-tantra 25.13)
For this kingdom is indeed beset by calamity and filled with the violation of others' wives;
yet he who acts as the charioteer there is slain and put to death.
While the lower and higher [energies] weep, the higher one indeed beholds there;
resorting to the path of the eldest (jyeṣṭhā), it proceeds by means of manifold methods.
Overwhelmed by the burden of phlegm and bile, and further assailed by wind,
this [being] is led along a terrible path and goes toward the mouth of Khecarī.
One shall behold the worlds from heaven down to the nether regions (pātāla), the realms of the Piśācas, the city of the Vidyādharas, and flowering groves and forests.
The assembly of the circle of Yoginīs was filled with the sounds of dancing and singing;
he had attained the royal consecration, with the parasol raised and the fly-whisks waved.
The person, whose self is overwhelmed by the burden of wind and bile, stands upon the path;
the charioteer perceives everything, but it is another who experiences [the results].
Or else, overcome by a burden of wind, he goes and is led far away;
terrified by the sun, he traverses the uneven mountain as if it were level.
Even while limping, he is broken with effort and dies;
or else, overcome by wind and phlegm, he is driven by another charioteer.
He sees a path entirely infested with snakes, tigers, and wolves;
he is devoured by the snakes, or he dies, or even is carried away.
In this way, the person-self (pudgala-ātman), well-established and dependent upon the aggregates,
is joined with a proven charioteer and follows the control of the higher and the lower.
Impelled by that Supreme Self, he sports with all things moving and unmoving;
thus has been clearly explained the definitive teaching on the Supreme Self, together with its secret.
That which has not been explained to anyone is the illusory nature of the world;
those who do not find the Śrīmata fall into error at every step.
In the space of the beyond (parākāśa) is indeed the supreme Self; in the space of mantra is the intermediate (parāpara);
in the space of power (śaktyākāśa) one is well-perfected; and when the state of the word (padabhāva) is reached, the intellect becomes fully realized.
Established in the path of the elemental ether, the individual self is nothing at all;
these five have been taught by Śambhu, while Śambhu himself is the uniform flavor everywhere.
The Lord of the Sixth is supreme, the manifest omniscient one; he is both transcendent and immanent, devoid of characteristics and beyond designation, for he is Śambhu through his grace.
Śrī Kubjikā said:
"Having been authorized and consecrated, a hero who desires the state of a hero and is a practitioner of mantra should observe the vow of the Vidyā; tell me how that is to be done."

The illustrious Bhairava said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme vow of the Vidyā. One may be one with matted hair, shaven-headed, or wearing a topknot; one may be smeared with ashes, a celibate student, or a graduate who has completed his studies. *Kubjikā-tantra* 25.30.
Whether established in a vow or not established in a vow, in whatever state he may be, he bestows success;
likewise, whether wearing the five mudrās, devoted to ashes, or naked as the sky.
Whether wearing rags or bark garments, or adorned with all kinds of ornaments;
whether soiled or clean, or decorated with clothes and jewelry.
"In whatever attire the supreme practitioner conducts himself, that very thing is declared to be his vow; such is the certainty of the scripture. (Kubjika-tantra 25.33)
Whatever ornament he wears or whatever he speaks with his voice—that is declared to be his conduct and his mantras as well; of this there is no doubt.
The supreme power called Vidyā is established in two divisions:
she who is the presiding principle devoid of the power of consciousness (cicchakti), and she who is auspicious, colorless yet abiding within the phonemes.
O beloved, by means of that through which one who abides in the castes attains [liberation], that is the vow of knowledge;
having performed the practice, the entire world is established within the castes and those beyond the castes.

"Vow" (vratam) is said to mean "state of being" (bhāva); by that, it is known as the "vow of knowledge" (vidyā-vrata). *Cic* [is derived from] the root *ci*, meaning "to accumulate," while *vida* means "knowledge"; thus, it is that which awakens the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). (Kubjikā-tantra 25.37)
Those devoted to the observance see a mass of colorless and red light, the embodiment of the Vidyā-mantra; he is called one who has mastered the Vidyā. (Kubjikātantra 25.38)
Because it awakens the power of consciousness from the immeasurable seven thousand million vidyās, that which is colorless has attained the state of being colored.
Kuṇḍalinī alone is declared to be the supreme, whose form is knowledge (vidyā).
Therefore, O Goddess, the auspicious vow of the enclosure of knowledge has been proclaimed. (KubjT 25.40)
He who proceeds on the path of knowledge through the ritual actions prescribed by the scriptures—
meditation, worship, recitation, fire-offerings, and the observance of the pledges— KubjT_25.41.
This is declared to be the vow of knowledge (vidyā-vrata); it is not otherwise, O Vīranāyikā.
Knowledge should be understood as residing in the womb (yoni), moving to the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta).
O beloved, at all the places of observance, he performed the vow of knowledge (vidyāvrata);
[therein reside] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
These are indeed the stations of the vow where she moves in her supreme state;
having known that supreme station, he is one who has truly fulfilled the observance of the vidyā-vow.
O Goddess, there are five mudrās, and from that arises the fivefold cause;
adorned with them, one should abide in the heart, established in the five mudrās.
Adorned with these, the practitioner, resorting to a sacred field (*kṣetra*), should wander about—
in a cremation ground, a forest, a well, a garden, or even in a temple.
In an empty Rājagṛha, on a mountain peak,
at a crossroads, at the junction of three paths, in a village street, or likewise on the shore of the great ocean, the mantra-practitioner [should perform the rite].
On the bank of a confluence of rivers, or at a solitary tree, or in a forest;
likewise at a single liṅga, or in a grove, or by means of eight fields in succession.
Prayāga, Varuṇā, Kolā, Bhīmanādā, Jayantikā,
Caritre, Aṃraka, and Koṭīvarṣa as the eighth.
A practitioner desiring the siddhi of the yoginīs should wander about with these;
holding a khaṭvāṅga and observing silence, he should always wander with speed.
The hand-drum, the noose, the khaṭvāṅga, the trident, as well as the shield,
the iron arrow, the knife, the discus, the goad, the mace, and the bow.
The mace, the dagger, the spear, as well as the staff and the water-pot—
these are the most excellent weapons that one should carry at the time of ritual practice.
The excellent vow, numbering as many as the weapons, consists of a rite performed every five days;
the practitioner of mantra should observe it for twelve days, or from the beginning of a fortnight or a month.
For six months, or a year, or two years, or indeed three;
likewise four, five, six, seven, or even eight [years]. (Kubjika-tantra 25.54)
Whether for nine, twelve, five, or eleven years, the mantra-practitioner should practice for twelve years; even one who has killed a Brahmin attains accomplishment.
O Goddess of the gods, within a single year he is worshipped by the lords of the mandalas;
[his] country, servants, city, and village, along with his ministers and leaders, [are likewise honored].
O beautiful one, leader of the gods, the king together with his excellent harem becomes submissive;
and after two years, the daughters of the yakṣas are accomplished.
Three times a year, he beholds those auspicious Daitya women from the seven netherworlds,
who are intoxicated with passion and whose eyes are rolling with lust.
Moving with the gait of an elephant in rut, possessing inexhaustible youth,
they become agitated at the sight of the lord of practitioners and instantly surrender their lives.
One should accomplish the worlds beginning with Brahmā in four, five, and six [years];
O lady of excellent hips, those established up to Rudra are accomplished in the seventh year.
"They are accomplished for the lord of practitioners," thus it is proclaimed in the scripture;
in the eighth [chapter] is that called Īśvara, and in the ninth is Sadāśiva.
In the tenth [house], having become a school, it plays greatly in the sky;
O Goddess, in the tenth and eleventh, it is endowed with twelve qualities.
Endowed with the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest, he goes together with the sky-farers;
for the yogi is imperishable, invincible, all-pervading, and auspicious, and he sports at will.
O beloved, this fruit for one established in the vow has indeed been described by me;
now listen to how it comes about through the path of yoga.
The cremation ground is said to be the house, and the body is proclaimed to be the home;
yet one whose mind is fixed on the cremation ground wanders about without rest.
The body is said to be "kaṃ"; at its end, one who is established in mantra intensely leads [the breath] and perceives the world of speech, including all that is moving and unmoving.
O beloved, that which is situated at the end of the body is called the forest (kānana) by him;
the mind is designated as the well, for it forms many volitions.
Therein, the field-dweller (kṣetrī) proceeds as the support; therefore it is renowned as the "well" (kūpa).
It is active, situated at the navel of the mind, in the center of all living beings.
"Neti" is that which has attained the supreme; therefore it is called Udyāna.
It constantly bestows the nectar situated in the sky within the body.

And because one wanders at the end of the lineage through the bonds of the self consisting of dharma and adharma, O Goddess, for that reason it is always declared that the embodied being is the family of the gods (devakula). KUBJATĀNTRA 25.70.
Furthermore, the King is designated as the Self (ātman) on the thirty-sixth path;
he is the Lord, abounding in qualities such as sound and the like, residing within the treasury of the mind.
When that [state] is established, they abide; with that very [state], one goes.
Always engaged in the state beyond mind (*unmanatva*), it is described as the "mind" (*manas*) that is empty. *Kubjikātantra* 25.72.
Therefore, O Beloved, Rājagṛha is empty in the state of the Transmental (unmanatva);
one should take hold of the peak of that mountain, which is the mouth of the Guru.
By that synonym, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, the mountain peak is remembered;
it becomes the crossroads, O Goddess, where Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrikā reside.
The wandering [deity] associated with Ambikā consists of the individual soul;
by that, the group of four is proclaimed, and this is declared to be the Path.
O Kuleśvarī, the path is said to be the three channels beginning with Iḍā;
situated on this triple path, he wanders eternally, performing coming and going.
He who, abiding in the single state at the junction of the three paths, performs [this practice], attains success.
The village is said to be the body, and the self is remembered as the body. (Kubjikātantra 25.77)
The Ālaya is the abode of all sentient beings, the source of pleasure and pain, high and low;
it moves up and down like the foundation of a street, the Lord of the World.
By that, the channel (nāḍī) beginning with Brahmā is remembered as the "street" (rathyā) of the Self;
the bank is declared to be the "shore" (taṭa), and the flow of the ocean is called the "outflow" (sindhūccāra).
At the end of suffering, there is the shore beyond dissolution known as the ocean;
there, at the end of speech, is the pervasive Lord Śiva, the supreme cause.
The practitioner of mantra remains constantly there, where the practice is revealed;
it is the supreme Kuṇḍalinī who resounds within the internal support.
That river, having become a flood, flows eternally within the ocean of the sky;
its union with the Supreme is proclaimed as the state of Unmanā.
Their union is declared to be the river;
the shore, however, belongs to the one who is present there, she who is the all-pervasive, supreme power (vibhvī parā kalā).
That which has transcended it becomes all-pervasive; this is declared to be the "riverbank.
A single tree is fully described as such, and here it is called the "single power" (ekā śaktiḥ).
The tree is said to be the sense organ; the tree is remembered as power (śakti).
It has gone to destruction in the supreme sky, which is mindless and free from affliction.
Therefore, O Goddess, I have declared that through the practice of the Single Tree, there is but one supreme reality—the all-pervading Lord who is the support of the *liṅga*, O Beloved. (KubjT 25.86)
One should wander day and night, without rest, again and again; this is declared to be the "Single Liṅga" (ekaliṅga). Now I shall describe to you the "Ṣaṇḍa."
The heart is said to be the lake, and the lotus there indeed has eight petals;
O Goddess of Gods, by means of the udāna breath, it is in bloom, and that [lotus] is the sun.
The primordial power, Manonmanī, who is called Haṃsā, resorts to and delights in the lotus situated in the heart, which is centered upon the individual soul (pudgala). KubjT_25.89.
That has been described as the *ṣaṇḍa* in the scripture; now I shall describe the fields (*kṣetra*) to you.
A field is called that which is supremely peaceful, the body conjoined with reality (*tattva*). (Kubjikātantra 25.90)
The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) wanders eternally, established in the movement through the eight locations;
it is for this reason, O Goddess, that these are proclaimed as the "Eight Fields" (kṣetrāṣṭaka). 25.91.
Those which are pīṭhas are the kṣetras, and the kṣetras are declared to be the pīṭhas;
however, the designations of names and synonyms differ from treatise to treatise.
Prayāga is situated in the navel, Varuṇā in the region of the heart;
Kolāgiri is located in the throat, and Bhīmanāda in the palate.
Those who have realized the Self should know that the place called Jayantī is located in the Bindu, Caritraka in the Nāda, and Ekāmra in the center of Śakti. (Kubjikātantra 25.94)
That which has come from the mouth of the Guru is declared as the eighth, namely Koṭivarṣa;
these places have been described by me as pertaining to the inner self and dependent upon the individual soul.
O Dear One, as long as one does not thus discover the internal seat (pīṭha), by which the eternal [Lord] residing in the heart-center wanders constantly, [so long does one remain bound]. KubjT_25.96.
How could there be any establishment of that [duality] for one who, though wandering through the three worlds,
perceives neither external nor internal existence, nor the distinction between the internal and the external?
O Dear One, external seats are proclaimed for the purpose of worldly engagement;
but when one perceives the pure internal state with the mind, [then the external is transcended].
Then, however, one sees subtle rays of light externally;
they provide a gathering, or else the sacrificial pap according to the rite for bound souls.
They bestow the oral tradition or even reveal the sacred site;
however, if one should wander the earth with an impure disposition, [the result is different].
O Goddess, it does not grant its vision to the mind anywhere;
and even while seeing, O Mistress of the Gods, though they look, they do not see.
The goddesses possess mixed characteristics; they cannot be known [individually] when combined.
Their power is declared to be manifest only through their collective grace.

In every village, as well as in the forest, in the city, at the crossroads, in the capital, in the hamlet, in the marketplace, and likewise in the sacred seats (pīṭha), the fields (kṣetra), and the woods; KubjT_25.103.
And likewise in the gardens and groves previously mentioned,
rays of the nature of knowledge arise in every place.
O fair-hipped one, they are said to exist in earth, water, fire, air, and space; their number is not known.
Indeed, they arise in many ways according to the division of their seats;
they are constantly devoted to food and drink, and they sport even among the lowest castes.
Therefore, O Goddess, I have described the sacred seats (pīṭhas) according to their external form:
they know the house of a courtesan as the seat named Prayāga, and Varuṇā as Sauṇḍikī.
Kollā is Kaivartikī, while Khaṭṭakī is Aṭṭahāsa;
one should know that Jayantī is Kandukī, and Caritra is the house of Rajakī.
Ekāmraka, Śippī, Koṭākhyā, and Kauṣaṭī are the fields situated in the east; the Knower of Wisdom should perceive them as such. (Kubjika-tantra 25.109)
The external division has been described; now hear concerning the householder.
Prayāga is in the Middle Country, where the Varuṇā river takes its stand at the gateway.
Kolāpura is Kañjinī, Cullī is Aṭṭahāsaka;
Caritra is to be known as Peṣaṇī, and Ekāmra is remembered as Kaṇḍanī.
Devikoṭṭa and Gharaṭṭa are secondary fields; hear now of others:
Vardhamānī, Upālambhī, Dehalī, and likewise Muśala.
If one desires prosperity for oneself, one should not touch with one's foot these items in their respective order: a bed, a winnowing basket, a millstone, and a water-pot.
One should avoid from afar the wind from a broom or a winnowing basket;
for [the obstructors], being carried by the wind, enter [the site] thinking there is a vulnerability in the practitioner.
The Siddhayoginīs take away obstacles; therefore, for the sake of spiritual welfare, one should grasp the auspicious Kaṇikā, known as Śiravā, which is the abode of Kālikālā.
Resorting to Kālañjara and Mahākāla as the established locations of the sacred fields (kṣetra),
he [perceives] the multitude of seats (pīṭha) and secondary seats (upapīṭha) situated in cities, in houses, and within the body.
It should be known that this bestows the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation through the *cumbaka* alone.
Thus, O lady of excellent vows, the sacred seats (*pīṭhas*) and fields (*kṣetras*) have been described externally.
A wise person who knows the mantras should always travel to these places, which are to be constantly honored; he should always satisfy them with various kinds of food, edibles, grains, and drinks.
The stability of these [practices] and the immeasurability of those yogins come to pass here;
of this there is no doubt, for they are indeed bestowers of boons upon the practitioner.
For the practitioner who follows the prescribed path and observes the vows and pledges, the goddesses, when gratified and honored, indeed grant [their boons] within six months. (Kubjikātantra 25.120)
O Dear One, after having satisfied the Guru, the best of practitioners should deliberate [upon this].
Now, I shall further explain the terminology of those who speak of the flow of the channels.
I shall tell you how both the internal and the external are known in their true nature; listen, O long-eyed one.
One should internalize the external; the practice of vows is the means of accomplishment.
When this is done, success will arise—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
I shall describe the khaṭvāṅga, the supreme means for attaining the power of moving through the air;
listen to how it comes to pass from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head. *Kubjikāmatatantra* 25.124.
O lady of beautiful hips, because he acts like a bed (khaṭvā) upon his veins and all other limbs, even down to the major and minor members of the body, he is therefore called Khaṭvāṅgin.
One should always abide in silence, with the supreme and the non-supreme hidden within the heart;
by that, O noble lady, one is to be known as a "silent sage" (maunī) amidst all states of being.
It wanders through the body with speed, without rest, again and again; therefore, I have described this wandering of the *pudgala* as "vega" (impulse). (Kubjika-tantra 25.127)
I shall explain the hand-drum (ḍamaruka) as it is described in the scripture:
the one called Amā is the supreme, subtle digit that carries the nectar of immortality.
The Self moves within that drop; when the drop emits its sound, the Great Souls situated in the Visarga say, "Speak! KubjT_25.129.
Therefore, the hand-drum (ḍamaruka) is said to exist in that state which is beyond the mind and free from affliction;
for one in whom Kuṇḍalinī, whose form is illusory, resides at the navel.
This has been specified as the noose; now hear about the sword.
Stationed in space, it cuts the nooses, while the bewildering [weapon] acts with the weapon of emission.
O Kuleśvarī, she who is stainless like a sword has entered into the midst of the sky;
that imperishable power attains union with Brahman.
Therefore, O Leader of the Gods, this weapon is called the sword (khaḍga);
it is the one supreme Śakti alone, moving in three paths within the circle of the wheel.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and likewise Raudrī, whose natures are will, knowledge, and action—
these are known as the trident and the three paths, representing the three powers in their proper sequence.
O Dear One, she who has the nature of space, who moves through the sky, who is peaceful and stainless, wanders;
therefore, the name "Kheṭaka" is established at the end of the twelve.
The *nārā* and the utterance of *śakti*, established as the nature of the instruments,
pierce the five causes indeed by means of *nirodhinī*.
Therefore, O fair-faced one, it is called *nārāca* by way of synonym;
for it is the *kartarī*, the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), by which it cuts through the fetters.
That supreme and most subtle digit (kalā) is the ultimate awakener of mantras; it should be known by the practitioner as the scissor (kartarī) in the form of the cutter (kartṛ). 25.138.
She moves at the end of the twelve [fingers], and in due order she releases the principles (tattvas);
she who is Parāparā, established like a goad, revolves eternally within the wheel.
The Goddess, residing in every limb and situated both externally and internally,
constantly performs her activity while one is seated as well as when lying down.
O Dear One, relying on the positions of running, leaping, obstructing, and the goad,
the sound situated in the state of the mace moves upward in the form of a line.
Having pierced that, there is an upward movement called Muṣala toward Sadāśiva;
it is indeed called Manā, the bow, by which one pierces the supreme target.
Having filled [the vessel] with the supreme organ of mind and sight, together with the emission (visarga),
by means of the instrument ending in *phaṭ* and abiding in the emission with a beautiful resonance.
By means of this [mantra], which is purified by two seasons and situated within the forest,
and by means of this concluding instrument, the Kaṭṭārikā is both supreme and non-supreme.
O fair-eyed one, through the *gadā* [mudrā], one attains union with reality (*tattvasāyojya*).
Indeed, when one has gone to the supreme aperture (*parā randhra*), it bestows auspicious nectar (*amṛta*). (KubjT 25.145)
But those who have gone with the mace do not return;
for power, by virtue of its inherent nature, always leads the self toward itself.
But when that state is pierced by the application of yoga through power (śakti) by the Lord of the Gods,
there is a straight line like a staff, the imperishable state of the end of sound (nādānta).
O observer of good vows, one should proceed by that path with the staff-bearer;
it is known as the body (kaṃ), situated in the form of a circle.
In this regard, O lady of excellent hips, the path must be purified by the wise;
she who is the supreme purity beginning with Kula is situated within the heart of the entire path.
Therefore, O auspicious lady, this has been told; it is known as the *kamaṇḍalu*.
These subtle weapons have thus been clearly explained by way of their synonyms.
O Goddess, I have explained to you the subtle *kalā* residing in the practitioner of the pledge (*samāyin*), the most subtle leader, according to the division of the higher and the lower.
I shall describe the auspicious characteristics of the female messengers (dūtīs) externally; likewise, hear now the definitive [teaching] regarding them within the inner self.
A mother, a daughter, a sister, one born together, as well as one born later, a washerwoman, a leather-worker, a woman of the Mātaṅga caste, and a woman of the highest caste. KubjT_25.153.
One should partake of food, drink, and edibles together with the Śaktis;
the twice-born and the low-born alike shall eat the sacrificial porridge (caru) in one place.
The practitioner himself must perform that which he desires for supreme accomplishment.
The venerable Kubjikā said: "O God, what has been told is base and improper for those who speak according to the scriptures;
O Supreme Lord, this conduct which has been described is intended for the bound souls (paśus)."
O Great Lord, when that indeed occurs for ascetics, it is truly a marvel.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
"Excellent, O Goddess of great wisdom! Out of affection for you, O leader of the gods, I shall explain this most difficult question in brief."
The Power (Śakti), established like a mother, is the form of the womb of the universe;
for within her everything has arisen—the entire realm of speech, including both the moving and the unmoving.
Therefore, she is renowned as "Mātā" (Mother) and is called the Supreme Goddess;
she is the source of emergence and the daughter because she milks the world.
The daughter is the second, and she is called the sister;
she is of the nature of the *bhaga*, supreme and subtle, not fashioned by anyone else.
Arising from herself and born of her own accord, she is therefore called the Innate (sahajā) digit;
abiding within all beings, the supreme (parā) one exists as that which reaches the end.
And standing before them was a certain supreme goddess born of the lowest caste;
O Umā, she was the washerwoman Mahāntī, entirely free from passion and darkness.
She who moves about, colored by that very limb which is made of skin, is the one called Carma-kārī; she is also called Mātaṅgī.
Mātaṅgī is said to be the messenger (dūtī) who always and eternally resides within the self, situated on the path at the end of the song; likewise, she is called Agrajanmī.
Among all the scriptures, she who has arisen as the foremost is the leader;
there can be nothing else there, for she is the primordial power, Manonmanī.
She is proclaimed as the First-born (Agrajanmā), for she indeed flows with immortality;
O Goddess, she is called Śakti by another name, possessing the attributes of that [First-born]. KUBJIKĀ-TANTRA 25.166.
O Dear One, those fools who practice without knowing the power born of the body, which resides in many places,
are declared to be mere beasts.
O Goddess, those who mock the Śiva-vow are unworthy of company and should not be spoken to;
one must not share food or drink with them.
Thus disciplined, one should always remain with a mind delighted by *madirā*;
for *madirā* is the Supreme Power (*parā śakti*), by whom the three worlds are enchanted.
For that state of equality with bliss is accomplished for one whose mind is intoxicated by wine;
there is no doubt about this, just as Bhairava has declared. (Kubjika-tantra 25.170)

For the yogin who is satisfied by the nectar of knowledge and has accomplished his purpose, there is nothing whatsoever left to be done; if there is anything still to be done, he is not a knower of reality.
Now I shall further explain another state that awakens knowledge:
Ghoṣaṇī, Piṅgalā, Vidyunmālā, and Candriṇī.
The goddess Mano’nugā, Sukṛtā, Saumyā, Nirañjanā, Nirālambā, and another, Mahābalā. (Kubjikā-tantra 25.173)
Helā, Lolā, Līlā, and Bodhābodhavatī—
these are declared to be the stainless, manifest Mothers.
Bestowers of the accomplishment of command within the lineage of the Accomplishment of Command (Ājñāsiddhi-kula) are Ghoṣaṇī, Ghoṣamārgasthā, Śikhā, Dhūmrā, and Piṅgalā. (Kubjikātantra 25.175)
At night it illuminates the white [light] and is called "the garland of lightning";
together with the moon within the womb of the moon, it is the twilight-point (sandhyā-bindu) that follows the mind.
When the eyes are closed, that which is drunk is declared by the virtuous to be the gentle sound of Kaṃsa,
as well as the stainless bell.
The one called Haṃsā is indeed supportless, while Kiṅkiṇī is of great power;
she arises in the region of the anus and always bestows accomplishment.
On the path of sound, that which is called the swan is said to be "play" (helā);
the sound within that is proclaimed by the name "unsteady" (lolā).

Līlā is said to be the atomic (āṇavā) [power], which bestows the state of moving through the sky; she who possesses both consciousness and unconsciousness is indeed Cītkṛtā, located in the region of the ears.
They call the Self "the swan" (haṃsa), while the awakener is the form of Māyā; Kuṇḍalinī is fully described as Rudra-śakti, and the drop (bindu) is the point. 25.181.
He who is seen in the sky, resplendent with a form of light,
illuminating the vault of heaven with the shape of an unbroken orb.
That is declared to be immovable, established by way of its immovability;
these states have been fully described as they arise in succession.
O Kubjikā, for one who knows the supreme state, who understands the beyond, who is well-guarded, and who honors the guru, success comes swiftly; it is not otherwise—this is my word.
Just as one experiences the happiness obtained from a father, that very happiness is enjoyed by oneself;
the happiness by which death occurs here in this world is called meditative absorption (dhyāna).
The venerable Bhairava said:
"O lady of excellent hips, all this which was difficult to attain has been made manifest.
You, moreover, having descended [as an incarnation], must fully illuminate the flood of the Krama."
Having become a guardian of that which is to be well-guarded, worship the Krama and become a destroyer of enemies.
O Kubjā, you who are supreme and the mother of the great flood, I have been impelled by you; you are Kubjā, the supreme curver, and I am yours, while you are mine again.
The fourfold sequence taught by you is the path of the Krama; its sequence is indeed as it has come down to me, and the supreme flood of the Krama has been received as a command, O sinless one.
This Pārameśvara Tantra is one hundred crores in extent;
indeed, its divisions and subdivisions will be manifold.
In this Kalpa, O lady of excellent limbs, there exists the characteristic compendium of the Sūtras consisting of twenty-four thousand verses; however, it is not indeed manifest.
"But, O blessed lady, you must perform [this] in the four seats;
however, reveal it unknown [to others], so that it may remain most secret. (KubjT 25.191)
O Goddess, this most wonderful tantra is exceedingly difficult to find;
in whatever land it remains, that land shall become a partaker of enjoyment.
How much more so when he who dwells within the city, residing in the heart as the householder, abides as its Lord; for him, the city becomes equal to a sacred seat (pīṭha).
That house and the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha) should be understood by those belonging to the lineage;
and through the scriptures, mandalas, and so forth, the supreme current of the Lord (pārameśvara-ogha) is to be worshipped.
In whatever place this extremely rare divine tradition resides,
it is indeed worshipped with divine [offerings], provided that it remains strictly secret.
If on the eighth or the fourteenth day one performs worship according to the prescribed rite,
